4.title: Abraham: The Father of All Who Believe
4.overview:
If justification is by faith and not by works of the law, Paul faces an immediate objection from Jewish readers: what about Abraham? Abraham is the father of the Jewish nation, the recipient of the covenant, the model of obedience. If he was justified by his works, then surely righteousness is earned, not given. Romans 4 is Paul's extended answer — and it is devastating in its exegetical precision and its theological reach.

The answer is simple and irrefutable: Abraham was justified by faith before he was circumcised (Genesis 15:6 precedes Genesis 17), and before the law was given (by four centuries). The very man whom Judaism claimed as the exemplar of covenant faithfulness is in fact the exemplar of justifying faith — and therefore the father not only of circumcised Jewish believers but of all Gentile believers as well. The gospel does not contradict the covenant with Abraham; it fulfils it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — Abraham Justified by Faith, Not Works or Circumcision
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul's argument from Abraham is both simple and lethal to the works-righteousness position. He goes directly to Genesis 15:6: "Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness." The verb "counted" (Greek: logizomai; Hebrew: chashab) is an accounting term — to reckon to someone's account. God reckoned Abraham righteous — not because Abraham had earned it but because Abraham believed. The righteousness was credited; it was not achieved.

Paul then deploys a second argument from David. Psalm 32:1–2 speaks of the blessedness of the man whose sins are not counted against him. David was not speaking of a man who earned God's favour; he was speaking of a man who received forgiveness he did not deserve. Blessed is the man whose iniquity is forgiven — not whose record is clean. The whole Old Testament agrees: righteousness before God is received, not achieved.

The third and clinching argument concerns the timing of Abraham's circumcision. The justification of Genesis 15:6 precedes the circumcision of Genesis 17 by perhaps fourteen to twenty-four years. Abraham was declared righteous while still uncircumcised — which means circumcision was a sign and seal of a righteousness already received by faith, not the means by which that righteousness was obtained. This means Abraham is the father of all who believe, circumcised or not: his pattern is faith, not ethnicity.

And at the centre of it stands a phrase so shocking that Paul can only have chosen it deliberately: God “justifies the ungodly” (v. 5). Not the sincere, not the searching, not the imperfect but well-intentioned. The ungodly — the very people the God of the Old Testament had sworn he would not acquit, since his own law had called the justifying of the wicked an abomination. Paul is not softening the difficulty; he is naming it in the strongest available terms, because the cross has already answered it (3:25–26). This is the sentence the whole chapter is arranged around, and every reader who has ever wondered whether he is too far gone should notice which category is being justified here.
verseByVerse.theology:
Imputation: The Reckoning of Righteousness

The word logizomai (count, reckon, credit, impute) appears eleven times in Romans 4. This is deliberate. The doctrine of imputation — that God credits Christ's righteousness to the believing sinner's account — is the hinge of the doctrine of justification. Luther's language of the "wonderful exchange" captures it: Christ takes our sin; we receive his righteousness. Not infused into us (as Rome taught), but credited to us — declared righteous in Christ, clothed in a righteousness that is not ours by achievement but ours by gift. Luther called this the "alien righteousness" (iustitia aliena) — foreign to us by nature, ours by grace.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul's appeal to Abraham was the ultimate trump card in Jewish theological discussion. If Abraham himself was justified by faith and not by works, the works-righteousness position has lost its founding father. Paul turns the Jewish trump card against itself. Now: Every form of religious merit-earning — "I'm basically a good person," "I attend church," "I pray every day," "I've never done anything really terrible" — collapses before Romans 4. Abraham, the father of the faithful, stood before God with nothing but faith in the promise. So must we.

verseByVerse.quote: What then shall we say was gained by Abraham, our forefather according to the flesh? For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about, but not before God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham, the father of Israel, had nothing to boast of before God: he too was justified by faith.

Abraham. The test case. Jewish tradition saw him as righteous by obedience; Paul goes back to the text.

Not before God. Before people Abraham might boast; before God, no one can.
verseByVerse.note: Jewish teachers held up Abraham as the great example of a righteous man.

verseByVerse.quote: For what does the Scripture say? "Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness." Now to the one who works, his wages are not counted as a gift but as his due.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Scripture says Abraham believed God and it was credited to him as righteousness; to a worker, wages are owed, not credited as a gift.

Genesis 15:6. Before circumcision, before the law, before Isaac.

Counted. Logizomai, credited to an account: used eleven times in the chapter.

Wages and gift. Two economies: earning and receiving. Salvation belongs to the second.
verseByVerse.note: “Counted” is a bookkeeping word: credited to his account.

parallels.desc: he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness

verseByVerse.quote: And to the one who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness,
verseByVerse.commentary:
God justifies the ungodly, not the godly, and the one who stops working and trusts him has faith counted as righteousness.

Does not work. Not idleness, but not working for acceptance.

Justifies the ungodly. A shocking phrase: God declares guilty people righteous, because Christ bore their sin (3:25–26).

Where Christians differ: what is counted? Some read “faith counted as righteousness” as if faith itself were the righteousness. Reformed theology holds that faith is the instrument that receives Christ’s righteousness, which is imputed to the believer (5:19; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Philippians 3:9). Verdict: the imputed righteousness of Christ, received by faith.

For worship. If you feel ungodly, good: God justifies the ungodly. Trust him.

parallels.desc: I will not acquit the wicked

verseByVerse.quote: just as David also speaks of the blessing of the one to whom God counts righteousness apart from works: "Blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven, and whose sins are covered;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
David too speaks of the blessedness of those whom God counts righteous apart from works, whose sins are forgiven and covered.

Psalm 32:1–2. Written by an adulterer and murderer.

Covered. Hidden from God’s judicial sight.

parallels.desc: blessed is the one whose transgression is forgiven

verseByVerse.quote: "blessed is the man against whom the Lord will not count his sin."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed is the person whose sin the Lord will not count against him.

Not counted. The other side of imputation: our sin not counted to us, because it was counted to Christ.

On a Tuesday. When conscience accuses you of a confessed sin, answer with this verse.

parallels.desc: blessed is the man against whom the LORD counts no iniquity

verseByVerse.quote: Is this blessing then only for the circumcised, or also for the uncircumcised? For we say that faith was counted to Abraham as righteousness. How then was it counted to him? Was it before or after he had been circumcised? It was not after, but before he was circumcised.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham was counted righteous before he was circumcised, so the blessing is for Gentiles too.

Before circumcision. Genesis 15:6 came at least fourteen years before Genesis 17.
verseByVerse.note: Abraham was declared righteous in Genesis 15 and circumcised in Genesis 17, some years later.

verseByVerse.quote: He received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith while he was still uncircumcised. The purpose was to make him the father of all who believe without being circumcised, so that righteousness would be counted to them as well, and to make him the father of the circumcised who are not merely circumcised but who also walk in the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham had before he was circumcised.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Circumcision was a sign and seal of the righteousness Abraham already had by faith, making him father of all who believe, circumcised or not.

Sign and seal. Circumcision confirmed what faith had already received.

Where Christians differ: signs and seals. Paedobaptists argue that as circumcision was given to infants as a covenant sign and seal, so baptism should be. Credobaptists answer that here circumcision sealed Abraham’s own prior faith, and the new covenant sign belongs to those who believe. Verdict: the app’s credobaptist view, held charitably: the sign follows faith, as it did for Abraham; paedobaptist brothers and sisters read the covenant differently in good faith.

Father of all who believe. Gentile and Jew.
verseByVerse.note: A seal marked ownership and confirmed that something was genuine.

parallels.desc: the sign of the covenant

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–25 — The Promise Through Faith: Abraham's Hope Against Hope
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul argues that God’s promise that Abraham and his descendants would inherit the world never depended on keeping the law but on the righteousness that comes by faith. If it rested on law, faith would be pointless and the promise void, since the law exposes transgression and brings wrath. So the promise rests on grace through faith, and it is guaranteed to all Abraham’s offspring, Jews and Gentiles who share his faith, for he is the father of many nations. Abraham trusted the God who gives life to the dead and creates out of nothing. Though he was about a hundred and Sarah was barren, he kept hoping when there was no human ground for hope, grew strong in faith, gave God glory and was fully convinced God would do what he had promised. That is why it was counted to him as righteousness, and Scripture records it for our sake too: righteousness will be counted to us who trust the God who raised Jesus, who was handed over for our sins and raised for our justification.
verseByVerse.theology:
Faith and the Resurrection

Romans 4:24–25 ties justification directly to the resurrection of Jesus. Christ was raised "for our justification" — His resurrection is not merely the proof of his deity but the declaration that his atoning work was accepted by the Father. The resurrection is the Father's public vindication of the Son's sacrifice. This means that Christian faith is not merely belief in the ethical teachings of Jesus or even in his death; it is faith in the God who raised him from the dead. Easter is not the happy ending of a sad story; it is the announcement that the story of sin and death and wrath has been definitively answered.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The promise to Abraham that he would be "heir of the world" (v. 13) goes beyond what Genesis explicitly states but draws on the expansive reading of the Abrahamic covenant in Jewish tradition. Paul is claiming that the full scope of that promise — a redeemed humanity, a renewed creation — is fulfilled in Christ and received by faith. The Jewish hope for the world is the Christian gospel. Now: Abraham's "hope against hope" (v. 18) is the model for Christian faith in every situation where the circumstances shout impossibility. The God who gave life to Abraham's dead body and Sarah's dead womb is the same God who raises the dead today — physically at the last day, spiritually in every conversion. No situation is beyond him.

verseByVerse.quote: For the promise to Abraham and his offspring that he would be heir of the world did not come through the law but through the righteousness of faith. For if it is the adherents of the law who are to be the heirs, faith is null and the promise is void.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The promise that Abraham’s family would inherit the world came through the righteousness of faith, not the law; otherwise faith is pointless.

Heir of the world. The promise of the land expanded to the whole earth (Matthew 5:5).

Void. If inheritance depends on law-keeping, no one inherits.

verseByVerse.quote: For the law brings wrath, but where there is no law there is no transgression. That is why it depends on faith, in order that the promise may rest on grace and be guaranteed to all his offspring — not only to the adherent of the law but also to the one who shares the faith of Abraham, who is the father of us all,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law brings wrath by exposing transgression, so the promise rests on faith and grace, guaranteed to all Abraham’s children.

The law brings wrath. It defines sin and condemns it.

Guaranteed. Because it rests on grace, not on our performance.

verseByVerse.quote: as it is written, "I have made you the father of many nations" — in the presence of the God in whom he believed, who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist. In hope he believed against hope, that he should become the father of many nations, as he had been told, "So shall your offspring be."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham believed the God who gives life to the dead and calls into being things that do not exist.

Father of many nations. Genesis 17:5: fulfilled in the worldwide church.

Gives life to the dead. Abraham’s faith was resurrection faith (Hebrews 11:19).

Calls into existence. The Creator speaks and it is.

Hoped against hope. Hope in God beyond all human hope.

parallels.desc: the father of a multitude of nations
so shall your offspring be

verseByVerse.quote: He did not weaken in faith when he considered his own body, which was as good as dead (since he was about a hundred years old), or when he considered the barrenness of Sarah's womb. No unbelief made him waver concerning the promise of God, but he grew strong in his faith as he gave glory to God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham faced the facts of his own and Sarah’s barrenness, yet did not waver, but grew strong in faith, giving glory to God.

Considered his body. Faith is not denying facts but trusting God above them.

Did not waver. Despite Genesis 16 and 17:17: Paul sees his faith as a whole.

Gave glory to God. Faith honours God by taking him at his word.

verseByVerse.quote: fully convinced that God was able to do what he had promised.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham was fully convinced that God could do what he had promised.

Fully convinced. The essence of faith: confidence in God’s power and faithfulness.

On a Tuesday. Which promise of God do you most need to believe today?

parallels.desc: is anything too hard for the LORD?

verseByVerse.quote: That is why his faith “was counted to him as righteousness.” But the words “it was counted to him” were not written for his sake alone, but for ours also. — Romans 4:22–24a
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham’s faith was counted as righteousness, and Scripture recorded this not only for his sake but for ours.

For our sake. Old Testament stories are written for us (15:4; 1 Corinthians 10:11).

verseByVerse.quote: It will be counted to us who believe in him who raised from the dead Jesus our Lord, who was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification. — Romans 4:24b–25
verseByVerse.commentary:
Righteousness will be credited to us who believe in the God who raised Jesus, who was handed over for our sins and raised for our justification.

Delivered up for our trespasses. Isaiah 53:5, 12: his death dealt with our sins.

Raised for our justification. The resurrection is God’s verdict that the sacrifice was accepted, and the risen Christ lives to apply it.

For worship. The cross and the empty tomb together are your acquittal.

5.title: Peace, Joy, and the Two Adams
5.overview:
Romans 5 is the hinge of the letter. Behind us lie three chapters of diagnosis and one chapter of remedy; ahead lie three chapters of Christian experience and life. Chapter 5 stands at the turning point, summarising the achievements of justification (vv. 1–11) before setting those achievements within the grandest possible framework: the story of two men, Adam and Christ, whose actions determined the destiny of all humanity (vv. 12–21).

The opening "therefore" connects everything that follows to everything Paul has argued. Because we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God. We have access to grace. We stand in hope. We can even boast in our sufferings. And the love of God — poured out in our hearts by the Holy Spirit — is the guarantee that the hope will not put us to shame. The person justified by faith does not merely have a changed legal status; she has entered a new world, a new relationship, a new story whose ending is already written.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Peace, Access, Hope, and the Love of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ." This sentence is the great sigh of relief at the centre of the letter. Three chapters of accumulated guilt — the Gentile without excuse, the moralist self-condemned, the universal verdict of Scripture, the silencing of every mouth — and now: peace. Not merely the absence of war, but the shalom of a relationship fully restored. The hostility between the holy God and the sinful creature has been dealt with at the cross, and the one who has received the verdict of justification stands in the peace of a fully settled relationship with God.

Paul adds to peace the gift of access (v. 2) — "through him we have also obtained access by faith into this grace in which we stand." Access was a technical term for the privilege of being brought into the presence of a king. The justified sinner has not merely been acquitted; she has been given permanent, unimpeded access to the throne of God. She does not approach on the basis of her spiritual performance on any given day; she stands in grace — a position of favour that does not fluctuate with her feelings or her faithfulness.

The boasting in sufferings (vv. 3–5) is one of the most counter-intuitive things Paul writes. He does not merely say we can endure suffering; he says we rejoice in it — because suffering produces endurance, endurance produces character, character produces hope, and hope does not put us to shame because the love of God has been poured into our hearts by the Holy Spirit. The chain is unbreakable. And the certainty of hope rests not on our own resilience but on the Spirit-given experience of being loved by God.

And then Paul does something the rest of the section depends on: he proves that love rather than asserting it. Verses 6 to 8 fix the timing of the cross — Christ died for us while we were still weak, still ungodly, still sinners. Not after we improved, and not in anticipation of our improving. He sets it against the best human parallel he can find and shows that there is none: one might barely die for a good man, but God shows his love in that while we were still sinners Christ died for us (v. 8). From there the argument runs from the harder thing to the easier. If God did that for enemies, the lesser question of whether he will finish the work in friends answers itself — since we have now been justified by his blood, much more shall we be saved from wrath through him (vv. 9–10). The section ends where it must: not with the benefits but with the giver. We rejoice, finally, not in peace or access or hope, but in God himself, through whom we have now received reconciliation (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology:
Peace with God and the Assurance of Faith

Romans 5:1 is a foundation stone of the Reformed doctrine of assurance. The believer has peace with God — not the peace she feels on spiritually good days, but the objective peace established by the accomplished work of Christ received by faith. The Reformation recovered this against the Roman Catholic teaching that assurance is presumption: on the contrary, to doubt one's justification when God has spoken the verdict is to call God's word into question. As Calvin taught, faith without assurance is not the faith of the New Testament. The peace of Romans 5:1 is not a feeling; it is a fact grounded in the finished work of Christ.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The first-century world had no shortage of philosophical frameworks for enduring suffering — Stoic resignation, Epicurean avoidance, Platonic transcendence. None of them grounded suffering in the love of a personal God or gave it redemptive purpose. Paul's rejoicing in suffering (vv. 3–5) was genuinely new: suffering has a trajectory, and that trajectory ends in hope that is guaranteed by the Spirit. Now: In an age that treats suffering as the enemy of the good life, to be medicated, minimised, or avoided at all costs, Romans 5:3–5 offers a radically different framework. Suffering is not the enemy of Christian hope; it is one of its primary instruments. The Christian who suffers well — who endures, who builds character, who hopes — is not an anomaly but a disciple.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ. Through him we have also obtained access by faith into this grace in which we stand... — Romans 5:1–2
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because we have been justified by faith, “we have peace with God” — the war between the holy God and the sinner is over. Through Christ we also have “access” into the grace in which we now stand, and we “rejoice in hope of the glory of God.” Peace behind us, firm ground beneath us, glory ahead.

“Therefore.” This word carries four chapters. From 1:18 to 4:25 Paul argued the case: the charge, the evidence, every mouth stopped, the verdict, and the provision by which the guilty are declared righteous. Chapters 5–8 describe what it is like to live inside that verdict. Paul is no longer arguing that you can be justified. He is telling you what is true of you because you are.

The footnote. Some manuscripts read “let us have peace.” In Greek the difference is one vowel, pronounced the same in Paul’s day, so a scribe taking dictation could easily write either. Nearly all translations rightly read “we have”: Paul is drawing a conclusion, not giving an exhortation. Even the other reading would mean “enjoy the peace you have,” never “try to obtain it.”

Peace with God, not just peace about God. This is not a calm feeling but the objective end of hostility. It ran both ways, differently. On our side, real enmity: “hostile in mind, doing evil deeds” (Colossians 1:21). On God’s side, not temper but settled judicial opposition — his wrath (1:18). Christ made peace “by the blood of his cross” (Colossians 1:20). That is why it is peace and not a ceasefire. A ceasefire can be revoked on an afternoon’s notice. A treaty settles the terms, and this one was signed in blood by the offended party.

Access. Nobody simply walked in to see a king; you were brought in by someone with the standing to do it. The word holds both the privilege and the fact that it is not yours. And the tense is completed: the introduction has been made. You do not reapply each morning to see whether today you may approach.

A place to stand. “This grace in which we stand” — grace is pictured as a floor, beneath you and bearing your weight. Nobody spends the day generating the floor. You do not have to re-establish your position with God every morning, any more than re-lay the floorboards before crossing the room.

The glory restored. “Hope of the glory of God” answers 3:23 word for word: “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” The phrase that stated our ruin now describes our future. Not only forgiveness for falling short of glory, but the glory itself, restored to the creature made for it.

A test. Which describes your ordinary week: “I am trying to get right with God,” or “I am right with God”? Sincere Christians say both; only the second is true. If your spiritual life hums with anxious effort, a project not yet finished, you are living in chapters 1–4 with a doctrine from chapter 5. Hear Paul’s first word: therefore. The case is closed. Your job is not to secure the peace but to live in it — start by praying today as someone already welcome.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “let us have peace.”

parallels.desc: the effect of righteousness will be peace

verseByVerse.quote: Not only that, but we rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope,
verseByVerse.commentary:
We also rejoice in our sufferings, because suffering produces endurance, endurance produces proven character, and character produces hope. Paul does not call suffering good. He says that, held by God, it does a work in us that ends in hope.

What Paul does not say. He does not say suffering is good, or should be sought, or that a Christian should feel positive about a diagnosis. Scripture never calls evil good; Jesus wept at a grave he was about to empty. And he does not say rejoice because of suffering. The word is in: joy found inside a situation that stays bad, because of something else that is true about it.

Not automatic. Paul is not promising that every sufferer gets stronger. Anyone who has watched a man come out of a hard decade smaller and harder knows better. Suffering produces bitterness as often as endurance. The difference is not how much it hurts but what the sufferer is holding while it lasts — which is why the paragraph ends with God’s love poured into the heart by the Spirit (v. 5).

Endurance. Not passive resignation. The word means “remaining under” — staying beneath a weight instead of crawling out. There is no way to develop it in the abstract; nobody became patient in a comfortable year. Several qualities we most want are made only in conditions we would never choose.

Character. A metalworker’s word: metal that has passed the test and is proved — the opposite of the failed mind of 1:28. A test does not create the quality; it demonstrates it, including to the man himself. Most of us don’t know what we believe until something tries to take it away. That is why a Christian who has been through something often has a settledness no reading produces. He is not cleverer. He has been tested and holds the certificate.

Hope comes last. We would expect hope to produce endurance. Paul says hope is the result. It makes sense once you have lived it. A tested believer has evidence: he was where he was sure he could not go on, he went on, and looking back he sees he was carried. Hope is not optimism about the future. It is a conclusion drawn from the past.

A test. Write down the three hardest things you have been through as a Christian. Beside each, write what you feared would happen — losing your faith, not coping, never being happy again. Then write what actually happened. Most people find the feared thing did not happen, and they cannot now reconstruct how they got through. That is the point: you were carried, and you have already forgotten. Keep the list. It is the raw material of hope.

For someone in it now. If you are suffering and can find no joy in it at all, you have not failed this passage. Paul describes a trajectory, not a mood on demand. Endurance mostly looks like simply not leaving. If today you have not walked away from God — if you are still, however raggedly, holding on — the first link is being forged in you now, and it won’t feel like anything while it happens.

verseByVerse.quote: and hope does not put us to shame, because God's love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This hope “does not put us to shame” — it will not turn out to be misplaced — “because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.” What makes hope safe is not our strength but what God has already done inside us.

Not put to shame. In the Old Testament, being put to shame is what happens to someone whose confidence proves misplaced — who trusted an ally who never came, or a god who could not answer. Every hope is a bet, and most eventually expose the person who made them. This one will not — not because we hope sincerely, but because of who holds the other end.

Outside the chain. Paul might have said hope is safe because you have come through before. Instead he points to something given: God’s love poured into our hearts. The chain of vv. 3–4 is real, but it is not what makes hope safe.

His love for us. This is not our love for God welling up, but his love for us poured in — the sense of being loved by God arriving as experience, not just inference. And “poured” is extravagant: the verb used of the Spirit poured out at Pentecost and of Christ’s blood “poured out” for many. Not a careful dose. And it “has been poured” — done, with lasting results. The reservoir was filled before today and is not drained by a bad week.

“I’ve never felt that.” Many faithful Christians conclude this has not happened to them. Three things. First, it is not one particular experience. It shows in the man surprised to find he wants to pray; in the conviction, on an ordinary Tuesday, that you are not facing your life alone; in tears at a hymn line sung a hundred times; in the fact that you mind about your sin at all. None announces itself as God’s love poured out, and all of them are. Second, temperament and health are real. Some feel everything strongly, some very little, and depression, exhaustion or grief can flatten feeling. Scripture never makes intensity of feeling the measure of anything, and a man whose illness has taken his feelings has not lost the Spirit given to him. Third, the evidence is not only inward. Do you call God Father and mean it? That is the Spirit (8:15). Do you want holiness while failing at it? Is Christ more precious to you than he was at nineteen? Those are not achievements. They are symptoms.

A test. Don’t ask whether you feel loved. Ask when you last noticed something that would be inexplicable if God were not real and did not care — not a miracle, but comfort arriving at the right moment, a peace you could not account for, a verse that landed as though addressed to you. Most Christians have a small collection and have never counted them because each seems too slight. Count them this week. That is the pouring, and it has gone on longer than you thought.

Why it holds. A chain from suffering to hope would be cruel if it ran on human strength, because those who most need it have least. It doesn’t. Beneath it is love poured in by a Spirit given, not earned — which is why the person at the bottom can still be told his hope will not let him down.

parallels.desc: in you they trusted and were not put to shame

verseByVerse.quote: For while we were still weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly. For one will scarcely die for a righteous person — though perhaps for a good person one would dare even to die —
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ died for us “while we were still weak” — helpless to save ourselves — “at the right time,” and “for the ungodly.” Paul compares this with the best of human love: someone might perhaps die for a good person. God’s love is not a bigger amount of that love. It is a different kind.

Proof, not feeling. Verse 5 spoke of love felt inside. A sceptic, or a Christian on a bad night, might say inward feelings prove nothing. So Paul goes outside us: the proof is a death, in public, at a datable moment, and its force lies in when it happened.

What we were at the time. Paul repeats the timing: “still weak,” “ungodly,” and in v. 8 “still sinners.” Each is a state we were in at that hour. If Christ had died for the repentant, the cross would prove God responds to repentance. If for the promising, that he has an eye for potential. He died for the helpless, opposed and guilty — which proves something about God and nothing about us. And “weak” should not be softened. It means without strength, like an invalid who cannot get himself to the water. Not someone needing help, but someone who could not contribute to his own rescue.

The search in v. 7. This is not padding. Paul goes looking for the highest human love he can find, to measure God’s against it, and qualifies himself twice. For a righteous person — upright, admirable — one will scarcely die. Perhaps for a good person — warm and generous, someone you are fond of — someone might dare. Even that is hedged with “perhaps” and “dare.”

Our ceiling. His estimate is right. People do die for others — a mother for her child, a soldier for his comrade, occasionally a stranger in a river. But there is always something in the other person that draws it out. Our love responds to worth or belonging. Nobody has laid down his life for someone he found contemptible, who had wronged him, and who would not be grateful.

A different kind of love. Ours is drawn out; God’s originates. Ours responds to something; his creates the something it will later delight in. So “What does God see in me?” has no answer — not because the answer is disappointing, but because the question assumes the wrong mechanism. He was not looking for something to see.

A test. When you try to believe God loves you, notice what you reach for as the reason. Most of us produce something, even unspoken: I’ve been trying, I mean well, I’m not as bad as I might be, at least I care. Set it beside verse 6: Christ died for the weak, the ungodly, sinners — three categories without a single reason in them. Whatever you were holding did not secure this and cannot maintain it. Put it down.

The comfort. If God’s love were like ours, something in you would have drawn it out, and something in you could exhaust it. A love with a reason can lose its reason. A love shown at a specific hour to people who were then helpless and hostile has nothing in you to lose.

parallels.desc: when the fullness of time had come

verseByVerse.quote: but God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” God proves his love not with words but with an event — his Son’s death — and at the worst possible moment: not after we cleaned up or made the first move, but while we were still in the act.

A standing exhibit. “Shows” means put on display, and it is present tense: God goes on showing his love this way. The cross is not a historical fact from which we infer God was once well disposed. It is still held up, still the answer when someone is at the bottom of himself.

Why a death. God has shown kindness in many ways; the sun rises on evil and good alike. But to prove he loved people who hated him, nothing less than his Son’s death would do. That tells you the size of the claim.

His own love, his own cost. The Greek says God shows his own love, and later Paul names the cost: “He who did not spare his own Son” (8:32). The cost fell inside God himself. Anybody can be generous with someone else’s son.

Is it just to punish the innocent? People ask honestly: how can it be loving for God to punish an innocent man instead of the guilty? But this is no third party conscripted. The Judge did not find a substitute; he became one. The one owed the debt paid it, in his Son, by agreement within the Godhead. Nobody was volunteered. That is the only arrangement in which mercy costs the one who shows it.

“Still.” Not “when we were sinners,” as if describing a former category, but still — mid-course, in the act. The cross was aimed at your life at its worst. It was not aimed at the person you have since become, and it is not waiting for the person you hope to be.

Two moments to reach for it. First, when you have failed badly and cannot bring yourself to pray. The accusation always says: not like this, not after this. Answer: the love was shown when I was doing exactly this, and worse, with no intention of stopping. This week’s failure is not news to God; it was in the file when the price was set. Second, for the respectable: believers who have never doubted God’s love and quietly think it reasonable — they go to church, give, pray, mean well. That confidence rests on an assessment, and assessments can be revised. Verse 8 removes it, which feels like loss and is the only route to a peace that does not depend on how the year went.

A test. Say aloud: “God loved me at my worst hour; nothing I have done since has improved his opinion; nothing I do next can lower it.” Which clause do you want to argue with? Most people trip on the second. We accept that our sins don’t disqualify us more easily than that our progress doesn’t impress him. That resistance shows where you are still living on your reputation.

The only demonstration. God does not point to a sunset or a harvest. He points to one afternoon, one man, one hill outside Jerusalem, and a death reserved for slaves and rebels, and says: that is what I am like. He has never seen the need to offer a second proof.

verseByVerse.quote: Since, therefore, we have now been justified by his blood, much more shall we be saved by him from the wrath of God. For if while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son, much more, now that we are reconciled, shall we be saved by his life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If God justified us by Christ’s blood, “much more” will he save us from wrath. If he reconciled us when we were his enemies, by his Son’s death, “much more” will he save us, now that we are reconciled, “by his life.” God has already done the hard part. Finishing it is the easy part.

From the greater to the lesser. This was a standard way of reasoning: what a big thing already done implies about something smaller. If a man has given you his house, he will not quibble about the key.

We have it backwards. We instinctively assume the hard part is still ahead: the cross is settled, but will I make it — will faith hold, will the next twenty years go well enough, will I be acceptable at the end? Paul says we have it inverted. The hard part was reconciling enemies, and that is done. What remains is God finishing his work in people who are now his friends. It is unthinkable that he would fail at the easy end of his own work.

Enemies. Paul has been escalating: weak, ungodly, sinners, and now enemies — the least flattering. God did not just find us lost and pity us. He found us in arms against him and made peace at his own expense. “Reconciled” is the word for parties once at odds and no longer.

His death and his life. We were reconciled by his death; we shall be saved by his life. Your future does not rest on a transaction finished by a dead man but on a living one who is not idle: “he always lives to make intercession” for those who come to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). Your security does not depend on your grip on Christ. It depends on a man alive right now whose present occupation is you.

“I might not last.” Nearly every serious Christian carries this fear: not that God is unwilling, but that I am unreliable, I have decades to go, and I know myself. If finishing depended on you, the fear would be reasonable. This argument takes it out of your hands. The one who did the hard part when you were his enemy is doing the rest now that you are his child.

A guard. This is no invitation to drift. Paul will spend chapters 6 and 12–15 on what is required. He is saying where the guarantee lies. You are still called to endure, and you can, because the outcome does not hang on the quality of your enduring. A man rowing a boat that is also under tow rows better, not worse.

A test. Ask what you think would have to happen for you to end up lost. If an answer comes quickly — a sin serious enough, coldness long enough, a falling away far enough — notice what it assumes: that the deciding factor at the end will be something about you. Set it beside verse 10. God did the impossible while you were his enemy. Whatever you imagined is a smaller obstacle than the one he has already cleared. Twice Paul says “much more.” That is not encouragement; it is arithmetic.

verseByVerse.quote: More than that, we also rejoice in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
More than that, “we also rejoice in God” himself, through Christ, through whom we have “received reconciliation.” The best gift of the gospel is not on the list of gifts. It is God.

Three rejoicings. We rejoice in hope of glory (v. 2) — joy about the future. We rejoice in sufferings (v. 3) — joy in the present, even at its worst. Now we rejoice in God. The first two are joy in what God gives. The third is joy in God himself, and Paul marks the step with “more than that,” as though everything before was preliminary.

Loving the gifts. You can be delighted with the benefits of Christianity and have little appetite for God. A man can be glad of forgiveness, relieved about judgment, grateful for peace, attached to his church, comforted in trouble — and all of it can be love of the gifts. That is not hypocrisy; the gifts are magnificent and meant to be enjoyed. But it can be tested.

A test. Suppose God gave you everything you have ever asked him for — health, the child restored, the marriage healed, fruitful work, the fear lifted — and then was himself absent. No sense of him, no dealings with him. Would that be enough? If yes, what you have wanted is Christianity’s results. If the honest answer is no — something essential would be missing from a world where everything went well and God was not there — you have found what verse 11 is about. That preference cannot be manufactured. Nobody talks himself into wanting God more than his gifts. If you are unsure, ask God for it, and spend some of your prayer this week simply enjoying him rather than asking.

Received. Not achieved, not negotiated. Reconciliation is not a settlement where two aggrieved parties each move some way. One party was wholly in the wrong and did not want terms; the other made peace at his own cost and handed it to the offender as a gift. There was nothing to do but take delivery.

Now. “We have now been justified” (v. 9), “now that we are reconciled” (v. 10), “we have now received” (v. 11) — three times in three verses. Whatever remains unfinished in the Christian life, and chapters 6–8 are honest about how much, the relationship is not among it. It was settled while you were an enemy and delivered before you understood it.

The road and the Giver. Paul has listed what the justified possess: peace, access, a place to stand, hope, endurance, character, love poured in, rescue from wrath, reconciliation. Then he sets the inventory aside to say the best of it is not on the list. The gifts were always the road to the Giver.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–21 — Death in Adam, Life in Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The argument that begins in v. 12 is the most theologically ambitious in the entire letter. Paul steps back from the individual experience of justification and places it within a cosmic, historical framework: the story of two men, Adam and Christ, whose representative actions determined the status and destiny of everyone who belongs to them. This is the doctrine of federal headship — the two-Adam theology that is foundational to the Reformed understanding of both sin and salvation.

The parallel is deliberate and asymmetrical. Adam sinned; condemnation and death spread to all. Christ obeyed; righteousness and life are given to all who are in him. But the parallel is asymmetrical because grace exceeds sin in every dimension: "the free gift is not like the trespass" (v. 15). The trespass brought condemnation; the gift brings justification for many trespasses. Adam's one sin brought death; Christ's one act of righteousness brings the free gift of life. Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more (v. 20). The gospel is not simply the repair of the damage done by Adam; it is a new creation that surpasses Eden.

The phrase "as sin reigned in death, grace also might reign through righteousness leading to eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord" (v. 21) is the conclusion to which the whole argument has been driving. Sin had a reign — a dominion, a kingdom of death. Grace now has a counter-reign — a dominion of life and righteousness. The believer has been transferred from one kingdom to the other. Adam is no longer her representative head; Christ is. She bears the condemnation of neither Adam's sin (fully atoned) nor her own (fully forgiven). She stands under the reign of grace, heading toward the eternal life that is the gift of her new federal head.
verseByVerse.theology:
Federal Headship: The Solidarity of Adam and Christ

Romans 5:12–21 is the biblical foundation of the Reformed doctrine of original sin and the imputation of Adam's guilt. Paul teaches that death spread to all because all sinned in Adam — not merely by imitating his example, but by being represented by him. Adam was the covenantal head of humanity; his act was our act in the only sense that matters covenantally. This is why all die, even infants who have not sinned in the way Adam sinned (v. 14). The parallel with Christ is the point: just as we were condemned in Adam by imputation, we are justified in Christ by imputation. The same covenantal logic that makes us sinners in Adam makes us righteous in Christ. You cannot reject one side of the parallel without undermining the other.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Adam-Christ typology was deeply embedded in Jewish theology of Paul's day — the figure of Adam as the representative of humanity was well established. Paul takes this shared theological framework and uses it to explain both the universality of sin and the universality of the gospel's offer: as Adam's headship was universal (all who are human bear his guilt), so Christ's headship is available to all (all who are in him receive his righteousness). Now: The doctrine of original sin is the one Christian teaching that can be empirically verified by reading any newspaper. Every generation produces fresh evidence that something has gone profoundly wrong with the human race at its root. Romans 5:12–21 names it: Adam. And then offers the only remedy: Christ. The diagnosis and the cure are inseparable.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, just as sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men because all sinned — for sin indeed was in the world before the law was given, but sin is not counted where there is no law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul begins his comparison of Adam and Christ. Through one man, Adam, sin entered the world, and death came through sin, and so death spread to everyone “because all sinned.” Sin was in the world even before Moses’ law. Adam’s act and our condition are bound together — and that is the pattern by which Christ will save.

Was Adam a real man? Some Christians read Adam as a symbol of every person, or as a figure in a story that need not be history, often to fit evolutionary accounts of human origins. But Paul’s argument depends on a real Adam. He sets one man’s act against another’s: one trespass against one act of righteousness (v. 18). If the first man and his disobedience are only a picture, the parallel breaks, and so does the comfort, because Christ’s obedience was a real act in history. Paul treats Adam the same way elsewhere (1 Cor 15:22; 1 Tim 2:13–14), and Luke traces Jesus’ genealogy back to him (Luke 3:38).

What death spread? More than the grave. God warned Adam that in the day he ate he would die (Gen 2:17). He died at once in his relationship with God, and in his body years later. So death here includes physical death, the spiritual death of being cut off from God (Eph 2:1), and, apart from Christ, the eternal death that is the wages of sin (6:23). That is why the answer at the end of the chapter is not only resurrection but eternal life (v. 21).

“Because all sinned” — how? Christians have answered three ways. (1) Pelagius: each person dies for his own sins; Adam only set a bad example, and his guilt is not counted to anyone else. (2) Augustine, reading the Latin “in whom all sinned”: all humanity sinned in Adam. Later Reformed theology (the Westminster divines, Owen) framed this as federal headship: Adam stood as our covenant representative, and his sin is counted to his descendants as Christ’s obedience is counted to believers. (3) Natural or “seminal” headship: we sinned in Adam because all human nature was present in him. The Greek is better rendered “because,” but Paul’s own explanation in v. 19 settles the substance: “by the one man’s disobedience the many were made sinners.” Our standing as sinners rests on Adam’s act, not only on our own. Federal headship best explains this and Paul’s Adam–Christ symmetry. And the symmetry is the comfort: if it is unjust to be condemned for another man’s act, you must also give up the only ground on which you can be saved — another Man’s righteousness counted to you.

An unfinished sentence. Paul starts “just as…” and does not finish until v. 18. Verses 13–17 are a parenthesis clearing obstacles. If you have lost the thread here, the fault is not yours; it really is interrupted.

Death as the evidence. Paul’s argument runs on a fact anyone can check: death reaches everyone — every civilisation, temperament, degree of virtue, every infant. And between Adam and Moses, with no written law to charge anyone under, people still died (v. 13). Their deaths must trace back to something other than offences formally charged. That is the point.

“I never voted for Adam.” That is how the objection is actually felt. Two answers. First, representation is the fabric of ordinary life. A nation goes to war on a government’s decision and everyone bears the consequences. Children inherit language, nationality, debts and reputation. We accept inherited goods readily and object loudly to inherited liability. Second, nobody can claim he would have done otherwise. Every one of us has stood where Adam stood — God’s word on one side, our preference on the other — and chosen as he did, repeatedly, knowingly. Adam’s act is the first instance of a choice we have each ratified.

A test. Ask what you believe death is. Most people say it is natural — part of the cycle. Then watch them at a graveside. Nobody stands at a funeral thinking “this is how it should be.” We grieve as though something has been done wrong, a person taken. That instinct is not sentimentality. Scripture agrees with it: death is “the last enemy to be destroyed” (1 Corinthians 15:26). Let your grief be honest, and let it point you to the One who defeats that enemy.

Standing alone. Insist on standing alone, judged only on your own record, and you would be safe from Adam — and alone with your own file, which Romans 1–3 has described. The principle you would abolish to escape Adam is the one by which another’s righteousness is credited to you. Both men acted before you were consulted. Only one acted on your behalf on purpose.
verseByVerse.note: “One man” is Adam.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those whose sinning was not like the transgression of Adam, who was a type of the one who was to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Death “reigned” from Adam to Moses, even over people who had not broken an explicit command as Adam had. So something more than personal lawbreaking was at work: a shared ruin. And Adam was “a type of the one who was to come” — a pattern of Christ, whose union with his people works the opposite way, bringing life.

Death reigned. Paul uses the word for a king’s rule, and uses it four more times before the chapter ends. Death is not just a biological full stop but a power with territory and subjects. It does not only take you at the end; it governs a whole life before it arrives — setting a limit on every plan, giving every love its ache, standing behind much of what people do to secure themselves.

The proof. Adam broke an explicit command with an explicit penalty. Between Adam and Moses there was no such published command — and people died anyway. Their deaths cannot be explained by offences charged under a code that did not exist.

What about infants? This question is usually asked by someone with a name and a date in mind, and it deserves an honest answer. The verse does say they die: the solidarity of ruin is why infants are mortal at all. But it does not say they are condemned. Paul’s subject is death’s reign, not the final destiny of individuals, and reading this paragraph as a roll of the lost has caused great grief. Scripture gives real hope, though not a formula. When David’s child died, he stopped fasting, washed, worshipped and said, “I shall go to him, but he will not return to me” (2 Samuel 12:23) — expectation, not resignation. Jesus took children in his arms and said, “to such belongs the kingdom of God” (Mark 10:14). “Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?” (Genesis 18:25). God judges by the light given (2:12), and where there was no capacity to receive any, the case is wholly in the hands of the One who himself became an infant. Reformed writers have generally held that such children are saved — not because they are innocent, which this chapter denies, but by sovereign mercy through the same Christ. Scripture does not state this in so many words, and we should not pretend it does. It is a hope resting on God’s character, the only place a hope was ever safe.

If you have a grave in mind. Hear both halves. Yes, this passage explains why that death happened: it is the reign of an enemy, and your grief is not a failure of faith but an accurate response to an intruder. And no, this passage is not a verdict on that child. The One who will decide is the One who wept at a friend’s tomb while fully intending to empty it.

A type of Christ. Everything said of Adam here is catastrophe, and yet Paul calls him a pattern of Christ — not in his sin, but in the shape of his significance: one man, one act, a whole race affected. God did not respond to the disaster by abolishing the mechanism that produced it. He kept it and sent a second Man to stand at its head. What you might have complained about in Eden is what makes your salvation possible.
verseByVerse.note: A “type” is a pattern or foreshadowing: Adam, head of the old humanity, foreshadows Christ, head of the new.

parallels.desc: the first man Adam, the last Adam

verseByVerse.quote: But the free gift is not like the trespass. For if many died through one man's trespass, much more have the grace of God and the free gift by the grace of that one man Jesus Christ abounded for many. And the free gift is not like the result of that one man's sin. For the judgment following one trespass brought condemnation, but the free gift following many trespasses brought justification.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Twice Paul says the gift is “not like” the trespass. Adam’s one sin brought condemnation; Christ’s gift came after “many trespasses” and brought justification. The two sides are not the same size. Grace overflows what sin ruined.

Paul breaks his own parallel. He has built a neat symmetry — one man, one act, a race affected — and now stops twice to say it does not balance. A tidy symmetry would suggest Christ merely undoes Adam, that the gospel is a repair job returning us to where we started. Paul will not have it.

The arithmetic runs backward. Adam faced one command and broke it: one trespass, then condemnation. Christ faced the accumulated sins of all he came to save: many trespasses, then acquittal. If one sin was enough to ruin the race, you would expect many sins to be proportionately harder to deal with. It is the reverse. One was enough to condemn, and countless were not too many to forgive.

“Can he forgive this much?” Many Christians privately fear not whether God can forgive sin but whether he can forgive this much of it — the man converted at fifty who keeps counting the years, the believer returning to the same failure who suspects there must be a limit. This verse answers with arithmetic. Grace is not calibrated to the size of the debt and does not run short beyond some quantity. It was never measured against the sin. It is measured against the worth of the One who gives it.

Much more. The gift does not just equal the trespass; it “abounded” — overflowed the container. The gospel is not the restoration of Eden. Adam lost a garden; we are promised a city. Adam had innocence, fragile and lost in an afternoon; the believer has a righteousness not his own, which he therefore cannot forfeit. We end not where Adam began but further on — redeemed, not just restored.

A test. After your last serious failure, how did you talk to yourself? Did you calculate: how much ground have I lost, how long before things are normal, how many good weeks does this cost? That is Adam’s arithmetic, reasonable inside a system that runs on your record. These verses say you are not in that system. There is no ground to make up, because the ground was never yours, and no amount at which the gift runs out. Confess it, receive the forgiveness, and go on today without the penance of a bad week.

The scales were broken on purpose. If Adam and Christ balanced, the Christian life would be anxious accounting with the outcome in doubt. They don’t. God broke the scales by putting his own Son on one side.

verseByVerse.quote: For if, because of one man's trespass, death reigned through that one man, much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and the free gift of righteousness reign in life through the one man Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Through one man’s trespass death reigned. “Much more” will those who receive “the abundance of grace and the free gift of righteousness” themselves “reign in life” through Jesus Christ. Under Adam, death ruled us. In Christ, we will rule.

The parallel breaks upward. The tidy version would be: death reigned through Adam, so life will reign through Christ. Paul writes instead that those who receive will themselves reign. Under Adam we were the territory being ruled. Under Christ we are not just freed subjects; we are given a throne.

Back to what we were made for. Salvation does not return us to safe neutrality. It restores what Genesis described before anything went wrong, when the creature in God’s image was told to have dominion (Genesis 1:28). Adam was made to rule and ended a subject of death. The man in Christ was a subject of death and ends by ruling.

Now and not yet. “Will reign” is future. Anyone who looks at his life and sees little sovereignty is reading it correctly. But “those who receive” is present: receiving now, reigning later — a king in exile whose title is granted and whose coronation date he does not know.

One condition: receive. It is the only verb we perform in the sentence, and it contributes nothing. Grace is given, righteousness is a gift, the reign is conferred. Paul’s nouns make refusal absurd: not just grace but “the abundance of grace,” not just righteousness but “the free gift” of it.

A test. What do you expect to be doing a thousand years from now? Many Christians imagine something passive — rest, an endless service, pleasant weightlessness. Paul says reign, and the New Testament gives it content: authority over cities (Luke 19:17), judging angels (1 Corinthians 6:3), work that matters. A hope that is only relief will not carry you through a hard decade. Picture the real one, and let it make your present work matter.

A guard. This is not a promise that Christians command their circumstances now — that faith gives power over illness, money or other people, and a defeated-looking life means you failed to claim your authority. The verb is future. The men who wrote these letters were beaten, imprisoned and executed, and Paul will soon describe creation and Christians groaning together (8:22–23). Reigning in life is a destination, not a technique.

The throne death sat on. In Adam, death was king — a thorough ruler that takes everything and gives nothing back. In Christ you receive, and what you finally receive is the throne death was sitting on.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, as one trespass led to condemnation for all men, so one act of righteousness leads to justification and life for all men. For as by the one man's disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man's obedience the many will be made righteous. — Romans 5:18–19
verseByVerse.commentary:
As one trespass led to condemnation for all, so one act of righteousness leads to justification and life for all. By one man’s disobedience “the many were made sinners”; by one man’s obedience “the many will be made righteous.” Each representative’s act determines the standing of all who belong to him.

The sentence finished. Paul began “just as” at v. 12 and broke off. Now the “so” arrives. Everything between was parenthesis.

Does “all men” mean everyone is saved? Read alone, this is the plainest-sounding universalism in the New Testament, and people who have believed it have usually not been frivolous. But three things settle it. First, the previous verse says the gift belongs to “those who receive” it (v. 17) — an unnecessary limit if everyone receives it. Second, Paul’s next sentence swaps “all” for “the many” in both halves; he is contrasting two humanities, not counting heads. Third, the same apostle wrote of the day of wrath (2:5), vessels of wrath (9:22), and those who “will suffer the punishment of eternal destruction” (2 Thessalonians 1:9). A sentence must be read with its author.

What “all” means. Each act is complete within its own sphere. Adam’s trespass reaches every person in Adam, with no exceptions — none too remote or too late. Christ’s obedience reaches, just as completely, every person in Christ. Neither representative leaves anyone out of his own people — which is exactly what you want to know if you fear you might be an exception at the edges of the second group.

Christ’s obedience. Verse 19 says not that Christ died for our sins, though Paul believes it, but that he obeyed. So his whole life counts, not only the six hours on the cross: perfect love for God and neighbour, temptations refused in the wilderness with no one watching, ordinary years in a workshop, every commandment kept in the only human life that ever kept them all.

More than pardon. A pardon cancels a record and leaves the man with none. The New Testament describes an exchange: your record counted to him, his to you (cf. 2 Corinthians 5:21). You stand before God not only with nothing charged against you but as one who has kept the law. The Reformers spoke of Christ’s passive obedience (what he suffered) and active obedience (what he did). Both are needed, because a clean slate with no righteousness is not yet fit for God’s presence. “Made sinners” and “made righteous” describe standing before God, not first of all inner character: a real verdict assigned on the basis of a real representative. This is imputation, working the same way in both directions.

A test. Which do you actually believe about yourself: “God has forgiven me,” or “God is pleased with me in Christ, as he is pleased with his Son”? Nearly every Christian can say the first. The second can sound almost presumptuous, yet it is the plain implication of verse 19 (cf. 8:1; Ephesians 1:6). Notice which you can say without flinching. The gap is the part of this verse you have not yet believed. Pray the second sentence until it stops sounding strange.

Alike in structure, unlike in everything else. One man’s disobedience put you in a position you never chose. One man’s obedience gives you a position you could never earn. You contributed to neither — the offence of this passage, and its whole comfort.

parallels.desc: shall my servant make many to be accounted righteous

verseByVerse.quote: Now the law came in to increase the trespass, but where sin increased, grace abounded all the more, so that, as sin reigned in death, grace also might reign through righteousness leading to eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord. — Romans 5:20–21
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law “came in to increase the trespass” — to expose sin and make it plain. But “where sin increased, grace abounded all the more,” so that as sin reigned in death, grace now reigns “through righteousness leading to eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.” No depth of sin is beyond grace, and grace does not leave sin in charge.

A shocking purpose. “The law came in to increase the trespass” is a statement of purpose, not a side effect. God gave the law at Sinai, with fire and a shaking mountain, so that sin would increase. If that does not jolt you, you read it too quickly. And “came in” means came in alongside — entering a story already under way. The law is not the main plot. It arrived between Adam and Christ with a defined job.

How the law increases sin. First, by drawing the line: “where there is no law there is no transgression” (4:15), so the law turns wrongdoing into chargeable offence. Second, as chapter 7 will describe, a prohibition provokes. Tell someone not to, and something wakes in him that was asleep — the cupboard you had no interest in until you were told not to open it. The law does not create the appetite. It exposes it, and in exposing it inflames it.

Why God would do that. A vague sin is not brought for forgiveness — not because God cannot forgive it, but because nobody asks. A man with a general sense that he is not all he should be goes nowhere in particular with it. The law turns the fog into an itemised bill specific enough to bring to a Saviour. Sin had to be made visible before grace could be seen to be enough.

Grace super-abounded. Sin increased; grace did not merely increase but overflowed beyond measure — Paul adds an extra prefix to an already strong verb. Wherever sin has gone, grace has gone further.

For those who think they are the exception. The one who came to Christ late, having done damage that cannot be undone. The believer with the same failure for the fifteenth year. The person with one thing in his past never said aloud to another human being, who assumes it lies outside the ordinary terms. This verse is aimed exactly at the places where sin went deepest: grace got there and went further. If that is you, tell God that thing today by name, and then tell one trusted believer.

The guard built in. Paul knows what a certain mind will do with this: more sin, more grace — why not oblige? He answers in the next line (6:1), but the answer is already here: grace reigns “through righteousness.” It does not reign by suspending righteousness. Grace is not permission; it is a dominion, and a dominion has a character.

Two reigns. Sin reigned in death; grace reigns through righteousness to eternal life. A reign is not a mood or an influence but a government you live under. You do not negotiate with it; you are transferred from one to another. The chapter ends on a name: “through Jesus Christ our Lord.” Sin’s reign was long, and it ended in a graveyard the size of the world. The new King took his throne by dying, and spends his crown giving life away.
