6.title: Dead to Sin, Alive to God
6.overview:
Romans 6 opens with the most dangerous question the gospel generates: "What shall we say then? Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound?" If grace covers all sin, and more sin produces more grace, why not sin freely? Paul's answer — "By no means!" — is the most vehement denial in the letter. The question misunderstands both the nature of grace and the nature of the union with Christ that is the foundation of the justified life.

The answer Paul gives is not primarily ethical (you should not sin) but theological (you cannot sin in the way that question imagines, because of who you now are in Christ). Union with Christ in his death and resurrection has changed the believer's fundamental status with respect to sin. She has died to it. It no longer has jurisdiction over her. The command that follows — "So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus" — is not a technique for sin management but a theological reality to be reckoned with and lived from.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — United with Christ in Death and Resurrection
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul's answer to the antinomian question is grounded in baptism — not as a magical ritual but as the enacted sign of the believer's union with Christ in his death and resurrection. "Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?" Baptism is the visible declaration of an invisible reality: the believer has been co-crucified with Christ, co-buried with him, and co-raised with him into newness of life. These are not future aspirations; they are present realities that define who the Christian is.

The key concept is "our old self was crucified with him" (v. 6) — the person we were in Adam, defined by sin's dominion, is dead. Not sick, not weakened, not being rehabilitated — dead. Sin still exists in the believer (7:14–25 will be painfully honest about this), but sin no longer reigns. The one who is in Christ has been transferred out of sin's kingdom and into grace's kingdom. She is not a sinner desperately trying to become a saint; she is a saint who still struggles with sin. The identity has changed, even while the struggle continues.

The imperatives of vv. 11–14 flow from the indicatives of vv. 1–10. "Consider yourselves dead to sin" (v. 11) — reckon it, take it into account, live from this reality. "Let not sin therefore reign" (v. 12) — the fact that sin no longer must reign does not mean the battle is over; it means the battle is now winnable. "Present yourselves to God" (v. 13) — the person whose old self has been crucified with Christ is now free to offer herself as a living sacrifice to the God she could not truly serve before.

Two things at the edges of the section carry the argument and should not be lost. The first is that Paul grounds our security in Christ’s experience before he applies anything to ours: the death he died he died to sin once for all, and being raised from the dead he will never die again — death no longer has dominion over him (vv. 9–10). That is the anchor. Our dying and rising are real because they are participation in his, and his cannot be undone or repeated. The second is the promise the section ends on: sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace (v. 14). It is stated as a fact about the future rather than a target to aim at — and the reason given is the opposite of what any moralist would expect. Sin loses its grip not because the rules have been tightened but because the government has changed.
verseByVerse.theology:
Union with Christ: The Foundation of Sanctification

Romans 6 grounds sanctification in union with Christ, not in moral effort or spiritual discipline alone. The Reformed tradition has always insisted that justification and sanctification, though distinct, are inseparable — both are fruits of union with Christ. John Murray's landmark study Redemption Accomplished and Applied showed that union with Christ is not an add-on to the Christian life but its very foundation: every blessing of salvation flows from being in Christ. We are justified in Christ, sanctified in Christ, glorified in Christ. The call to holiness in Romans 6 is not the demand to earn what we have not yet received; it is the call to live consistently with what is already true of us in Christ.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The antinomian objection Paul addresses — "let us sin that grace may abound" — was apparently a real misreading of his gospel in his own day (v. 1 and 3:8). Some had heard his message of free grace and concluded that moral behaviour was irrelevant. Paul's reply is not to retreat into moralism but to deepen the gospel: the same grace that justifies also transforms. Grace is not a license; it is a power that liberates from the dominion of sin. Now: The same objection recurs whenever grace is preached with full biblical clarity. The person who is never accused of antinomianism by those who prefer a works-based gospel has probably not yet preached grace clearly enough. But Paul's answer stands: grace does not produce moral indifference; it produces the only genuine moral transformation available — the transformation of a person who has died and risen with Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: What shall we say then? Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound? By no means! How can we who died to sin still live in it?
verseByVerse.commentary:
If grace abounds where sin increases, should we keep sinning so grace can abound? “By no means!” Paul does not answer “you must not” but “how can we?” Those who have died to sin cannot go on living in it, because union with Christ has changed their whole relationship to sin.

A real objection. Paul has heard this before; he reported it as an actual slander at 3:8. You only get this objection if you have said something that sounds dangerously like “God accepts the ungodly and their record contributes nothing” — which is what Paul has said for five chapters. A gospel never once misheard this way may not yet have been stated clearly.

A question, not a fence. Paul did not soften 5:20 to avoid the objection. Now he answers it, and the shape matters. “You must not” is a fence. “How can we?” is an incongruity. You don’t forbid a man released from a life sentence to sleep in his old cell. You ask why on earth he would want to.

“Continue in sin.” The verb means to remain, to keep living somewhere. Paul is not asking whether a Christian ever sins; chapter 7 is painfully clear that he does. He is asking whether a Christian takes up residence in it — not whether you have trespassed, but whether you have built a house on the property.

What “died to sin” does not mean. It does not mean sin no longer attracts you, the pull has gone, or you can no longer do what you did last year. The man who wrote this also wrote chapter 7.

What it does mean. Death ends a jurisdiction. A dead man is beyond the reach of the court that had a warrant out for him. Think of sin as a former employer, not a departed feeling. He still has your number, rings often, and knows what to say. What he has lost is not his voice but his authority. He can make suggestions; he can no longer give orders you are obliged to obey — not because you grew stronger, but because you don’t work there any more. And “died” is past tense: done to you, dated at a cross, applied when you were united to Christ. Every command in this chapter comes after it.

A test. Don’t ask whether you sinned this week; you did. Ask whether there is anything you have stopped fighting — not lost to repeatedly, but quietly stopped contesting. Something you have made room for and no longer bring to God, because you have privately decided this is just how things are. That is not a lapse. It is an address. Paul’s question is not “how could you?” but “how can you still live there?” Name it to God today and move out.

The objection has it backwards. The man who hears of free grace and decides he may now sin as he likes still regards sin as the good thing he is giving up and grace as a permission slip. You were not let off a punishment and left in the same house. You were taken out of the house.
verseByVerse.note: Paul answers a charge his teaching of grace invited.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone baptised into Christ was baptised into his death. We were buried with him, so that as Christ was raised by the glory of the Father, we too might “walk in newness of life.” Baptism marks our union with Christ in his death and resurrection, and that union is the ground of a new way of living.

“Do you not know?” Paul is reminding them of something they were told at the start and are not using. That is the commonest condition in the Christian life: not shortage of information, but not standing on what we already have.

Does baptism itself unite us to Christ? Roman Catholic and Lutheran Christians say that it does: in the rite God gives new birth and joins the person to Christ. Others, Martyn Lloyd-Jones among them, think Paul means not water baptism at all but the Spirit’s baptism into Christ (1 Cor 12:13). The more likely reading is that Paul means water baptism, but as the sign and seal of a union God brings about by the Spirit through faith. That is why Colossians says we were “raised with him through faith in the powerful working of God” (Col 2:12), and why Abraham’s sign followed his faith (4:11). Even when Peter says that baptism “now saves you,” he explains at once: “not as a removal of dirt from the body but as an appeal to God for a good conscience” (1 Pet 3:21). The water does not save; Christ does, and baptism is where his saving is publicly declared. The picture of burial and rising fits immersion best, and it fits a person who has already come to faith; Christians who baptize infants see the sign as God’s promise to the children of believers (cf. 4:11), but the dying and rising Paul describes here is something the baptized have entered by faith.

“Into.” Baptised into Christ, into his death. Not because of it or in memory of it. Paul is not describing a benefit sent to you from a distance but your being placed inside an event. What happened to Christ counts as having happened to you, because you are in him. That is why Romans can say you died, were buried and were raised, in events that took place in Judea before you existed.

Why mention burial? Burial is how a society confirms that a death is real and final. A man in a coma may recover; a man in the ground has been publicly given up. The burial is the certificate. Paul wants no possibility left that the old life is merely convalescing.

Walking. Paul does not say we were raised to feel new or have new experiences, but to “walk in newness of life.” Walking is the least dramatic verb there is: ordinary, repetitive, getting you somewhere over time. The new life shows itself not as an event but as a gait.

“By the glory of the Father.” Not just his power. Glory is the full weight of who God is. The raising of Jesus expressed the Father’s whole character, his verdict on his Son. And the same glory stands behind your new life. The energy available for an ordinary Christian’s Tuesday is the energy that emptied the tomb.

A test. Take the sin you fight most often. What do you say to yourself when tempted? Most of us say “I must not” — a fence, and fences get climbed. This passage gives a different sentence: “I am not that man any more; that man is buried.” It is not a stronger effort but a truer description. Notice which comes to you unprompted. If it is always the first, you know the doctrine of this chapter but have not started using it. Start using it today.

parallels.desc: buried with him in baptism

verseByVerse.quote: For if we have been united with him in a death like his, we shall certainly be united with him in a resurrection like his. We know that our old self was crucified with him in order that the body of sin might be brought to nothing, so that we would no longer be enslaved to sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If we have been united with Christ in his death, we will certainly be united with him in his resurrection. Our “old self” — the person we were in Adam — was crucified with him, so that “the body of sin might be brought to nothing” and we would no longer be slaves to sin.

Grown together. The word for “united” means grown together, like a graft cut into another tree’s stock until both share one life. Not a partnership but a shared life. What happens to the tree happens to the branch, because the branch lives on sap it did not produce. His death is your death for the same reason his life is your life. And so the resurrection follows with no further condition. Nobody was ever joined to Christ for the funeral and left out of the resurrection.

“Then why does he keep getting up?” Paul says the old self is dead. My experience says he was in the kitchen this morning in a bad temper. Two distinctions clear this up.

First: the old self is not the same as remaining sin. The old self is not a compartment of you that survives alongside the new one. It is the whole person you were under Adam. That person has been executed; his position and jurisdiction are gone. What remains are the habits, appetites and reflexes he trained into your body over years. A country can change government overnight, and on Monday the old regime’s officials are still at their desks, still know the procedures, and will keep running things the old way unless somebody stops them. Their authority is gone. Their filing cabinets are not.

Second: “brought to nothing,” not destroyed. The word means rendered powerless, put out of a job. Paul does not say sin is gone, that its pull has stopped, or that you won’t lose this week. He says it has been deposed. A deposed power that still has supporters in the country is exactly what you experience: real fighting, real losses, and a war whose outcome is not in doubt.

The fight is evidence. A struggle does not show the doctrine has failed. It shows there are two parties. A man wholly under sin does not fight it; he simply lives, and the accusations that trouble you would not trouble him. That you resist, grieve and get up again is what this passage predicts. You are not failing to be dead. You are meeting the resistance of a regime that has already lost.

A test. Think of the last time you sinned in your most habitual way. What did it produce afterwards — relief and no further thought, or a heaviness that would not settle until it was dealt with? The second is the sign not of a weak Christian but of a live one. Corpses don’t ache. Take that heaviness straight to God rather than carrying it.

Freedom is the aim. “So that we would no longer be enslaved to sin.” Not only pardon but release from service. If the Christian life feels like a fight rather than a holiday, it is because you have been freed from an owner who has not yet accepted the verdict.
verseByVerse.note: The “old self” (literally “old man”) is the person we were in Adam before union with Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: For one who has died has been set free from sin. Now if we have died with Christ, we believe that we will also live with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“One who has died has been set free from sin.” Death ends legal obligation: a dead man owes no more taxes and stands before no more courts. And if we have died with Christ, “we believe that we will also live with him.” The life to come is the other side of a death that has already happened.

A commonplace. Every ancient legal system knew that death dissolves obligation. A creditor may chase a debtor across three provinces and has no case against a corpse. The claim was valid yesterday. It has not been forgiven; the person it was filed against is simply out of the court’s reach.

Stronger than a written-off debt. We usually picture forgiveness as a generous creditor writing off a debt — true, and Romans says so. But here Paul’s point is stronger: the debtor has died. Sin is not standing at the counter having its claim waived. It is discovering that the man it came for is not available, and never will be.

“We believe.” Up to now Paul has argued: we know, do you not know. Now he says we believe. He is not weakening the claim, but being honest about how the second half is held. The death is behind us and can be argued from. The life with him is ahead and must be trusted, because nobody has seen it yet. The real difficulty is not believing Christ died, but believing this ends well for you — a life beyond your own grave, with him, in a body. Paul offers no proof, but a link: if the first is true of you, the second follows, because both are one union with one Person.

Dated and undated. Your death with Christ is dated. Your life with him is not yet dated, and is no less certain.

A test. When you think quietly about your own death, what arrives? Not what you would say at a funeral, but what comes when it is your own. If it is a blank, a vague hope, or a subject you avoid, that is not necessarily unbelief. But Paul, as mortal as you, wrote “we believe that we will also live with him” as the settled second half of something already begun (cf. 2 Timothy 2:11). The Christian’s confidence about the far side is not bravery. It is arithmetic on a union already in force. Read 1 Corinthians 15 this week and let it fill in the picture.

verseByVerse.quote: We know that Christ, being raised from the dead, will never die again; death no longer has dominion over him. For the death he died he died to sin, once for all, but the life he lives he lives to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ, raised from the dead, “will never die again; death no longer has dominion over him.” He died to sin “once for all,” and now he lives to God. Our security rests on these facts about him.

Look at him, not you. Paul has been making claims about us — you died, were buried, will live — and a reader might ask how firm they are. So he spends two verses on Christ. If you want to know how permanent your position is, don’t examine your position. Examine his.

Never again. That had never been true of anyone. Lazarus came out of a tomb and in time died again; so did the widow’s son at Nain. Every earlier raising was a postponement. Jesus’ resurrection is the only one that did not end in a second funeral. Death has run every human story and lost one, permanently.

Once for all. Once in a way that settles the matter and forbids repetition. A thing that must be repeated has not worked. The old sacrifices ran on repetition because nothing was finished; the same priest offered the same blood next year to the same queue of people (Hebrews 10:1–4). This death ended the queue.

“He died to sin.” This cannot mean for him what it means for us. We die to sin as people leaving a master who owned us. He never sinned and was never owned. What ended at the cross was his relationship to sin as the one who had taken responsibility for it. He entered its territory voluntarily, bore its full penalty, and when it was paid, the matter was closed. Sin has no remaining claim on him.

Why this matters for you. If you are in him, sin’s claim on you was settled in the same transaction and cannot be reopened, for the same reason it cannot be reopened against him. Your security is not that you have moved beyond sin’s reach by progress. The account was closed on a Friday in Jerusalem and the receipt issued on the Sunday.

A test. When you are anxious about your standing with God, what do you look at? Almost all of us look inward — the state of our faith, last week, whether we feel anything, whether the repentance was sincere enough. That really does fluctuate, so the anxiety never ends. Paul looks at what happened to Christ, once, and cannot change. Next time the accusation comes, don’t ask “How am I doing?” Ask “Is he still risen?” The answer does not depend on your week.

Living to God. “The life he lives he lives to God” — not against sin or in reaction to it, but toward God. The negative is finished. That is the pattern Paul is about to ask of you, which is why he has spent ten verses on what is true before giving a single command. The wounds are still on him — the only scars that no longer mean anything is wrong.

verseByVerse.quote: So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus. Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, to make you obey its passions.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So “consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus.” Count as true what already is true. Therefore do not let sin reign in your body, making you obey its desires. The command rests on the fact: because sin has been dethroned, do not let it rule.

“Consider” is an accountant’s word. It is the verb of chapter 4, where Abraham’s faith “was counted to him as righteousness.” God has been doing the reckoning; now Paul tells you to do some. An accountant who enters a sum not in the account commits fraud; the entry is honest only if the money is there. So Paul is not asking you to pretend, visualise or talk yourself into a mood. He is telling you to write down what is already the case. Reckoning never creates the fact. It brings your books into line with it.

The first command is to believe something. This is the chapter’s first imperative, after ten verses of what is true. And it is not an action but an act of mind. A man who doesn’t know who he is will fight the wrong war all his life.

Both halves. Dead to sin and alive to God. Most attempts at holiness are only negative — a list of things not done — and they fail, because a life cannot be organised around an absence. You cannot warm a room by removing the cold. You are alive to God: available to him, responsive, in the room with him. Fight sin without cultivating that, and sin wins on ground you have left empty.

Reign, not presence. “Let not sin reign” would be pointless unless sin were trying. Paul assumes a daily campaign to restore a deposed regime. And he forbids not sin’s presence — chapter 7 explains why that is not yet on offer — but its reign. The question is not whether sin is present; it will be until you are buried. It is whether it is giving orders that are obeyed. A defeated army in the hills is a real danger. It is not the government.

How sin rules. By making you “obey its passions.” It cannot compel a Christian; it can only persuade, presenting a desire as though it were an order. That is why temptation rarely feels like a summons from an enemy and usually feels like just wanting something. The lie is usually about your position: that you have no real choice, that this is just how you are.

A test. Next time you are tempted, don’t start by measuring the pull; that number will always discourage you. Say two sentences, in words: “I am dead to this. I am alive to God.” Then notice what happens when the temptation is named as an ex-employer’s request rather than a master’s order. It may not vanish; usually it doesn’t. But it has been correctly classified, and much of the Christian fight is simply refusing a false description of who you are. The books have been correct in heaven since the cross. Bring your copy into line.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not present your members to sin as instruments for unrighteousness, but present yourselves to God as those who have been brought from death to life, and your members to God as instruments for righteousness. For sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stop offering the parts of your body to sin as tools of wrongdoing. Offer yourselves to God, as people brought from death to life, and your bodies to him as tools of righteousness. And a promise: “sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace.”

Two kinds of command. The first is a standing prohibition: stop going on presenting your members to sin — break a habit already in progress. The second is a decisive act: present yourselves to God, once, as a thing done rather than a policy. Daily refusal of a worn groove; a single, dateable handing-over.

Members. Paul means the parts of the body — hands, tongue, eyes, feet — the actual equipment you sin and serve with. Holiness in Romans 6 is not mainly a state of mind. It is what your hands did this afternoon.

Weapons. “Instruments” here usually means weapons, a soldier’s equipment. Your body is not neutral ground in the war between two regimes. It will be used by one side or the other today; there is no option in which it is used by nobody.

From death to life. You don’t present a corpse to God for service; it has to be raised first, and it has been. So this surrender is not the desperate effort of someone trying to be good enough. It is the natural act of someone given a life he did not have, deciding what to do with it.

A promise, not a command. “Sin will have no dominion over you.” Paul stops commanding and states an outcome. Not “ought not” or “will not if you are diligent” — will not. Take that sentence to bed on the evening of a bad failure.

Why grace, not more law. Every instinct says: to stop sin, you need more law — firmer rules, sharper accountability. Paul says law keeps sin in power. It tells you what is right and gives no ability to do it; it provokes what it forbids (5:20); and it keeps you under a condemnation that makes honest repentance almost impossible, because someone who thinks he is one failure from being finished cannot afford to look honestly at himself. Sin thrives on that. Grace dismantles it.

A guard. Under grace does not mean the commandments have no claim on you; Paul gives three commands in two verses and many more later. Nor does it mean you won’t sin, which is why v. 13 is written. It means your standing does not depend on your performance, so your failures cannot destroy you, so you are finally free to fight them without terror — the only condition in which anyone has fought them successfully.

A test. When you fail badly, what do you reach for? Most of us reach for law: a tighter rule, a new system, a resolution with more teeth. Count how often you have done that and how long each lasted. Paul’s remedy runs the other way: go back to what is true of you — brought from death to life, not under law — and present the same members to God again today. It feels too easy because it costs no self-punishment, and self-punishment is the one payment sin always accepts, since it keeps you looking at yourself.
verseByVerse.note: “Members” means the parts of the body — hands, eyes, tongue — used for good or evil.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–23 — Slaves of Righteousness: Freedom and Its Direction
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The question of v. 15 replays the question of v. 1 in a new key: "Are we to sin because we are not under law but under grace?" This is the libertarian version of the antinomian objection — if the law is not our master, then surely we are free to do anything. Paul's answer is again a flat denial, followed by a theological argument: freedom from sin does not mean freedom from all master; it means a change of master. Every human being serves either sin or righteousness — there is no neutral ground, no autonomous freedom that is subject to nothing.

The language of slavery runs throughout the passage and is deliberately shocking. Sin is a slave-master. Righteousness is a slave-master. The difference is in the direction: slavery to sin leads to death; slavery to righteousness leads to life and holiness. The Christian is not more free than the unbeliever in the sense of being subject to nothing; she is more free in the sense that she now serves the master whose yoke is easy and whose burden is light — the master whose service is perfect freedom.

The concluding verse is one of the most famous in the letter: "For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord." The contrast between wages and gift is the contrast between law and gospel. Death is what sin earns — a wage paid in proportion to the work done. Eternal life is what God gives — a gift, free, unearned, proportionate not to the recipient's merit but to the giver's generosity. The entire letter is in this sentence.
verseByVerse.theology:
Grace and the New Obedience

Romans 6:15–23 establishes that grace does not produce lawlessness but a new and deeper obedience — obedience that flows from a changed heart rather than a legal compulsion. The Reformers distinguished between the "old obedience" (driven by fear of punishment and desire for reward) and the "new obedience" (driven by love for God and gratitude for grace). Calvin was particularly insistent that the justified Christian is not released from obedience but liberated for it — the law now functions as a guide for the regenerate, not as a court that condemns. The third use of the law: the Christian, freed from condemnation, embraces the law as the expression of the will of the God she loves.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul's slavery metaphor was immediately intelligible to a first-century audience in which slavery was the defining social institution. Every person knew what it meant to be owned by a master, to have their labour and their body subject to another's will. Paul's redeployment of this metaphor is arresting: you were a slave before, and you are a slave now — the only question is whose slave you are. The liberated Christian is not autonomous; she is re-owned, by a Master who purchased her with his own blood. Now: The modern West prizes autonomy above almost everything — the right to define oneself, to determine one's own values, to answer to no authority beyond the self. Romans 6 is a direct challenge to this: the autonomous self is a myth. Every person serves something — appetite, ambition, approval, comfort, identity. The gospel does not offer escape from all masters; it offers the only master worth serving.

verseByVerse.quote: What then? Are we to sin because we are not under law but under grace? By no means! Do you not know that if you present yourselves to anyone as obedient slaves, you are slaves of the one whom you obey, either of sin, which leads to death, or of obedience, which leads to righteousness?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Should we sin, then, because we are under grace, not law? “By no means!” Whoever you obey, you are that one’s slave — either of sin, which leads to death, or of obedience, which leads to righteousness. Freedom from law is not freedom from all masters. It is a change of master.

Can a Christian give himself back to sin and so lose his salvation? Arminian Christians read the verse that way: a believer who keeps presenting himself to sin becomes its slave again, and the end of that road is death. But Paul is describing two kinds of people, not one person changing sides. He goes straight on: “you who were once slaves of sin have become obedient from the heart” (v. 17). A Christian still sins, sometimes badly, but sin is no longer his master (v. 14). Someone who gives himself to sin without struggle or repentance is not showing that he has lost his salvation; he is raising the question whether he ever had it (1 John 2:19). The warning is real, and God uses it to keep his own (cf. 8:38–39).

A subtler objection. At v. 1 the question was whether to continue in sin. Here it is whether to sin — an occasional liberty, “this once won’t matter.” It is the more plausible version, and most of us have made it without noticing.

Every yielding is an enlistment. Paul doesn’t argue about the size of the act. He points to what obedience does: present yourself to someone as an obedient slave and you are his slave. Each act of yielding is a small enlistment. “Can I get away with this once?” is the wrong question. The issue was never whether you would be caught, but what you were becoming while you did it. Nobody decides to become an alcoholic; he decides, thousands of times, to have a drink. Nobody chooses to become untrustworthy with confidences; he chooses to repeat one interesting thing. Habits are made by decisions about single occasions.

No third option. Paul offers two masters and no independent territory. The idea of serving nothing — self-directed, answerable only to your preferences — is not even presented as a possibility. And he is right. The man who has thrown off every outside authority is ruled by his appetites, which never say thank you and never say enough. Look at what governs a free modern person’s choices: what he wants, what others think, how he wants to be seen, what he fears losing. That is not the absence of a master. It is four of them, none chosen and none resignable.

What freedom is. We use “freedom” to mean no constraint. Paul means being under the right authority — owned by the One you were made for, the only condition in which a creature works properly. A fish in a net is constrained. A fish on the riverbank is free of the water and dying of it.

A test. Over the last month, what actually decided your choices where it cost you something? Trace three or four real decisions to their reasons: how you spent an evening, what you didn’t say, the money, the awkward conversation. Whatever turns up repeatedly at the end of those chains is a master. Almost nobody finds only one, and almost nobody finds the one he would have named. Bring what you find to the Master who bought you, who is the one owner in history who died for his slave.

verseByVerse.quote: But thanks be to God, that you who were once slaves of sin have become obedient from the heart to the standard of teaching to which you were committed, and, having been set free from sin, have become slaves of righteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Thanks be to God” that you who were once slaves of sin have become “obedient from the heart” to the teaching you were handed over to, and, set free from sin, have become slaves of righteousness. The change of master is God’s work, and it reaches the heart.

God gets the thanks. These Christians turned from a wicked past and now obey sincerely. Paul does not congratulate them; he thanks God. The only one commended in a sentence about their obedience is someone else. That follows from the chapter: a slave does not transfer himself, and a dead man does not decide to be raised. If they obey from the heart, it is because they were given a different heart. Next time you catch yourself pleased with your spiritual progress, remember: the progress may be real, but it is not yours to be proud of. Thank God for it.

From the heart. Ancient slaves obeyed with their hands. Nobody expected agreement; what a slave thought in the evening was his own affair. Paul says these slaves obey from the heart — which breaks the metaphor on purpose. The new Master has done what no owner ever managed: he has changed what the servant wants.

Poured into a mould. “The standard of teaching to which you were committed” — literally, the pattern you were handed over to. The word is the mould into which molten metal is poured, or the die that stamps a coin. And the direction is the reverse of what we would write. We would say the teaching was delivered to them. Paul says they were delivered to the teaching. The gospel is not a substance you store; it is a shape you are poured into, and what comes out bears its impression.

Why teaching matters. If teaching is a mould, what you steadily attend to will steadily form you, whether or not you are trying. Nobody sits under years of preaching and stays unshaped; the only question is what shape. That is why a Christian cannot be indifferent to what is taught where he worships. You are not just evaluating a message. You are standing in a mould. Choose it carefully.

A test. Take an area where you are currently doing the right thing. What would happen if the outside pressure came off — if no one would ever know, the person you would disappoint weren’t watching, there were no consequence? Would you still do it? Obedience that survives the removal of the audience is from the heart. Obedience that doesn’t is compliance — what the old master got.

A guard. That test can become a whip. Nobody obeys from the heart perfectly; motives in this life come mixed, and someone who waits for pure motives will never act. The answer to mixed motives is not to stop obeying but to bring them, mixed, to the God who is changing them — and to notice, as evidence, that you mind about the mixture at all. A slave who merely complies does not lie awake examining his sincerity.

verseByVerse.quote: I am speaking in human terms, because of your natural limitations. For just as you once presented your members as slaves to impurity and to lawlessness leading to more lawlessness, so now present your members as slaves to righteousness leading to sanctification. For when you were slaves of sin, you were free in regard to righteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul uses the slavery picture because we understand concrete images. Once you offered your bodies to impurity and lawlessness, leading to ever more lawlessness. Now offer them to righteousness, leading to holiness. When you were slaves of sin, you were “free” from righteousness — and look where that freedom led.

“Speaking in human terms.” Paul has built a whole argument on slavery and now half-withdraws it. Not because it is wrong, but because no image from a brutal human institution can carry what it is to belong to God. Slavery conveys ownership, obligation and total claim, all true. It cannot convey that the Master is a Father, that the service is freedom, or that the slave is loved. That is a good rule for every biblical image: find what it was chosen to convey, and don’t make it say what it was never built to say.

“Your natural limitations.” Literally, “the weakness of your flesh.” Not an insult. We think in pictures and grasp ownership more easily than union, so we need concrete images. God has arranged his book accordingly — full of vineyards, sheep, courtrooms, marriages and slaves rather than definitions.

Sin escalates. Impurity led to “lawlessness leading to more lawlessness.” Sin does not deliver and then rest. What satisfied last year does not satisfy this year; the appetite grows by being fed. Anyone who has watched addiction knows this, and it is not limited to obvious vices. The man who shades the truth in small ways needs larger departures to serve the same purpose. A habit of criticism needs fresh material. Pornography is the clearest modern example because the escalation is so measurable, but the same law operates in ambition and temper. Increase is not an abuse of sin; it is what sin does.

Righteousness compounds too. “Present your members as slaves to righteousness leading to sanctification.” The same escalating grammar runs upward. What you resisted with difficulty at thirty is not the same size at fifty — not because you are impressive, but because ten thousand small refusals have worn a channel. Neither slope is fast. Both are real.

A test. Take something you struggle with and compare it not with last week but with five years ago. Does it cost you more to sin than it used to, or less? Does it take more to satisfy, or less? And is there anything that used to be a battle and is now largely settled, because it stopped being a live question? Those answers show which slope you are on more accurately than any audit of the last seven days. Choose one small refusal today; it is how the channel is worn.

That freedom. “When you were slaves of sin, you were free in regard to righteousness.” Paul says it flatly. Free from any obligation to be good — and the previous verse just showed where that liberty was going. Next time freedom is offered as escape from God’s claims, remember: it is genuinely available, and Paul has told you what it produces.
verseByVerse.note: Slavery was part of everyday life across the Roman world; many in the church were slaves or former slaves.

verseByVerse.quote: But what fruit were you getting at that time from the things of which you are now ashamed? For the end of those things is death. But now that you have been set free from sin and have become slaves of God, the fruit you get leads to sanctification and its end, eternal life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What fruit did you get from the things you are now ashamed of? Their end is death. But now, freed from sin and enslaved to God, you bear fruit that leads to holiness, and its end is eternal life. Same structure — master, service, fruit, end — opposite results.

Sin never offers a retrospective. Paul asks rather than lectures, and the answer has to come from the reader. Sin lives entirely in the future tense: what this will feel like, how much better the evening will be. It never volunteers the morning after. So Paul makes them look back — and the expected answer may be devastating: nothing. Not bad fruit; no fruit. Sin is a season of work with an empty barn at the end, and only shame left in the hand.

Your own inventory. Think of something you did that you would not want said aloud. What did it actually yield — not what it promised, but what you have now because of it? Usually the honest list reads: an hour that no longer exists, a relationship changed by a degree nobody else noticed, a memory that arrives uninvited years later. That is the harvest.

Shame. Guilt says “I did something bad.” Shame says “I cannot look at it.” It is the impulse to turn the face away, as Adam did in the garden, and why sin needs concealment to survive. Nobody hides what has done him good.

A guard. Paul speaks of what you are “now ashamed” of — Christians looking back at a life they have left — and he spends one sentence on it, then moves to the fruit they bear now. If you are a believer who cannot stop replaying an old sin at night, this verse is not asking that of you. The shame here is diagnostic, not punitive: it shows the old master for what he is, so that you look at the new one. Chapter 8 says there is now no condemnation, and it adds no exceptions.

Change the master. The same four stages run both ways. Sin as master: service, fruit of shame, end in death. God as master: service, fruit of sanctification, end in eternal life. Only the first term changes, and everything downstream follows. That is why this chapter spends twenty verses on ownership rather than techniques for behaving better.

Fruit grows slowly. Paul uses a farming picture, not a mechanical one. Fruit is slow and seasonal and not produced by the branch straining. Nobody grew an apple by effort. It appears because the tree is alive, attached, and has stood in the right place long enough (cf. John 15:4–5). If your sanctification looks discouragingly gradual, you are not assembling something; you are growing, and growth isn’t visible on the timescale at which we inspect ourselves. Stay attached: keep to the Word, prayer and the church, and let the seasons do their work.

verseByVerse.quote: For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord. — Romans 6:23
verseByVerse.commentary:
“The wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.” Sin pays what it owes: death. God gives what we could never earn: eternal life — and that life is found in a Person, Jesus Christ.

A soldier’s pay. “Wages” is the word for a soldier’s ration money, paid out at intervals during the campaign. Sin does not pay its people in one settlement at the end. It pays in instalments, on time, as you go. We picture death as a bill arriving at the end of life. But sin has been paying all along in its own currency: the friendship that thinned and was never mended, the wonder that dulled, the prayer that got harder to say, the person you can no longer be honest with. Those are not warnings of a future wage. They are the wage, paid in small coin, on schedule. The final payment is the same currency, in full.

The parallel broken. The tidy version would be “the wages of righteousness is eternal life.” Nobody has earned that wage, so Paul changes the noun: not wages but free gift. The sentence does not balance, and the gospel is in the imbalance. Hell is earned and heaven is not. Nobody will be in hell who did not work for it, and nobody in heaven who did. That offends many at first, but it is the only arrangement in which God is both just and merciful (3:26).

In a Person. The verse ends with a name: “in Christ Jesus our Lord.” Eternal life is not a substance God hands you at conversion to keep independently, like money taken home. It is in a Person — “I am the resurrection and the life” (John 11:25); “Whoever has the Son has life” (1 John 5:12). So it is not stored anywhere you could lose it or in an account you could overdraw. To have it you must have him, and if you have him you cannot have less of it than he has.

The last word is “Lord.” Twenty-three verses about two masters, two slaveries, two harvests, two ends, and Paul finishes by naming the Owner. Not “our Saviour,” though he is, but “our Lord.” The chapter has been about whom you belong to.

A test. Which half of the verse do you expect to receive, and why? If your reason includes anything about yourself — you have tried, you believe the right things, you are not as bad as some — you have answered from the first half, where things are earned. The only answer the verse allows is a name that is not yours.

No third category. No wages of moderate sin, no partial gift, no arrangement for those in between. Everyone is drawing one of two things: a wage earned or a gift not earned. The wage is being paid now, in instalments. The gift is held in a Person who is alive and cannot be lost. If you have been drawing the wage, stop and receive the gift today. Nobody has ever earned the second half of this verse — which is exactly why it can be relied on.
verseByVerse.note: Wages were the regular pay of a soldier or labourer — what is earned. A gift is not.

6.text: <sup>1</sup>What shall we say then? Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound?<sup>2</sup>By no means! How can we who died to sin still live in it?<sup>3</sup>Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?<sup>4</sup>We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life.<sup>5</sup>For if we have been united with him in a death like his, we shall certainly be united with him in a resurrection like his.<sup>6</sup>We know that our old self was crucified with him in order that the body of sin might be brought to nothing, so that we would no longer be enslaved to sin.<sup>7</sup>For one who has died has been set free from sin.<sup>8</sup>Now if we have died with Christ, we believe that we will also live with him.<sup>9</sup>We know that Christ, being raised from the dead, will never die again; death no longer has dominion over him.<sup>10</sup>For the death he died he died to sin, once for all, but the life he lives he lives to God.<sup>11</sup>So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus.<sup>12</sup>Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, to make you obey its passions.<sup>13</sup>Do not present your members to sin as instruments for unrighteousness, but present yourselves to God as those who have been brought from death to life, and your members to God as instruments for righteousness.<sup>14</sup>For sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace.<sup>15</sup>What then? Are we to sin because we are not under law but under grace? By no means!<sup>16</sup>Do you not know that if you present yourselves to anyone as obedient slaves, you are slaves of the one whom you obey, either of sin, which leads to death, or of obedience, which leads to righteousness?<sup>17</sup>But thanks be to God, that you who were once slaves of sin have become obedient from the heart to the standard of teaching to which you were committed,<sup>18</sup>and, having been set free from sin, have become slaves of righteousness.<sup>19</sup>I am speaking in human terms, because of your natural limitations. For just as you once presented your members as slaves to impurity and to lawlessness leading to more lawlessness, so now present your members as slaves to righteousness leading to sanctification.<sup>20</sup>For when you were slaves of sin, you were free in regard to righteousness.<sup>21</sup>But what fruit were you getting at that time from the things of which you are now ashamed? 7.title: The Law, the Flesh, and the Struggle Within
7.overview:
Romans 7 is one of the most debated chapters in the New Testament. The first six verses use the analogy of marriage to explain the Christian's release from the law — just as death dissolves a marriage, so the death of the old self has dissolved the law's claim on the believer. Verses 7–25 then address the relationship between the law and sin in a passage of such raw psychological honesty that it has divided interpreters for centuries: is Paul describing his experience before or after his conversion?

The Reformed tradition, following Luther and Calvin, has generally argued that vv. 7–25 describe the experience of the regenerate person — not as the normal steady state of the mature Christian, but as the honest account of the ongoing struggle that even the believer has with indwelling sin. The person who says "I delight in the law of God in my inner being" (v. 22) is not an unregenerate person; the unregenerate person has no such delight. The chapter is not a counsel of despair but a radical honesty about the nature of the Christian struggle — which ends, in v. 25, with the triumphant answer: thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Released from the Law to Bear Fruit for God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul uses the analogy of marriage to make a point about the law's jurisdiction. A woman is bound to her husband by law as long as he lives; if he dies, she is free to marry another. In the same way, the Christian has "died" to the law through her union with Christ's death — she is no longer bound to the law as a system of earning and condemnation. She is now married to another — to Christ who was raised from the dead — so that she might bear fruit for God.

The point is not that the law is bad (v. 7 will explicitly deny this) but that the law was never the instrument of life. Under the law's jurisdiction, the sinful passions "aroused by the law were at work in our members to bear fruit for death" (v. 5). This does not mean the law created those sinful passions; it means that the sinful nature, encountering prohibition, is provoked — not helped — by the law. The law reveals and aggravates what is already there; it cannot remove it.

But now — freed from the law, joined to Christ — the Christian serves "in the new way of the Spirit and not in the old way of the written code" (v. 6). This is not antinomianism; it is the fulfilment of Jeremiah 31 and Ezekiel 36 — the new covenant in which the law is written on the heart by the Spirit, not merely imposed from without by the letter. The motive for obedience has changed: from fear of penalty to love of the God who has shown such grace.
verseByVerse.theology:
Death to Law: Liberation for Obedience

The believer's death to the law (vv. 4, 6) has been the source of great misunderstanding. Paul is not teaching that the Christian is released from the moral content of the law — he will demonstrate in chapters 12–15 that the redeemed life is the life of love, which is the fulfilment of the law (13:8–10). He is teaching that the believer's relationship to the law has changed: no longer subject to it as a court that condemns, the Christian is now free to embrace its moral demands as the expression of the will of the God she loves. Calvin's third use of the law: a guide for the regenerate, not a goad for the condemned.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The marriage analogy was immediately accessible to Paul's Jewish readers, for whom marriage law was well understood. The death that dissolves the marriage — the death of the old self in union with Christ's death — was the theologically startling element. Paul is saying: you belong to a new husband now. The old master (law as condemning power) is dead to you; the new master (Christ) is alive to you. Serve him accordingly. Now: Many Christians live as though they are still married to the law — haunted by condemnation, driven by religious duty, exhausted by the performance of obligation. Romans 7:1–6 is the declaration of liberty: you have died to that system. You are joined to Christ. Serve him from love, not from fear.

verseByVerse.quote: Or do you not know, brothers — for I am speaking to those who know the law — that the law is binding on a person only as long as he lives? For a married woman is bound by law to her husband while he lives, but if her husband dies she is released from the law of marriage.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul states a legal principle his readers know: law binds a person only while he lives. A married woman is bound to her husband while he lives; if he dies, she is released from the law of marriage. Death ends legal obligation. Paul will apply this to the Christian’s relationship to the law of Moses.

Respect for the law. Paul argues from what his readers already grant, and he will insist in this chapter that “the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good” (v. 12). He is not disparaging it. He is explaining how a good thing can be the wrong thing to be married to.

Why marriage? Paul has used debt and slavery already. He picks marriage, the Old Testament’s covenant image: Israel the wife, idolatry adultery, Hosea told to marry a woman who would betray him so the nation could see what it had done. Marriage carries what debt cannot: exclusive belonging, covenant rather than contract, and — as v. 4 will say — fruitfulness.

Don’t press the picture. In the illustration the husband dies and the wife goes free. In the application it is not the law that dies; “you also have died to the law” (v. 4). Paul is not building an allegory where every part lines up. He is establishing one principle — death dissolves legal obligation — and applying it. Whoever dies, the bond is over. Pushing an illustration further than its author meant is one of the commonest ways to misread the Bible.

Not a passage on divorce. Paul is citing a commonplace to make a point about the law, not legislating for someone whose marriage has ended. For that, go where it is actually taught (Matthew 19; 1 Corinthians 7).

Married to the law. Many Christians are, in practice, still married to the law. It is life with a spouse who is never satisfied. He is not cruel or wrong; his standards are reasonable and every criticism accurate. He just notices every failure and never says “well done.” He offers no help — he tells you what is required and leaves you to it. And you cannot leave, because he is right and you have nothing to plead. That produces a conscientious person, permanently tired, who cannot enjoy God and cannot admit it. The remedy is not that the spouse lowers his standards; the law stays holy. It is that the marriage has ended by a death, and you are joined to Someone else — “him who has been raised from the dead” (v. 4), who does not die and is not waiting to be satisfied.

A test. A woman long married to a severe man often goes on bracing for criticism years after the funeral. Take an ordinary act of obedience — your praying, your giving, your Sunday. Which husband is it done for? To avoid a bad conscience, keep something at bay, stay in credit? Or because you belong to Someone and want to be with him? The act is the same in both marriages. The person doing it is not. Pray today as the wife of the second husband.

parallels.desc: a wife is bound to her husband as long as he lives

verseByVerse.quote: Accordingly, she will be called an adulteress if she lives with another man while her husband is alive. But if her husband dies, she is free from that law, and if she marries another man she is not an adulteress.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While her husband lives, a woman who goes to another man is called an adulteress. If he dies, she is free, and marrying another man is not adultery. The same act is treachery in one case and blameless in the other. The only difference is a death.

A strong word. Paul uses “adulteress,” the strongest word for covenant betrayal. The bond is not a formality that lapses quietly. While the first husband lives, going to another is treachery. The law’s claim is that serious.

A change of category. Nothing about the woman has changed — her character, her history, perhaps even the man she goes to. What has changed is her standing, and standing is not a matter of degree. There is no partial adultery and no half-widow. A funeral moves her from bound to free. That is why Paul chose such uncomfortable language: he needs a change that is absolute, not gradual. Christians are not people the law is slowly letting off as they improve. The change is a change of category, made by a death, complete the day it happened.

Free to belong. She is “free from that law” — not free from all law or from belonging to anyone. She is free to marry again. Freedom here is never freedom from attachment; it is freedom to be attached to someone new.

Your peace is lawful. Some Christians carry a low-level sense that their happiness in Christ is somehow illegitimate — that they have got away with something, that a stricter accounting would find them out. Look at this woman in her second marriage. She is not living in a tolerated irregularity. “She is not an adulteress” — Paul uses the very word that would have accused her. Your standing with Christ is not a generous arrangement that would collapse under scrutiny. It would survive any court in the universe, because the death that made it lawful has already happened.

Overlooked or resolved? One way of holding the gospel says God has kindly overlooked the problem. The other says the problem has been legally resolved and there is nothing left to overlook. Only the second can be rested on at three in the morning, because what has been overlooked can always be looked at again.

Widowed, not divorced. She did not negotiate a release or walk out on an obligation. She was widowed. She has no case to answer and no reason to avoid the neighbours. That is your position toward the law: not that you escaped it, but that the bond ended the only way it could, by someone else’s death. Stop apologising for being loved.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise, my brothers, you also have died to the law through the body of Christ, so that you may belong to another, to him who has been raised from the dead, in order that we may bear fruit for God. For while we were living in the flesh, our sinful passions, aroused by the law, were at work in our members to bear fruit for death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You have died to the law through Christ’s body, so that you may belong to another — to Christ, raised from the dead — and bear fruit for God. Before, our sinful passions, stirred up by the law, worked in us to bear fruit for death. The law could diagnose and provoke but never cure.

Through a body. Not through a decision or a change of conviction, but through Christ’s body — an execution at a particular hour on a particular hill. Your release from the law is not a principle you grasped; it is a consequence of what happened to Someone’s body, and you were in him when it happened.

Belonging, not just liberty. The first purpose is “that you may belong to another.” Not freedom full stop; a widow left alone is not what Paul describes. The whole point of the death was a second marriage.

The risen husband. Paul identifies Christ as “him who has been raised from the dead” — because of the illustration. The first marriage ended by a death; this one cannot. This husband has been through death and come out, so the wife will not be widowed twice.

Fruit. The second purpose: “that we may bear fruit for God.” This changes what holiness is. Fruit is not manufactured by effort; it is the natural result of a union. That is why the New Testament seldom tells Christians to try harder and often tells them to abide, to stay joined (John 15:4–5).

Aroused, not restrained. “Our sinful passions, aroused by the law.” Applied to a sinful nature, the law does not produce holiness. It produces provocation, then failure, then fruit — for death. Both marriages are fertile. That is the horror of the first: it was productive, and you have the children to prove it.

A test. Take an area where you have made real moral effort — a habit fought, a temper managed, a discipline attempted. What did it produce over five years? Under the first husband the pattern is familiar: a rule, some success, a collapse, a worse collapse, then despair or a quiet lowering of the standard so the failure stops showing. Under the second it is slower and different: something you didn’t particularly work at has quietly changed, and you noticed afterwards. The first produces effort and shame. The second produces fruit, which grows while you sleep. Spend your effort on staying close to Christ.

A guard. This does not mean obedience no longer matters. The new marriage is not easier and nothing is unasked. The wife now belongs to Someone alive who can help her, instead of a husband who could only tell her what was required. The demands remain; the relationship in which they are met has changed completely.

verseByVerse.quote: But now we are released from the law, having died to that which held us captive, so that we serve in the new way of the Spirit and not in the old way of the written code.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“But now” we are released from the law, having died to what held us captive, so that we serve “in the new way of the Spirit and not in the old way of the written code.” We still serve. What changes is the source: not a rule outside us, but the Spirit within.

“But now.” The same words that opened the gospel at 3:21. Paul uses them where the argument turns from what was to what is, both times after describing something inescapable.

Held captive. The law is pictured as custody. A striking thing to say about a good law, which is why Paul spends the rest of the chapter clearing it of blame. The law was not designed as a jailer. It became a prison because of what we brought to it, as a mirror becomes unbearable to a man who cannot change his face.

Not Old Testament versus New. “The old way of the written code” versus “the new way of the Spirit” is not law-bad, Spirit-good. The written code is God’s word. Paul contrasts two ways of serving, and both have the same verb: we serve. The question was never whether a Christian obeys, but from what source.

A rule outside, a life inside. A written code can say what is required and can do nothing to make you want it — not a defect, but a limit of the medium. Instructions pinned to a wall have never moved anyone. The new covenant promised not clearer instructions but a new interior: “I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33); “I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes” (Ezekiel 36:27). The statutes don’t change. The walking does.

Pushing or driving. Most Christians default to the old way without deciding to: I must, I should, I ought, I’ll try. It produces a life that is disciplined and quietly joyless. The new way does not abolish the “shoulds.” It relocates the engine. It is the difference between a man driving a car and a man pushing one; on a flat road they can look alike for a long way.

A test. Take the last thing you did that you did not want to do — the visit, the apology, the gift, the honest word. Why did you do it? Because not doing it would make you feel bad about yourself, or someone would notice, or standards must be kept? Or because you belong to Christ and it would please him? You cannot tell from outside, and most of us will find a mixture, which is normal. Notice which one does the heavy lifting when you are tired — and ask the Spirit for the second.

The house you live in now. You have not been released into having no master and no obligation. You have been released into a house where the same things are asked, and Someone lives in you who wants them.

parallels.desc: the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–25 — The Law and the Ongoing Conflict
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"What then shall we say? That the law is sin? By no means!" Paul's defence of the law is passionate and complete: the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good (v. 12). The problem is not the law; the problem is sin — which used the good commandment as a foothold for its own agenda. When the commandment "you shall not covet" entered Paul's consciousness, it awakened the very covetousness it forbade. Not because the commandment was defective, but because sin is so pervasive that even the confrontation with prohibition provokes the prohibited desire.

The famous passage beginning in v. 14 — "For we know that the law is spiritual, but I am of the flesh, sold under sin. For I do not understand my own actions. For I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate" — is the most honest description of the experience of indwelling sin in all of Scripture. Whether Paul is describing pre-conversion or post-conversion experience has been debated exhaustively. The weight of the evidence — the delight in God's law (v. 22), the willing of the good (v. 18), the self-awareness of the conflict — points to the regenerate person, not the unregenerate.

The climax of the chapter is both a cry and a triumph: "Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord!" (vv. 24–25). The cry of anguish is honest; the gratitude that follows is immediate. Paul does not wallow in the wretchedness. He knows the answer. He has the answer. The very struggle he describes is the evidence that the Spirit is at work — because the person without the Spirit does not experience this conflict; she simply does what sin desires. The one who hates what she does and loves the law of God in her inner being is alive in Christ, even while she wars against the flesh.

Two things in the middle of the chapter carry the argument and should not be lost. The first is Paul’s conclusion at v. 13, which is the point of the whole autobiographical section: the law did not kill him, sin did — working death in him through what is good, so that sin might be shown to be sin and might become sinful beyond measure. That is the purpose of the exercise. The law was given partly to provoke sin into the open, where its true character could be seen; a disease that is invisible cannot be treated, and sin’s worst feature is exactly its capacity to use a holy commandment as its instrument. The second is the image at v. 23, which supplies the vocabulary for everything Christians have said since about the inner conflict: another law waging war against the law of the mind, and taking the man captive. Paul does not describe an imbalance or a tension. He describes a campaign, with two sides, prisoners, and territory — which is why the chapter can end in a cry rather than a conclusion.
verseByVerse.theology:
Indwelling Sin and the Doctrine of Sanctification

Romans 7:14–25 is the biblical foundation for the Reformed doctrine that sanctification is a lifelong struggle, not a crisis experience of eradication. John Wesley and the Holiness tradition argued for the possibility of entire sanctification — the complete eradication of the sinful nature — in this life. The Reformed tradition, following Augustine, Luther, and Calvin, has insisted that indwelling sin remains until glorification. This is not defeatism but realism: the Christian who understands this will not be surprised or destroyed by the ongoing struggle. She will be equipped to fight it with the means God has provided — the Word, prayer, the sacraments, the community of believers — rather than pretending it does not exist or despairing when it does.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The experience Paul describes in vv. 14–25 had a parallel in the literature of the day — Ovid's famous line, spoken by Medea: "I see the better and approve it; I follow the worse." But the philosophers' solution (more reason, more discipline, more willpower) is precisely what Paul finds inadequate. The problem is not ignorance; it is the power of indwelling sin that reason alone cannot overcome. The solution is not philosophy; it is the liberating power of "Jesus Christ our Lord" (v. 25). Now: The Christian who has experienced Romans 7 — who has tried harder, prayed more, committed afresh, and still found the same sins returning — is not a failure. She is a normal Christian, living in the honest tension between the new self and the old, between the delight in God's law and the drag of indwelling sin. The answer is not more effort; it is more Christ. Chapter 8 is the answer to chapter 7.

verseByVerse.quote: What then shall we say? That the law is sin? By no means! Yet if it had not been for the law, I would not have known sin. For I would not have known what it is to covet if the law had not said, "You shall not covet." But sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, produced in me all kinds of covetousness. For apart from the law, sin lies dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Is the law sin, then? “By no means!” But the law made sin known. Paul would not have known what coveting was if the law had not said “You shall not covet.” Sin used the commandment as a base to stir up every kind of coveting in him. Without the law, sin lay dormant. The fault is sin’s, not the law’s.

Paul states the objection fairly. He has just said the law arouses sinful passions (v. 5) and we are released from it (v. 6). Any fair reader would conclude that the law is the problem. Paul denies it as strongly as he can and then spends the rest of the chapter defending the law he has just called a captor.

Why the tenth commandment. Of the ten, it is the one nobody can be seen breaking. Stealing and adultery leave witnesses; coveting happens entirely inside. It is the commandment that exposed Paul. He could say that “as to righteousness under the law,” he was “blameless” (Philippians 3:6). He kept the other nine outwardly. The tenth got past his defences, because it asks what you want.

A bridgehead. “Seizing an opportunity” uses a military word for a base of operations. Sin does not just react to the commandment; it sets up camp on it. Something you had not thought about for months becomes interesting within an hour of being told it is off limits. A wet-paint sign creates an urge to touch. Tell a child not to put beans up his nose and you have given him an idea. But the sign does not corrupt the child. It brings into daylight what was already in him.

Dormant, not absent. “Apart from the law, sin lies dead.” A quiet conscience is not necessarily a clean heart. It may only mean nothing has yet woken what is sleeping. Most of us think highly of our patience until we live with the right person, and of our honesty until real money is involved.

A test. Don’t audit your behaviour; you will pass. Audit your wanting. In the last week, what did you wish you had, in a way that made your own life look thinner — someone’s marriage, their ease, their platform, their health, their children, the way things seem to work out for them? Nobody sees that or can charge you with it, which is exactly why Paul used this commandment to explain how a blameless man discovered he was lost. Name it to God, and thank him for three specific things he has given you instead.

The law exonerated. The law is holy and did not create the appetite. It walked into the house and turned the lights on. The problem is not God’s commandment but what we are: creatures in whom even a perfect word from God can be made a bridgehead by an enemy already inside.
verseByVerse.note: Coveting is the one commandment that concerns only the heart.

parallels.desc: you shall not covet

verseByVerse.quote: I was once alive apart from the law, but when the commandment came, sin came alive and I died. The very commandment that promised life proved to be death to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“I was once alive apart from the law, but when the commandment came, sin came alive and I died.” The commandment that promised life became death to Paul. The law was given for life — “if a person does them, he shall live by them” (Leviticus 18:5) — but sin turned it into the occasion of death.

A story told at every scale. The shape is: alive without the commandment, then the commandment, then death. That is Eden — a man in a garden, one command, death as promised. It is Israel — rescued from Egypt by mercy, then Sinai, then a golden calf before Moses was down the mountain. And it is a devout boy secure in a religious home until the tenth commandment reached where he actually lived.

Whose story? Paul is speaking of himself, but telling it in a way that echoes Adam and Israel. The “I” is too personal to be a figure of speech. How could Paul, blameless as a Pharisee (Phil 3:6), say “I was once alive apart from the law”? Not because he had never heard the law, but because he had never felt its weight. He knew its outward demands and kept them. The commandment came when he saw that the law also forbids coveting (v. 7), a sin of the heart he could not stop. Then he died: his confidence in his own righteousness was finished.

Are children innocent until they understand the law? No. Paul has already said that all die in Adam, even those who did not sin as Adam did (5:12–14); “alive” describes how things seemed, not his standing before God. Scripture gives no age of accountability. But it gives good ground for hope for those who die in infancy: David expected to go to his child (2 Sam 12:23), and the Judge of all the earth will do what is just (Gen 18:25).

The peace of not knowing. “I was once alive” describes how it felt, not how it was. Nobody who has not met the commandment in earnest thinks himself in danger — not because he has examined it, but because the question has never been put to him with force. There is a kind of peace that is only the absence of information.

Swapped places. “Sin came alive and I died.” Sin had been dormant (v. 8); now it stands up, and the man who thought himself alive is the corpse. The commandment did not change how much sin was in him. It changed which of them was standing.

“Death to me.” Paul does not say the commandment is death, but that it proved to be death to him. The same word that is life to someone who keeps it is death to someone who cannot — not because it changed, but because of what he was. The sunlight that ripens fruit blisters skin that cannot take it. Nothing is wrong with the light. That is why every attempt to fix humanity by improving the instruction has failed.

A test. When did the commandment come to you? Not when you first heard the Ten Commandments, but when one of them found you — when a sentence of God’s stopped being a general statement and became an accusation with your name on it. Some can date it; for others it came slowly over a year. But a Christian who has never been genuinely alarmed by anything God has said should ask whether he is standing in the first half of verse 9. It feels better and is more dangerous. Ask God to let his word reach you.

Dying is progress. The man alive at the start is lost; the man dead at the end will write about grace for nine chapters. God’s ordinary way of saving people is to let a commandment kill them first. The one never wounded by the law has not yet been helped by it.

parallels.desc: by doing them a person shall live

verseByVerse.quote: For sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me. So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sin used the commandment to deceive Paul and to kill him. Yet “the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good.” The culprit is sin, not the law — as the fault lies in the patient, not the prescription.

The serpent’s method. “Deceived me” echoes Eve: “The serpent deceived me, and I ate” (Genesis 3:13). Watch his method, because it has not changed. First he misquoted the command: “Did God actually say, ‘You shall not eat of any tree in the garden’?” (Genesis 3:1) — inflating it until God looked mean. Then he questioned the motive: “God knows that when you eat of it your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God” (Genesis 3:5) — he is holding out on you. Only then the flat denial: “You will not surely die” (Genesis 3:4).

Still in service. All three moves work today. The command is exaggerated until it sounds like deprivation for its own sake. God’s motive is questioned: he is restrictive, doesn’t want you happy, other people manage fine. And the consequence is quietly denied — not disproved, just pushed into the theoretical, no longer something that will actually happen to you.

Sin misinforms. Sin’s main work is not to overpower you but to misinform you. Nobody sins while clear-sighted about what he is doing and what it will cost. Every temptation contains a lie, usually not about the thing itself but about the arithmetic: this will satisfy, it won’t cost much, you can stop, God is unreasonable. So the answer to temptation is often simply telling yourself the truth, aloud if necessary, because what is under attack is your information.

Three adjectives. Paul has just described the commandment being used to kill him. The obvious conclusion lies ready — and he refuses it: holy, righteous and good. He defends the law more warmly than almost anything else in the letter. He was genuinely wounded, and he will not let his own experience be evidence against God. Most of us do the opposite: we take what hurt us and conclude something about God from it, and the conclusion always flatters us.

A test. Think of a commandment that has cost you something — that stood between you and what you wanted, or that you have failed so often you stopped hoping. What do you really think of it? Holy, righteous and good? Or is there an unspoken sense that it is excessive, that a reasonable God would have made an exception for your case? That resentment is the serpent’s second move, still working, in many believers who would sign any doctrinal statement. Read Psalm 19:7–11 aloud and ask God to make you agree with it about that command.

We are the danger. The verdict is not that the law is dangerous but that we are. Paul can describe the whole process, name himself as the casualty, and end by calling the weapon good.
verseByVerse.note: “Deceived” echoes the serpent’s deception of Eve.

parallels.desc: the serpent deceived me

verseByVerse.quote: Did that which is good, then, bring death to me? By no means! It was sin, producing death in me through what is good, in order that sin might be shown to be sin, and through the commandment might become sinful beyond measure.
verseByVerse.commentary:
