Did the good law bring death? “By no means!” Sin did, using what is good — so that sin would be exposed as sin and become, through the commandment, “sinful beyond measure.” The law cannot save, but it shows exactly what we need saving from.

Why give the law at all? If God knew the law would provoke sin rather than restrain it, why give it? Paul does not call it a miscalculation. He says it was the purpose: “in order that sin might be shown to be sin.”

Making the disease show itself. A sickness with no symptoms is not harmless; it is untreatable, because nobody sees a doctor for a condition he cannot feel. The cruellest illnesses are silent ones. The commandment forced a hidden thing to produce symptoms, the symptoms were violent, and that is why the patient finally went for help.

Sinful beyond measure. How does sin earn that description? Not by something spectacular — this passage is about a man wanting what he shouldn’t. By what it is willing to use. It took the holiest thing God had given, a good commandment designed for life, and turned it into an instrument of death.

Sin has strategy. We picture sin as weakness — appetite, lapse, a failed good intention. Paul describes something with strategy. It waits, seizes opportunities, deceives, and repurposes the best material available. Religion can be conscripted. Doctrine can be — a man may use accurate theology to avoid God. Even repentance can be, when it becomes a performance that manages guilt without reaching its cause.

A test. What good thing in your life is being used against you? Your work, a gift, which has become where you go to avoid a difficulty at home. Your theological knowledge, which is real, and has become a way of feeling superior to other Christians. Your service, which helps people, and has become how you avoid asking whether anyone knows you. Sin prefers good material because good material is not inspected. Name yours and bring it into the light.

Why serious Christians are blindsided. The man who has fought an obvious sin successfully for twenty years is often taken from an angle he never watched. He guarded the disreputable ground; the enemy was working through the commandment.

The purpose is revelation. God let sin have the commandment so a man could see what was in him and stop negotiating with it. Nobody is saved from a problem he doesn’t believe he has. The chapter ends in a cry for rescue — the first thing this man says that can be answered.

verseByVerse.quote: For we know that the law is spiritual, but I am of the flesh, sold under sin. For I do not understand my own actions. For I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law is spiritual, but “I am of the flesh, sold under sin.” Paul does not understand his own actions: he does not do what he wants, but the very thing he hates. Many, following Augustine and the Reformers, read this as the ongoing struggle of a Christian who loves God’s law and still finds sin at work in him.

Before or after conversion? This is one of the most debated passages in Scripture. Some read it as Paul’s pre-Christian struggle under the law, since Romans 6 has declared the believer “dead to sin” and “set free from sin.” But that reading cannot account for what this man does: he delights in God’s law in his inner being (v. 22), the language of a renewed heart, while “the mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God, for it does not submit to God’s law; indeed, it cannot” (8:7). And the cry of v. 24 is not the voice of someone comfortable in sin but of someone with a new nature who hates what his flesh keeps doing. Calvin, Luther, Owen and Sproul all read it as Christian experience — not Paul’s low point, but the ordinary condition of a believer with a renewed heart still living in unredeemed flesh.

The case against. Honesty requires stating the strongest objections. First, “sold under sin” is hard language for a man just described as “set free from sin” (6:18, 22). Second, v. 5 speaks of life “in the flesh” in the past tense, and vv. 14–25 seem to describe that very condition in the present. These are not trivial, and the answers are not knockdown. On the first: Paul is describing his flesh — the unredeemed part of him, which really is sold under sin until it is buried — not his standing before God, and he immediately distinguishes what he wills from what his flesh does. On the second: the present tenses run unbroken for twelve verses, just after a deliberate past tense, which is hard to explain if he has gone back to his pre-Christian life; and the delight of v. 22 remains the immovable obstacle for the other view.

The comfort survives either reading. If Paul describes the Christian, your experience of failure is normal and you are not disqualified. If he describes life under law, the passage shows what you have been rescued from and where to look instead of at yourself. Either way the answer arrives in the same sentence, and it is a Person, not a technique.

Two further questions. What does “the law is spiritual” mean? Not that it is vague or only inward, but that it comes from the Spirit of God and carries his holiness. That is why a person of the flesh cannot keep it, and why those who walk by the Spirit begin to fulfil it (8:4). And does this rule out sinless perfection in this life? Some in the Wesleyan and Holiness traditions teach that a believer can be so filled with love that he no longer sins deliberately, and they often read 7:14–25 as life before conversion or before that second blessing. But if this is the Christian’s experience, even an apostle was still fighting indwelling sin, and John says, “If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” (1 John 1:8). Sin’s rule is broken now; its presence ends only when we are glorified.

“I do not understand my own actions.” Not “I regret them” or “I can’t justify them” — he cannot make sense of them. That is the honest report of anyone who has fought a besetting sin. The strangest thing is not that it is powerful but that it is unintelligible. You did what you had genuinely resolved not to do, for reasons that seemed adequate and evaporate on inspection. And he does not do what he wants — so he wants the right thing. A man who wanted only the wrong thing would have no conflict to report.

A test. What does your sin do to you afterwards? If it produces this bafflement — “why did I do that? I didn’t even want it” — that is evidence of two parties, not one. Someone in you wanted otherwise. He did not exist before God put him there, and his presence is why it hurts.

A guard both ways. This is not a licence. Quoting Romans 7 to excuse a sin you have stopped fighting turns a description of anguish into a permission slip — and the anguish is what you no longer have. Nor is it a ceiling. Chapter 6 insists the Christian life does change, chapter 8 describes the Spirit putting sin to death, and obedience compounds over years (see on 6:19–20). This chapter describes the floor of Christian experience, not the ceiling.
verseByVerse.note: Christians have long debated whether Paul here describes life before conversion or the ongoing struggle of a believer; many, following Augustine and the Reformers, read it as the believer’s experience.

parallels.desc: the desires of the flesh are against the Spirit

verseByVerse.quote: Now if I do what I do not want, I agree with the law, that it is good. So now it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells within me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If I do what I don’t want to do, I am agreeing that the law is good. So “it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells within me.” This is not an excuse but a diagnosis: sin lives in the believer like an unwanted lodger, and it is not the real occupier of the house.

My failure proves the law good. Paul is still defending the law. If I do what I don’t want, my wanting is on the law’s side. My conscience voted for the commandment while my hands voted against it. Guilt, uncomfortable as it is, is evidence: the sound of a moral order being acknowledged by someone who has just broken it.

Not an excuse. “It is no longer I who do it” sounds like the oldest excuse in the world, and has been used as one. But Paul has spent the chapter accepting responsibility — I do, I keep on doing — and never asks to be let off. If you have caught yourself saying “that wasn’t the real me” about last Tuesday, you have found this verse’s counterfeit, not the verse. The tell: Paul’s sentence produces anguish and a cry for rescue. The excuse produces relief and no cry at all.

A lodger. “Dwells” means takes up residence — a settled inhabitant, not a visitor. Sin in a Christian is not an intruder who breaks a window and leaves. It has a room, has been there for years, knows the layout, and pays no rent. That explains why sin in a believer so often looks like habit rather than decision. A lodger doesn’t need inviting each time. Paul does not promise here that you can expel him. He says he is not the real occupier, and then cries out for Someone stronger to deal with him.

Holding two things. The distinction lets a Christian hold “I did that” and “that is not who I am” together. Most can manage only one. Hold the first alone and you get despair: I did it, so that is what I am. Hold the second alone and you get evasion: that’s not me, so it doesn’t count. Paul holds both: full responsibility, and an identity not defined by the failure. The first keeps you honest; the second keeps you standing.

And 1 John 3:9? How does this fit with John’s “No one born of God makes a practice of sinning” (1 John 3:9)? John is describing the settled direction of a life, not a sinless one; the same letter says that anyone who claims to have no sin deceives himself (1 John 1:8). Paul’s man hates the sin he does and fights it. What John rules out is the man who has made peace with it.

A test. After your last serious failure, where did you land? “That wasn’t really me, so there’s no need to make anything of it” — the dodge, which ends the conversation. Or “that was me, and it is also not what I am, and I want it out of my house” — which starts a conversation, and the next thing it produces is a prayer. Paul’s version of this doctrine has a prayer at the end. The counterfeit has a shrug.

verseByVerse.quote: For I know that nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh. For I have the desire to do what is right, but not the ability to carry it out. For I do not do the good I want, but the evil I do not want is what I keep on doing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh.” Paul has the desire to do right but not the ability. He does not do the good he wants, but keeps doing the evil he does not want. The problem is not lack of wanting but lack of power.

A careful correction. Paul starts “nothing good dwells in me” and then narrows it: “that is, in my flesh.” He won’t let the first half stand alone, because something good does dwell in a believer — the Spirit does, and the delight of v. 22. Many Christians say the sentence Paul refused to say: “There is nothing good in me at all.” It sounds humble and is not accurate. A man who believes there is nothing good in him anywhere has no basis for hope and no explanation for why he minds about his sin. The flesh is unimproved and unimprovable; the man is not the flesh.

What “flesh” means. Not the body, as if physical appetites were the problem and the mind were clean. The vice lists include pride, envy, gossip and malice, with no bodily component at all. Flesh is human nature organised without God — the whole self as it worked before grace. A thoroughly ascetic man can be entirely fleshly, and a man enjoying his dinner need not be.

Desire without ability. “I have the desire to do what is right, but not the ability to carry it out.” The desire is real. The ability is absent. That discovery undoes every self-improvement scheme. Most moral advice assumes the missing ingredient is wanting, so it supplies motivation: think of the consequences, remember who you are, try harder. Paul has the motivation and is drowning anyway. You only learn this by trying in earnest — on the fifth time of resolving the same thing with complete sincerity and failing by Thursday.

“Keep on doing.” The tense is continuous: a pattern with a history, the shape of a lifetime. That makes this passage either the most depressing or the most liberating in the New Testament, depending on what comes next.

A test. Take the sin you return to. Which is true: “I don’t really want to stop,” or “I want to stop and can’t”? Be honest; they need different medicine. If the first, the problem is affection, not ability, and the answer is repentance — you are enjoying it and have not yet decided otherwise. If the second, you are exactly where verse 18 is, and your wanting is not nothing. It is strong evidence God has been at work, because the desire was not there before and you did not manufacture it (Philippians 2:13).

No technique. Paul offers no method and no seven steps. He states the problem in its full hopelessness for five more verses, because the answer is not a better strategy but a Person, and he wants you to have exhausted every alternative before he names him.
verseByVerse.note: “Flesh” here means human nature in its fallen state, not the body as such.

verseByVerse.quote: Now if I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells within me. So I find it to be a law that when I want to do right, evil lies close at hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul repeats: if I do what I don’t want, it is sin living in me. And he finds “a law” — a reliable pattern — that “when I want to do right, evil lies close at hand.” The wish for good and the presence of evil come together. The way out is not self-improvement but deliverance.

A law like gravity. In Romans “law” has mostly meant Moses’ law. Here it means a regularity, like the law of gravity — something that operates whether you attend to it or not and makes no exceptions for people trying hard.

The timing. Not just that evil is always around. Evil arrives when the good is wanted. The intention and the opposition appear together, and the second is summoned by the first.

What every Christian has met. You resolve to pray more, and the next week is the busiest of the year. You decide to be patient with a particular person, and within thirty-six hours he becomes much more irritating. You resolve to work on your marriage, and the next fortnight brings more friction than the previous six. Nobody warned you that the decision itself would be the trigger, so you conclude the resolve was insincere, or God isn’t helping, or you imagined it.

Resistance means movement. Paul says it is a law. The moment you move toward the good, something moves to meet you, and that is not evidence the movement was false but that it was real. Nothing opposes a resolution nobody intends to keep. Drifting is downhill and meets no resistance. A man walking with the current is not aware of the river.

A guard. Not every difficulty after a good decision is a spiritual attack, and reading life that way makes people strange and frightened. Sometimes the week really was busy; sometimes the person is having a hard time that has nothing to do with you. Paul describes a pattern, not a decoder for events.

A test. Think of the last time you made a real spiritual resolve and it collapsed within a week or two. What did you conclude? Most of us conclude something about ourselves: I’m not serious, I never change, there’s no point starting again. Verse 21 reads the same evidence differently: the collapse followed the resolve because that is what this law does. The right response is not to stop resolving but to stop being surprised — and to start again today. A man who expects the counter-attack is not defeated by it.

verseByVerse.quote: For I delight in the law of God, in my inner being, but I see in my members another law waging war against the law of my mind and making me captive to the law of sin that dwells in my members.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“I delight in the law of God, in my inner being,” but another law in Paul’s body wages war against the law of his mind and takes him captive to sin. The delight is real, and so is the captivity. This is not hypocrisy but the anguish of a divided person.

The hinge of the debate. “I delight in the law of God” — not merely approve or concede, but delight. That is the language of Psalm 1:2 and Psalm 119. And it is exactly what the unconverted cannot do (8:7). Whatever else is disputed, the man of v. 22 is not that man.

War and captivity. The other law is “waging war” — a sustained campaign with strategy, not a series of accidents. And it is “making me captive,” the word for a soldier taken alive after a lost battle and marched where the victor chooses. Paul does not say he is tempted. He says he is taken prisoner — more humiliating and more accurate.

Where the battle is. The delight is in the inner being; the defeat happens “in my members” — hands, eyes, tongue, where habits live. That is the shape of most Christian failure. Nobody sins because his theology collapsed that morning. His convictions were intact; they just weren’t where the battle was fought.

Defend the right ground. If the war is in the members, that is where the defences belong. That is why the New Testament gives physical, unspiritual-sounding commands: “Flee from sexual immorality” (1 Corinthians 6:18); if your hand causes you to sin, “cut it off” (Matthew 5:30); “make no provision for the flesh” (13:14). Those are about your hands, your feet and your evening. Praying earnestly about a temptation while taking no practical steps to make it harder is fortifying the wrong position. Take one such step this week.

Both are real. A Christian who recognises himself in the captivity often concludes his delight must be false — someone who truly delighted in God’s law wouldn’t keep losing. Paul puts both in one sentence without contradiction. They happen in different places.

A test. Don’t ask whether you always obey; verse 23 has answered that. Ask what you feel about the commandment you keep breaking. Looking at the standard itself — not your failure — is there something in you that says “that is good, and I wish I were like that”? An unconverted man doesn’t think that; he thinks the standard is unreasonable or someone else’s business. If you agree with the very law that is defeating you, that agreement is the deepest thing in you, and it was put there. A prisoner of war has not changed sides. Everything depends on whether Someone is coming for him.

parallels.desc: his delight is in the law of the LORD

verseByVerse.quote: Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord! So then, I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh I serve the law of sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” The answer comes at once: “Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord!” The rescuer is a Person, not a technique. And Paul adds that the conflict goes on — with his mind he serves God’s law, with his flesh the law of sin — but the outcome is certain.

A Christian’s cry. Is this a Christian speaking? Yes, as the argument at vv. 14–15 shows: an unbeliever does not delight in God’s law or cry out to be rid of his sin like this. This is a regenerate man, still in a body where sin lives, longing for the day it is gone.

“Wretched.” Not self-pity. The word means worn out by hardship, battered by a struggle that has gone on too long. The risen Christ uses it of the church at Laodicea, which did not know it applied to them (Revelation 3:17). Paul knows, and he has stopped explaining himself.

A body of death. An old story, repeated for centuries, tells of tyrants who punished a murderer by binding his victim’s corpse to him, face to face, until the decay killed him. Whether or not Paul had it in mind, the picture fits: something dead strapped to a living man, which he cannot untie or outrun. He does not ask to be improved. He asks to be delivered, which is what you ask when the problem is attached to you.

Who, not what. Not which discipline, method, conference or resolution. Every technique has been tried: he knows the law, approves it, delights in it, wills the good, and is still carried off. The only remaining category of answer is a rescuer.

No interval. Cry and answer are separated by a question mark. No dark night, no qualifying period. And the answer is not “Jesus will rescue me one day” but thanks, in the present, for something already true — what a man says looking back at a rescue.

The war restated after the thanks. Paul does not announce that the struggle is over. He restates it: mind serving God’s law, flesh serving sin’s. Putting the tension after the thanksgiving says the deliverance is certain and not yet complete. You may be rescued and still be carrying the body. Chapter 8 opens on this same man, and its first word is “no condemnation.”

A test. What have you been asking for? If your prayers about your besetting sin are requests for equipment — help me try harder, give me strength to keep the resolution, make me more disciplined — you are still asking “what.” The prayer of this verse is different: the cry of someone who has given up on himself and wants a Person to come and get him. Pray it today, in those words, and then thank God for Jesus Christ our Lord. Most Christians don’t pray it until they have exhausted the other kind, which is why God so often lets them be exhausted.

That is a Christian. Wretched, bound to a corpse, and thanking God in the same breath — not a contradiction. Every other religion answers “who will deliver me?” with an instruction. The gospel answers with a Person, and then gives him to you.

7.text: <sup>1</sup>Or do you not know, brothers —for I am speaking to those who know the law—that the law is binding on a person only as long as he lives?<sup>2</sup>For a married woman is bound by law to her husband while he lives, but if her husband dies she is released from the law of marriage.<sup>3</sup>Accordingly, she will be called an adulteress if she lives with another man while her husband is alive. But if her husband dies, she is free from that law, and if she marries another man she is not an adulteress.<sup>4</sup>Likewise, my brothers, you also have died to the law through the body of Christ, so that you may belong to another, to him who has been raised from the dead, in order that we may bear fruit for God.<sup>5</sup>For while we were living in the flesh, our sinful passions, aroused by the law, were at work in our members to bear fruit for death.<sup>6</sup>But now we are released from the law, having died to that which held us captive, so that we serve in the new way of the Spirit and not in the old way of the written code.<sup>7</sup>What then shall we say? That the law is sin? By no means! Yet if it had not been for the law, I would not have known sin. For I would not have known what it is to covet if the law had not said, “You shall not covet.”<sup>8</sup>But sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, produced in me all kinds of covetousness. For apart from the law, sin lies dead.<sup>9</sup>I was once alive apart from the law, but when the commandment came, sin came alive and I died.<sup>10</sup>The very commandment that promised life proved to be death to me.<sup>11</sup>For sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me.<sup>12</sup>So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good.<sup>13</sup>Did that which is good, then, bring death to me? By no means! It was sin, producing death in me through what is good, in order that sin might be shown to be sin, and through the commandment might become sinful beyond measure.<sup>14</sup>For we know that the law is spiritual, but I am of the flesh, sold under sin.<sup>15</sup>For I do not understand my own actions. For I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate.<sup>16</sup>Now if I do what I do not want, I agree with the law, that it is good.<sup>17</sup>So now it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells within me.<sup>18</sup>For I know that nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh. For I have the desire to do what is right, but not the ability to carry it out.<sup>19</sup>For I do not do the good I want, but the evil I do not want is what I keep on doing.<sup>20</sup>Now if I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells within me.<sup>21</sup>So I find it to be a law that when I want to do right, evil lies close at hand.<sup>22</sup>For I delight in the law of God, in my inner being,<sup>23</sup>but I see in my members another law waging war against the law of my mind and making me captive to the law of sin that dwells in my members.<sup>24</sup>Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?<sup>25</sup>Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord! So then, I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh I serve the law of sin.

8.title: No Condemnation, All Glory
8.overview:
Romans 8 is the mountain peak of the New Testament. Commentators across twenty centuries have reached for superlatives and still found them inadequate. It begins with "no condemnation" and ends with "no separation" — and between those two impossibilities of loss, it contains the fullest and most glorious account of the Christian life available in Scripture: the Spirit, adoption, the groaning of creation, the golden chain of redemption, and the love of God from which nothing in the universe can separate us.

The movement of the chapter is from liberation (vv. 1–17) through present suffering (vv. 18–27) to eternal security (vv. 28–39). In each movement, the Spirit is central: He liberates (vv. 1–11), he adopts (vv. 14–17), he intercedes (vv. 26–27). And over all of it stands the sovereign love of a God who foreknew, predestined, called, justified, and will glorify — a chain that has never had a broken link and never will.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — No Condemnation: Life in the Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus." One sentence — and the whole of the gospel's comfort is here. Not less condemnation. Not reduced condemnation. No condemnation. The verdict is absolute, unconditional, and permanent. It rests not on the quality of the believer's life on any given day but on the finished work of Christ and the irreversible union with him by faith.

The reason for the "no condemnation" is the "law of the Spirit of life" which has set the believer free from "the law of sin and death" (v. 2). This is not two different legal codes but two different powers — the power of the Spirit that gives life versus the power of sin that produces death. Christ condemned sin in the flesh (v. 3) — He bore its penalty, exhausted its power, stripped it of its right to condemn — so that the Spirit-empowered believer might fulfil the righteous requirement of the law (v. 4).

The contrast between "flesh" and "Spirit" in vv. 5–11 is not between body and soul — Paul is not a Gnostic. It is between life oriented around the self and its capacities (flesh) and life oriented around God and his Spirit (Spirit). The mind set on the flesh is death; the mind set on the Spirit is life and peace. The Christian is not defined by the flesh but by the Spirit — "you, however, are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if in fact the Spirit of God dwells in you" (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology:
Definitive Justification and Ongoing Assurance

Romans 8:1 is the permanent foundation of the Reformed doctrine of assurance. The condemnation that does not exist for those in Christ is not merely past (sins before conversion) but total: nothing from the past, present, or future can generate condemnation for the one who is in Christ. This is because justification is not a process but an event — a forensic declaration that has been made and cannot be unmade. The Christian may sin grievously; she is not beyond discipline, but she is not in danger of condemnation. The Spirit she has received is the guarantee (v. 11) that what began in justification will be completed in glorification.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Jewish legal system that Paul's readers knew well had a concept of condemnation — the verdict of guilty rendered by a court against one who had violated the law. Paul takes this forensic language and applies it to the ultimate court: the tribunal of God. The verdict of "no condemnation" is the legal declaration of the divine Judge that the case is closed, the penalty has been paid, and the accused walks free — permanently. Now: Countless Christians live under a cloud of functional condemnation — not doubting their doctrinal justification but unable to feel free, perpetually haunted by past sins, unable to receive grace without qualifying it. Romans 8:1 is the word that cuts through all of this: not less condemnation, not reduced condemnation — none. Take it in. Live from it.

verseByVerse.quote: There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. For the law of the Spirit of life has set you free in Christ Jesus from the law of sin and death. — Romans 8:1–2
verseByVerse.commentary:
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.” Those united to Christ will never face God’s sentence, because it fell on Christ. And the Spirit, who gives life, has set them free from the power of sin and death.

“Therefore” — to whom? It reaches back not to a triumphant paragraph but to a man crying out that he is wretched and keeps doing what he hates (7:24). That is who this sentence is addressed to. He has not improved or turned a corner. He has cried out, and the answer is: no condemnation.

“Now.” Not one day, not when the struggle is resolved. Now — on the same page as the groaning, to a man who has just called his life captivity. Paul could have made this a reward for progress, and he wrote “now” instead. In Greek the sentence even begins with the denial: “None — therefore — now — condemnation.”

Nothing left to serve. “Condemnation” includes not only the guilty verdict but the sentence that follows. A man can be acquitted and still ruined by costs. This is an acquittal with no outstanding liability of any kind.

A footnote. Some older translations add “who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit.” Those are Paul’s words — in v. 4 — but the earliest and best manuscripts lack them here; a scribe’s eye likely picked them up from below. It matters. In v. 1 they would make the promise conditional on the quality of your walking. In v. 4 they describe the result of what God has done. The sentence stands unqualified.

Living under a cloud. Many believers hold this doctrine and live under something else. They cannot receive assurance without adding “yes, but I need to be more consistent.” They approach God as though reapplying each time. They find it easier to believe they are forgiven than that they are welcome. And when something goes wrong, their first instinct is to ask what they are being punished for. That last instinct reads providence through a cancelled verdict. Whatever the hard thing is, it is not God collecting a debt, because there is no debt.

Three things not to confuse. Condemnation, a judicial verdict, is gone entirely. Discipline remains, and it is evidence of sonship, not wrath: “the Lord disciplines the one he loves” (Hebrews 12:6). Consequences often remain in full. A man may be wholly forgiven and still lose the marriage or live with the conviction on his record. Telling him his forgiveness must be doubtful because his circumstances are hard is one of the cruellest mistakes a Christian can make.

A test. Say it in the first person: “There is no condemnation for me.” Listen to what your mind supplies next. If a “but” arrives, or an urge to add something about trying harder, that is the cloud. It is not unbelief; it is the residue of a marriage that has ended (see on 7:1–2), and it goes the way residues go — by being noticed and contradicted with this verse, again and again. Chapter 7 ended with a man tied to a corpse asking if anyone was coming. Chapter 8 begins with “no.”
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add “who walk not according to the flesh,” and that some read “me” for “you.”

verseByVerse.quote: For God has done what the law, weakened by the flesh, could not do. By sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin, he condemned sin in the flesh, in order that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit. — Romans 8:3–4
verseByVerse.commentary:
God did what the law could not do, because the law was weakened by our sinful nature. He sent his own Son in a real human body like ours, but without sin, as an offering for sin, and “condemned sin in the flesh.” He did this so that what the law rightly requires would be fulfilled in us, who now live by the Spirit.

Weakened by the flesh. The fault was not in the law but in the material it worked with. Perfect instructions are powerless before a man who cannot follow them. The law failed the way a ladder fails a man with no legs — which is to say, it did not fail.

“In the likeness of sinful flesh.” Paul places the word carefully. Not “in the likeness of flesh” — that would make the incarnation a costume, as some taught within a generation. Not “in sinful flesh” — that would put sin in the Son. Real flesh, in the same weakness and mortality as ours, without the sin. If what he took was not truly ours, he did not redeem ours; if it were sinful, he would have needed saving himself. He had to be near enough to be one of us and clean enough to help.

Where the condemnation went. Verse 1: no condemnation for those in Christ. Verse 3: God “condemned sin in the flesh.” Same root. The condemnation was not cancelled or waived; it was carried out. There is none in verse 1 because there was some in verse 3. And “in the flesh” is the arena: sin had held human nature since Eden and never been beaten there. God came into that territory, in that material, and beat it there — the second Adam winning on our ground what the first lost.

Fulfilled in us. Some readers, especially in the Reformed tradition, take this to mean Christ’s obedience counted as ours: he kept the law, and his record is credited to those in him. That is true, and v. 1 rests on it. But here the more likely reading is that Paul means the obedience the Spirit works in believers, because he goes straight on to describe those who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit. The two belong together. Christ’s righteousness counted to us is the ground; the Spirit’s work in us is the result. Note the wording: “in us,” not “by us.” The standard is not lowered. What it requires actually gets done, and the Spirit is the agent. That answers chapter 7: there a man had the desire without the ability; here the ability comes from outside him.

A test. Facing a sin you have repeatedly lost to, what do you reach for? If it is your own determination — a firmer resolve, a better system, a promise to yourself — you are using chapter 7’s resources, and the outcome is on record. Ask instead: what has been given to me that I am not using? The Spirit is not a reserve for emergencies. He is the standing condition of a Christian. Ask for his help before the temptation comes, not after.

“God has done.” The law could not, the flesh could not, chapter 7 could not. Then the subject of the sentence changes, and everything after it is in a different tense: not what must be attempted but what has been accomplished, in real flesh, on our ground, by Someone else.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “for sin” can also be rendered “as a sin offering.”

parallels.desc: the sin offering

verseByVerse.quote: For those who live according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh, but those who live according to the Spirit set their minds on the things of the Spirit. For to set the mind on the flesh is death, but to set the mind on the Spirit is life and peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who live by the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh; those who live by the Spirit set their minds on the things of the Spirit. The mind set on the flesh is death; the mind set on the Spirit is “life and peace.” The question is which way your mind habitually points.

“Set the mind.” The word covers more than thinking — what you care about, what you are drawn to, your whole disposition. It is where a person goes when nothing is requiring him to be anywhere. Not the stray thought on a train, but the direction a compass needle returns to when left alone.

The settings show in the gaps. Not at church or work, where the agenda is set for you, but in the unstructured minutes. What do you reach for when you wake at night? What fills the ten minutes in a queue, the drive with the radio off, the moment your hand goes to your phone before you’ve decided anything? Those intervals are the readout. A mind released goes where it lives.

“Is death.” Not “leads to” or “risks” death — is. A life organised around the self is not awaiting a sentence; it is already the thing it will be judged for, as drowning is not the punishment for being underwater.

“Life and peace.” We might have written “life and holiness.” Paul writes peace — the exact answer to chapter 7, a chapter of war: a law waging war, a man taken captive, a self divided. What ends the war is not a stronger will but a mind no longer set on the thing that was fighting it.

The battle is decided earlier. We think the fight against sin happens at the moment of temptation, and by then it is largely over. The mind arrives already set, and it was set during the hours that seemed to be about nothing. What a Christian feeds his attention on is not a minor matter of taste.

A test. Look at where your attention went yesterday — not your duties, your attention: the reading, watching, scrolling, the conversations you sought out. Add up the hours honestly. What would a stranger conclude about what you care about? This is not a call to joylessness. But nobody has set his mind on the Spirit by accident while setting his hours on everything else. Change one hour this week (cf. Colossians 3:1–2).

A guard. Paul describes two kinds of people, not a grading of Christians by concentration. The believer whose mind wanders in prayer, who finds Scripture hard going this month, is not the man whose mind is set on the flesh. The proof is that he minds. A mind truly set on the flesh does not lie awake troubled by how little it wants God. Wanting to want him is already the needle pointing the right way, however unsteadily.

verseByVerse.quote: For the mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God, for it does not submit to God's law; indeed, it cannot. Those who are in the flesh cannot please God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The mind set on the flesh is “hostile to God” and does not submit to his law — “indeed, it cannot.” Those in the flesh cannot please God. Without the Spirit, a person is not just unwilling but unable to turn to God.

Hostile. Paul does not mean everyone outside Christ consciously hates God; many are polite about him, some religious. He describes an orientation, not an emotion — like two magnets set against each other, so that the closer God comes, the more the flesh turns away. You can see it when God stops being a topic and starts making a claim. Discussed as an idea, he is interesting. Introduced as Someone with rights over the listener, the temperature changes.

“It cannot.” Paul could have said it does not submit — a statement about behaviour. He says it cannot — a statement about capacity. That is what makes the Christian faith unlike every programme of moral improvement. The natural man is not equipped to obey God, as a stone is not equipped to float.

Not an excuse. This inability does not reduce guilt, because it is not imposed from outside. It is the inability of someone who cannot bring himself to love a person he has decided to despise — real, total, and his own fault. “I was constitutionally incapable of wanting to” is no defence in any human relationship, and none here.

Why arguments don’t convert. If unbelief were a shortage of information, better arguments would fix it, and the intelligent would convert at higher rates, which they don’t. If it were lack of motivation, stronger appeals would fix it. Paul locates it in capacity. That is why the New Testament describes conversion as new birth, resurrection, a heart of flesh for a heart of stone (Ezekiel 36:26; John 3:3). Those are not exaggerations; they are the right language for an inability removed.

Praying for someone who won’t believe. You have explained it, lived it before them for years, answered objections, and new ones came. Verse 7 tells you why — not that you argued badly, but that what is needed is a change no persuasion can produce. That discourages only until you notice that the work is God’s, it is exactly what he does, and the person you pray for is not a harder case than you were (John 6:44). Keep praying, and keep loving them.

Why this doesn’t describe you. Read verse 8 and ask why it no longer describes you, since it once did. Nothing in your capacity changed by your own effort. Someone made the stone float. That is why Paul turns at once to “You, however” (v. 9). The bleak paragraph is there so that you know what it cost to find yourself in the next one.

verseByVerse.quote: You, however, are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if in fact the Spirit of God dwells in you. Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him. But if Christ is in you, although the body is dead because of sin, the Spirit is life because of righteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“You, however, are not in the flesh but in the Spirit,” if God’s Spirit lives in you. Anyone without the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him. And if Christ is in you, your body is still mortal because of sin, but the Spirit is life because of righteousness.

Three names, one presence. The Spirit of God dwells in you; anyone without the Spirit of Christ is not his; Christ is in you. Paul moves between them without explanation — the New Testament assumes the Trinity rather than arguing it. And to have the Spirit is to have Christ. He is not a lesser substitute while the Lord is elsewhere. The indwelling Spirit is how the risen Christ is present with his people.

A sentence that troubles consciences. “Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him.” It is a real dividing line. But it is often read by the wrong person — the anxious believer, who takes it as an exam he is probably failing — while the man who should be searched by it reads past it.

What it does not say. Not “anyone who does not feel the Spirit,” or has not had a particular experience, spoken in a particular way, or can point to a dated moment. Paul describes a possession, not a sensation, and possessions are verified by their effects.

How would I know? Not by introspection, which mostly reports on your temperament and how you slept. Look for effects the New Testament names. Do you call God Father and mean it (v. 15)? Do you love Christians you have nothing else in common with (1 John 3:14)? Do you mind about your sin, more than you used to? Is Christ more precious to you than he was at twenty? Does Scripture sometimes speak as though Someone were behind it? None is spectacular. All are supernatural, because nothing in the flesh produces them (vv. 7–8).

A test. Don’t ask whether you feel the Spirit. Ask where these things came from. If you find a desire for God you did not manufacture, that survives your worst weeks, and that you could not switch off if you tried, the question is not whether you have the Spirit but how else you would account for it. Thank God for it.

The body is still dying. Verse 10 admits: “the body is dead because of sin.” The Spirit does not fix everything now. Your body is ageing as you read and will fail. Any teaching that implies enough faith should keep a believer well has not read this verse. Yet both halves stand together — the body dead, the Spirit life — the shape of the Christian life: decaying and being renewed at once, sometimes felt on the same afternoon (2 Corinthians 4:16). Paul has conceded the body to death; next he says what will happen to it afterwards.

verseByVerse.quote: If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If the Spirit of the God who raised Jesus from the dead lives in you, then God will also give life to your mortal bodies through that Spirit. The same power that raised Jesus will raise you, body and all.

How Paul names God. Not the Almighty or the Creator but “him who raised Jesus from the dead” — twice in one sentence. Not elegant, and not meant to be. He fixes your attention on one historical act and tells you the same power lives in your body now.

The harder thing is done. Every Christian has the Spirit (v. 9). So the God who already did the harder thing has placed the means of the easier one inside you — the same reasoning as 5:9–10.

Your mortal body. Not your soul or some refined essence that survives the wreck. The body reading this — the bad knee, the thinning hair, the scan results, the one that tires at four in the afternoon. Christianity does not offer escape from the body. It offers the body back, repaired.

More Paul than Plato. Ask a congregation what happens when a believer dies and you will hear that the soul goes to be with the Lord — true (Philippians 1:23), but not the main thing the New Testament says. The hope of this letter is a raised body in a renewed creation, and the deposit on it is already lodged in the flesh that is wearing out.

How to regard your body now. If it is destined to be raised, it is not a shell to be resented or despised — nor something to worship and defend against time. It is going somewhere. That is steadier ground than either the contempt or the panic our culture offers. Look after it as something God means to keep.

For the ill and the ageing. If you are ill, or ageing badly, or watching someone you love dismantled by a named disease, this verse does not say the body doesn’t matter. It says it matters so much that God intends to raise it. The decline is real; Paul calls the body “mortal” in the same breath. But the Spirit in you is the Spirit who was in the tomb that Sunday, and he is there not only as comfort during the decline but as a deposit against its reversal. A God who has gone to that trouble will not lose track of the address.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–17 — Heirs with Christ: The Spirit of Adoption
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Spirit does not merely set us free from condemnation; he establishes our identity as children of God. "For you did not receive the spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, 'Abba! Father!'" (v. 15). The word Abba is the intimate Aramaic term for father — the word a child uses at the family table, in the moment of fear, in the unselfconscious familiarity of the parental relationship. Jesus used it in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36). His Spirit now enables his adopted brothers and sisters to use it too.

The adoption of which Paul speaks is not merely a legal status (though it is that — full legal rights as sons and daughters, co-heirs with Christ). It is a relational reality experienced in the present: the Spirit bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God. This inner witness — not our feelings but the Spirit's testimony — is the ground of Christian assurance at the deepest level. When we doubt our standing, when darkness presses in, when God feels distant — the Spirit within is still crying "Abba!" on our behalf.

"Heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ" (v. 17) — the inheritance is nothing less than God himself, shared with the Son. Everything that belongs to Christ by right of his eternal sonship is ours by right of our adoption. This is the logic behind Paul's bewildering statement in 1 Corinthians 3:21 — "all things are yours." The adopted child of God is heir to a universe, co-inheritor of a new creation. The suffering of the present age (v. 17 — "provided we suffer with him") is the path to that glory, not its obstacle.

The section does not begin there, however, and the two verses that open it are the hinge on which the rest turns. Paul first cancels an obligation: we are debtors — but not to the flesh. The old master has no further claim, which means every demand it still makes is made without authority. Then comes the one command in the passage, and it is not gentle: by the Spirit, put to death the deeds of the body (v. 13). This is the letter’s answer to the defeat of chapter 7, and it holds two things together that we habitually separate — the killing is genuinely ours to do, and the power to do it is not ours at all. And verse 14 then supplies the link to everything that follows: those who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God. The mortification of sin is not the price of sonship. It is the evidence of it, and the family likeness of people who are being led.
verseByVerse.theology:
Adoption and Assurance

The doctrine of adoption (huiothesia) is one of J.I. Packer's great themes in Knowing God: he argues that adoption is a higher privilege than justification, because justification changes our status before the court while adoption brings us into the family. Reformed writing on the Holy Spirit develops the same insight: the Spirit's primary work in the believer is to mediate the Trinitarian relationship — drawing the child into the love that the Father and the Son share, enabling her to cry "Abba" with the same intimacy that the eternal Son has always known. Assurance, at its deepest level, is not confidence in our own faith or our own experience; it is the Spirit-given knowledge that we are beloved children of the Father.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Roman adoption law in the first century was clear: an adopted son received full legal rights, the old debts were cancelled, the new family name was his, and the inheritance was secured. Paul's readers would have understood immediately the thoroughness of what adoption meant. No second-class status, no probationary period — full sonship, full inheritance, from the moment of adoption. Now: The "spirit of slavery" (v. 15) that produces fear is the functional religion of much nominal Christianity — the haunting sense that God is primarily a demanding judge to be appeased, that our standing depends on our performance, that we must earn our place at the table. Romans 8:15 is the antidote: not slaves, sons. Not fear, Abba. Not earning, inheriting.

verseByVerse.quote: So then, brothers, we are debtors, not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh. For if you live according to the flesh you will die, but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live. — Romans 8:12–13
verseByVerse.commentary:
We owe the flesh nothing. If you live by the flesh, you will die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live. Killing sin is our task, and it is done by the Spirit’s power, not by willpower alone.

An unfinished sentence. “We are debtors, not to the flesh…” and Paul stops. The obvious completion — “but to the Spirit” — is left for you to supply. You owe the flesh nothing. Every demand it still makes is made without standing, by a creditor whose debt was settled and who hopes you haven’t read the paperwork.

“Put to death.” A violent word: not manage, moderate or review. And continuous: keep putting to death. There is no version of the Christian life where this is dealt with once and never returns. John Owen’s summary of this verse is famous: be killing sin, or it will be killing you.

How, concretely. Most sin is not a decision but the last link in a chain, and by the time you reach the decision the outcome was settled several links earlier. So the fight is mainly upstream, where you still think clearly. Map the chain. Take the sin you keep returning to and ask what reliably comes before it: the hour, the room, the device, your state — tired, alone, resentful, unaccountable, just criticised, just successful. Most people can name the sin instantly and have never mapped what precedes it, which is why the same battle is lost the same way for years.

Attack the chain. That is what Jesus meant by cutting off and tearing out (Matthew 5:29–30): not mutilation, but removing access, nearly always possible and nearly always inconvenient. It is why the New Testament often says “flee” rather than “resist” (1 Corinthians 6:18; 2 Timothy 2:22). Some temptations you stand and fight; with others, standing to fight is the mistake.

By the Spirit. This keeps it from being self-improvement in religious language. An unbeliever could take the same practical steps. The difference is dependence: praying while you do them, and wanting not only to stop failing but to please a Person. A man can lock his phone away in the flesh’s strength, and the flesh will find another route within a month. The same act done in prayer, asking God for the desire you don’t yet have, is mortification.

A guard. “If you live according to the flesh you will die” can sound like a threat over every bad week. Paul describes a direction of life, not a tally of failures (see on 2:7–8). The chapter assumes you lose battles. The question is which way you face. A man putting sin to death badly and repeatedly is doing what this verse describes. A man who has stopped and made his peace is not.

A test with a pen. Name the sin. Write down the four things that usually happen before it. Choose one and make it harder this week — not the sin, the link before it. That is putting something to death rather than resolving about it. Both halves stand: in your own strength you will fail (chapter 7), and if you wait without lifting a hand, nothing happens either, because the verb is addressed to you. The Spirit does not do it instead of you. He does it through you, and the hands are yours.

parallels.desc: put to death what is earthly in you

verseByVerse.quote: For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God. For you did not receive the spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, "Abba! Father!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
All who are led by God’s Spirit are God’s sons. You did not receive a spirit of slavery that makes you afraid again, but the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, “Abba! Father!” Being led by the Spirit is the evidence that you are already God’s child.

Read the right way round. Paul does not say those led by the Spirit become sons, but that they are sons. The leading is the symptom; sonship the condition. Read backwards, it becomes a treadmill: am I being led enough to count?

What “led” means here. Not mainly guidance on decisions — which job, which house, which person. The context is v. 13: putting sin to death. The leading is being drawn, over time, toward holiness. A Christian who has never had a strong impression about a career move but has been slowly turning from the same sin for ten years is exactly whom this verse describes.

Falling back into fear. “Back” describes a relapse, the standing temptation of the Christian life. Nobody decides to relate to God as a slave; it happens by drift. It feels like being on probation — God broadly disappointed, the relationship under review, this week’s performance the evidence. That is the spirit of slavery, and it is not what you received.

Abba. Aramaic, the word used at home by a child who has not learned to be careful. Not baby-talk — grown men used it of their fathers — but unguarded. Paul writes in Greek to Greek speakers and leaves this one word untranslated, because they were already using it. Someone had taught Gentile converts an Aramaic word they had no other use for, and it is not hard to see why. Jesus used it in Gethsemane, face down, with the cup before him: “Abba, Father” (Mark 14:36) — the only place the Gospels record it on his lips, at the worst hour of his life. So it was never a word for good days. It is what the Son said in the dark, and the Spirit puts it in your mouth in the same conditions.

“We cry.” A strong word — not a recitation but something like an involuntary shout. The evidence of adoption is not a doctrine affirmed calmly but what comes out of you when you are frightened.

A test. What comes out of you in real fear — the phone at two in the morning, the scan result, the child late home and not answering? If the reflex, even wordless, is toward God rather than away — reaching for a Father rather than bracing for a Judge — that reflex was put there. No unconverted person produces it under pressure. Fear strips away what is learned and leaves what is there.

If “father” is a hard word for you. If your own father was frightening, absent or cruel, this verse hands you the warmest word in the language and it feels cold. Two things. God is called “Father of the fatherless” (Psalm 68:5) — a claim made in the absence of good fathers, not borrowed from them. And the comparison runs the other way from what we assume. God is the original; every human father is a more or less faithful copy. Yours may have been a poor likeness. That tells you nothing about the original, and this verse invites you to meet him. Begin your next prayer with the word “Father.”
verseByVerse.note: In Roman law an adopted son received full rights and inheritance, as if born into the family. “Abba” is the Aramaic word for “father,” used within the family.

parallels.desc: sons of the living God

verseByVerse.quote: The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God.” Two witnesses agree: your own sense of belonging to God, and the Holy Spirit himself. Assurance rests not on our feelings alone but on God’s own testimony.

Two witnesses. Israel’s law required two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15), and Paul has used courtroom language since chapter 1. Your own sense of being God’s child would not suffice alone; you are an interested party. A second Witness has been called, and he is not.

“What does this feel like?” Many faithful Christians conclude that whatever Paul describes has passed them by. But he does not describe a voice, a dated experience, or something you could arrange at a meeting. And “bears witness” is present and continuous — a testimony going on quietly underneath your Christian life, mostly below the level you notice.

A settledness. What it usually produces is not a feeling but a settledness: reading a promise God makes to his children and finding it does not bounce off — taking it as meant for you without arguing yourself into it. The instinct to reach for a Father under pressure (v. 15). The plain fact that you care whether God is pleased with you at all. None announces itself as a witness. All of it is one.

Heard in your own prayer. The Spirit’s witness is not usually a separate voice beside your thoughts. It is heard in them. When you pray “Father” and mean it, you are not working up a conviction and hoping the Spirit confirms it. That prayer is the confirmation. You may have been looking for the second Witness while he was speaking with your mouth.

Two guards. First, this cannot be manufactured and should not be faked. Teaching that presses people to claim an inner assurance they don’t have produces despair or pretence. If you lack it, the remedy is not to work at feeling it; assurance is God’s gift, often given in his time to those who have walked with him long. Second, the inner witness is no licence to ignore evidence. John wrote a whole letter of tests — do you love the brothers, keep his commandments, confess the Son — “that you may know” (1 John 5:13). Inner witness and outward fruit are the two witnesses agreeing. A man who claims deep assurance and whose life shows nothing of Christ has one witness, and it is the interested party.

A test. Don’t search your feelings; notice what you already do. Do you call him Father when nobody is listening? Does your sin trouble you as an offence against Someone rather than a broken rule? When you hear that God loves his children, does some part of you include yourself? Those are not achievements. They are the second Witness, testifying, mostly while you were not attending.

Children. Paul shifts from “sons” (v. 15), the legal word of adoption and rights, to “children,” the word of birth and family. The court has ruled, and the house has taken you in. It is the second that the Spirit spends his time telling you about.

verseByVerse.quote: ...and if children, then heirs — heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ, provided we suffer with him in order that we may also be glorified with him. — Romans 8:17
verseByVerse.commentary:
If we are God’s children, we are also his heirs — “heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ” — provided we suffer with him, so that we may also be glorified with him. Suffering is not the price of glory; it is the road to it, the road Christ walked first.

Heirs of God. An heir usually inherits what the deceased owned. Paul does not say we inherit God’s possessions but that we are heirs of God. The inheritance is not a portfolio; it is God himself.

Levi’s portion. Israel had a picture of this. When the land was divided, the other tribes received territory — this valley, that ridge, the olive terraces, the well. Levi received no land at all, and the reason given was the highest honour: “the LORD is their inheritance” (Deuteronomy 18:2). The others were given things God had made. Levi was given God. Paul tells every adopted child in Rome that they are all Levites now. And everything else you have can be taken by a diagnosis, a market, a war, or time. An inheritance that is God cannot be repossessed.

Fellow heirs with Christ. Not a junior share for newcomers. Joint heirs. What you receive is not calibrated to your service, maturity, or how well your Christian life has gone. It is calibrated to his. What the Son inherits by right of being the Son, the adopted receive by right of adoption — with no clause reducing the portion of those who came late or did badly.

“Provided we suffer with him.” This has frightened people it was never aimed at — usually those already suffering, who hear a demand for more. But Paul does not say “provided you suffer enough” or “of a religious kind.” He says suffer with him, and the weight is on the last word. It is not the quantity that counts but the company. Christ is not watching your suffering from a distance. He is in it, and he has been in worse.

A guard. Suffering with Christ does not mean accepting every affliction and staying put. It does not mean a woman should remain in a house where she is being harmed, that illness should go untreated, or that injustice should be borne quietly when it could be addressed. Paul avoided danger repeatedly, appealed to Caesar, and was let down a wall in a basket (Acts 9:25; 25:11). The verse describes the shape of the road, not a duty to seek wounds.

A test. Think of the hardest thing you have carried in five years. Has it driven you toward God or away? Not whether it felt good. Whether over time you have prayed more honestly, held this world more loosely, and longed for the day of glory more than before. That is what suffering with him looks like from inside — not a sign of punishment but of walking the road the Heir himself walked. Glory comes last in the sentence. The Son was not offered it without the road either.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–30 — Future Glory: Groaning, Intercession, and the Golden Chain
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The present sufferings are real — Paul does not minimise them — but they are not worth comparing to the glory that is to be revealed (v. 18). The entire creation groans, longing for the liberation that the resurrection of the children of God will bring. The believer groans too, in the Spirit, longing for the full redemption of the body. And the Spirit himself groans on behalf of believers with groanings too deep for words, interceding according to the will of God. Three levels of groaning: creation, believer, Spirit — all pointed toward the same consummation: the full glory of the children of God in the new creation.

"And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose" (v. 28). This verse has comforted more afflicted souls than almost any other in Scripture — and it has been more abused by careless application than almost any other. Paul is not promising that everything that happens to Christians will feel good or produce obvious benefit. He is promising that the God who is sovereign over all things is working in all things — the good and the bad, the joyful and the painful — toward a single end: the good of those he has called. The suffering is not outside his purposes; it is within them.

The "golden chain" of vv. 29–30 is the most concise summary of the Reformed ordo salutis in Scripture: foreknew, predestined, called, justified, glorified. Five links, each leading inevitably to the next, with no link missing and none reversible. The glorification is in the past tense — "he also glorified" — because it is as certain as if it had already happened. The God who foreknew in eternity past will glorify in eternity future, and nothing can interrupt the chain.
verseByVerse.theology:
Effectual Calling and the Golden Chain

Romans 8:29–30 is the biblical foundation for the Reformed doctrine of election and effectual calling. Foreknowledge here is not merely prior knowledge but prior relational knowing — the same sense in which God "knew" Israel (Amos 3:2) or the Shepherd knows his sheep (John 10:14). Those whom God foreknew with this special, electing love he predestined; those he predestined he called (effectually, inwardly, irresistibly); those he called he justified; those he justified he glorified. The chain is unbreakable. Every link is divine. The reason no one finally falls from grace is not that believers are strong enough to hold on, but that the God who foreknew and called them is powerful enough to keep what he has started.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The groaning of creation in vv. 19–22 draws on the Jewish understanding that the natural world was affected by human sin (Genesis 3:17–18) and will be renewed in the messianic age. Paul extends this vision: not just Israel but the whole creation waits for the redemption of God's children. The gospel is not merely the rescue of souls; it is the renewal of all things. Now: Romans 8:28 is one of the most misused verses in the Christian repertoire — invoked as a quick comfort for minor inconveniences and sometimes grotesquely applied to genuine catastrophe. Used rightly, it is not a promise that things will work out the way we hope; it is the promise of a sovereign God who is working toward his purpose in all things — and his purpose is better than our preferences.

verseByVerse.quote: For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul has done the sum: “the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us.” He does not call suffering small. He says the coming glory is of such a different order that the two cannot be weighed against each other.

“I consider.” The accountant’s verb of this letter — reckon, credit. Paul is not saying he feels his sufferings are light; he has worked it out. And he writes from inside the arithmetic: five times given thirty-nine lashes, three times beaten with rods, once stoned, three times shipwrecked (2 Corinthians 11:24–25). Nobody can say he values suffering cheaply because he has not met it.

Not a balance sheet. Paul does not say the sufferings are small, but that they are not in the same category as the glory — as you cannot weigh a colour against a sound. We often say the good will eventually outweigh the bad, and a grieving person feels the falseness at once: no amount of future pleasantness makes a dead child worth it. Paul is not proposing a trade. He is saying the coming thing makes the comparison itself break down.

Two more things. The sufferings belong to “this present time” — an age that is ending, not a permanent feature of the universe. And the glory is “to be revealed,” the word for drawing back a covering. It exists now and is out of sight. The honest thing to say about the present is not that it is fine, but that the curtain is still up. And it is revealed “to us” — not just a better world to look at, but a transformation of the one looking (v. 29).

Don’t use it as a stick. You can quote Romans 8:18 at a newly widowed woman in a way that is cruel, as though grief should stop making so much of itself. The paragraph forbids that: within eight verses creation groans, believers groan, and the Spirit himself groans. Paul is not asking anyone to minimise. He is putting something on the other side of the scale.

Store it for later. This verse is not a reply to someone’s pain in the first week. It is to be stored in advance and used by the sufferer himself on days when the trouble threatens to become the whole horizon. Notice Paul writes in the first person: “I consider.” He tells the conclusion he has reached about his own troubles, which is far more usable than an instruction about someone else’s.

A test. Take the heaviest thing you are carrying and try to finish this honestly: “Compared with what is coming, this is…” Most of us can’t — not because we doubt the glory, but because we have never spent time on it. We could describe our trouble in detail and couldn’t name four specific things we are promised. The sum needs both figures, and most Christians have only one. So we weigh a vague word against a vivid ache, and the ache wins. Read Revelation 21:1–7 this week and write down four things.

verseByVerse.quote: For the creation waits with eager longing for the revealing of the sons of God. For the creation was subjected to futility, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it, in hope
verseByVerse.commentary:
Creation itself waits eagerly for God’s children to be revealed. It was subjected to futility — not by its own choice, but by God, after Adam’s fall — “in hope.” The world’s brokenness is a sentence God passed, and it has an end.

Craning its neck. The word for “eager longing” is built on the word for “head”: someone craning forward at the front of a crowd on a platform, watching for the train. That is what Paul says the physical universe is doing — not decaying quietly, but waiting with its neck out.

Waiting for us. Creation is not waiting for its own repair but “for the revealing of the sons of God.” We usually think we are waiting for the world to improve. Paul says the world is waiting for us, because its liberation is tied to ours. It went down when we did and comes up the same way.

A hard sentence. “The creation was subjected to futility… because of him who subjected it.” That is God. The thorns of Genesis 3, the earthquakes, the diseases that kill children in countries that did nothing particular to deserve them — Paul traces none of it to blind chance or to the devil, but to God’s judicial act after Adam’s rebellion (Genesis 3:17–19). The honest thing is to let that stand.

Meaningful and bounded. But see what it saves you from. A universe damaged by accident has no one to appeal to and no reason to expect repair. A universe placed under futility by a Judge can be released by the same Judge, and the sentence has an end. Hence the last words: “in hope.” The subjection was passed with a view to release.

Futility. The same word the Greek Old Testament uses throughout Ecclesiastes for “vanity”: breath, vapour, what will not hold still. It is why every achievement has a hollow centre, the beautiful thing decays, the building needs repointing, and the body strong at thirty is not at seventy. Paul is not being pessimistic. He describes a world under sentence, which everyone knows whether or not they have a theology for it.

Your grief at the world. The sense that something is wrong with the way things are — grief at a ruined landscape, anger at a disease that shouldn’t exist, refusal to be reconciled to everything you love being temporary — is not immaturity or a failure to be spiritual. It is agreement with the apostle. Creation is groaning; you are meant to hear it.

A test. When you picture what God has promised, does the physical world appear in it? Many people describe a departure — souls elsewhere, this world discarded. Paul describes an arrival, and a world craning for it. If matter has no place in your hope, it is smaller than this chapter’s. The rivers, mountains and animals are not scenery to be struck at the end of the play. They are waiting to be included.
verseByVerse.note: The creation was subjected to futility when God cursed the ground after Adam’s sin.

parallels.desc: cursed is the ground because of you

verseByVerse.quote: that the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption and obtain the freedom of the glory of the children of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Creation will be “set free from its bondage to corruption” and brought into “the freedom of the glory of the children of God.” God does not plan to abandon the material world but to renew it, alongside his glorified children.

Bondage to decay. “Corruption” here means decay, the process by which things come apart. The apple browns, iron rusts, the photograph fades, memory blurs, the strong man weakens, and every living thing is on a schedule it did not choose. Paul calls it slavery — not an occasional misfortune but a condition nothing here escapes.

Not slowed — ended. Hold the promise against what is actually broken. No more funerals, because nothing left to bury. No scans, no waiting rooms, no results delivered by a doctor who has learned to arrange his face. No more watching a mind go while the body remains, or a body go while the mind remains. No more photographs of people you can’t ring. What this verse abolishes is not unpleasantness in general but the machinery by which everything good is taken from you.

Brought into our freedom. Creation is brought into the very liberty of God’s glorified children, as though the family estate were restored with the family. It is Genesis in reverse: the ground was cursed because of a man (Genesis 3:17), and it is released because of redeemed men. Both times the creature and its home go together.

A garden at both ends. The Bible opens in a garden and closes in a garden city, with a river, a tree, and leaves “for the healing of the nations” (Revelation 22:1–2). It does not open in a garden and close in a cloud. Any version of Christian hope in which believers finally leave the material world behind has the last chapter wrong.

Work on the world matters. If God means to redeem the material creation, work on material things is not a lower kind of work. The farmer, surgeon, engineer, conservationist, the man who repairs things properly — none is doing something merely temporary while the spiritual people do the real work. They are doing to a corner of creation, in a small way, what God intends for all of it. Their work is still not permanent; it is a signpost, which is a serious thing to be. Do yours well.

Will animals be there? Scripture pictures the new creation with animals in it: “The wolf shall dwell with the lamb” (Isa 11:6). Whether a particular pet will be raised, Scripture does not say, and we should not claim more than it does. But the hope of renewal shapes how we treat the world now. God put man in the garden “to work it and keep it” (Gen 2:15), and that rules out both worshipping the earth and wasting it carelessly.

A test of attention. Next time something in creation stops you — a sky, a piece of music, the face of someone asleep — notice the ache that comes with it, wishing it would hold still. That ache is not greed. It is the right response to beauty under sentence, and this verse answers it: the sentence is being lifted. What you love will not be taken permanently. It will be given back, without the decay.

verseByVerse.quote: For we know that the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now. And not only the creation, but we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole creation groans like a woman in labour. And we who have “the firstfruits of the Spirit” groan too, as we wait eagerly for our adoption — “the redemption of our bodies.” The groaning is not despair but labour: painful, and going somewhere.

Two kinds of screaming. In a hospital corridor, cries from a ward where something is ending and from a delivery room where something is beginning can sound the same. Paul says this world’s groan is the second kind. That is a claim about meaning, not volume. Labour pains are not less painful for being productive. And labour often gets worse before it ends; nobody promises the groaning of this age will taper off gently. The image is not for hurrying people.

We groan too. Paul puts Christians in the same sentence as earthquakes and decay — and not the immature or weak in faith, but “we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit.” The groaning is not evidence that your Christianity has gone wrong. It is evidence the Spirit is in you.

Firstfruits. A harvest word: the first sheaf brought in, genuinely the harvest and clearly not all of it (Leviticus 23:10). A man who has never tasted something doesn’t know what he is missing; the taste creates the hunger. So the Spirit does not settle you into contentment with this world. He makes you less at home in it. That is why the ache often grows as a Christian matures, and why the godliest people you have known were often the most homesick. If this world satisfies you less the older you get in faith, you have not lost ground. You have been given more of the firstfruits.

Adopted, and waiting for adoption. Verse 15 says we have received the Spirit of adoption. Here we wait for adoption — “the redemption of our bodies.” Both true. The adoption is legally complete and not yet fully experienced. The paperwork is signed; the child has not yet come home.

Our bodies. Not “our souls,” which most Christians would predict. The thing awaited is the part of you visibly losing. Your soul is not the part with a diagnosis.

A test. When you feel the groan — the flat Sunday evening, the sense that nothing here is quite it, grief without a clear cause — what do you conclude? Many treat it as a fault: ingratitude, failure to count blessings, something to medicate with distraction. Paul treats it as the Spirit’s work in you, running in the same direction as the groaning of the universe. You are not malfunctioning; you are in labour with everything God has made.
