Read Exodus 9:15–16 whole, spoken at the seventh plague: “For by now I could have put out my hand and struck you and your people with pestilence, and you would have been cut off from the earth. But for this purpose I have raised you up…” God is explaining to Pharaoh why he is still alive. It is not an announcement that a man was made in order to be destroyed. It accounts for the continued existence of a man who should already be dead — the patience Paul will speak of in v. 22.

The hardening. Exodus has both halves. God says he will harden Pharaoh’s heart (4:21; 7:3) and does (9:12; 10:1; 14:4). Pharaoh hardens his own heart again and again (8:15, 32; 9:34). In the narrative, through the first five plagues it is Pharaoh’s heart that hardens or Pharaoh who hardens it; the first time the LORD is said to harden it is the sixth (9:12), after Pharaoh has twice promised to let the people go and gone back on it (8:8, 28). That does not soften the doctrine — God announced it beforehand (4:21). But it shows its shape: the hardening is judicial. God confirms a man in the direction he insisted on going — Romans 1:24–28 in a single man.

“Has God hardened me?” If that question frightens you, notice what the fear shows. Pharaoh never asked it. Hardness doesn’t lie awake wondering whether it is hard. Alarm about your heart is a sign of feeling in it. And the remedy was never introspection. A heart of stone is not repaired by examining it more closely; it is replaced, as God promised: “I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh” (Ezekiel 36:26). Ask him for it today.

“That my name might be proclaimed.” Not a boast, but what happened. Forty years later in Jericho a Canaanite prostitute told two spies, “For we have heard how the LORD dried up the water of the Red Sea before you… our hearts melted” (Joshua 2:10–11). The news crossed a desert and a border into a doomed city. And it saved her. Rahab and her household came out alive, and her name is in the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:5). Pharaoh willed and ran harder than anyone in the story and it moved nothing. The mercy reached the last person anyone would have picked, by way of the hardest heart in the region.

parallels.desc: for this purpose I have raised you up

verseByVerse.quote: So then he has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills. You will say to me then, "Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
So God “has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills.” Then comes the hardest objection: “Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?” If God is that sovereign, how can people be held responsible?

The two halves are not equal. “He has mercy on whomever he wills” summarises God’s own self-declaration at Exodus 33:19. “He hardens whomever he wills” is Paul’s conclusion from the Pharaoh story. God nowhere announces himself as the One who hardens whom he will in the way he announces himself as merciful. Scripture is not even-handed between the two, and neither is this chapter; it returns at vv. 22–23. And hardening is never the opening move. It falls on a man who has already hardened himself, repeatedly, in daylight.

The objection at full strength. It is not a sneer; it is the sharpest thing anyone says in Romans. If God’s will cannot be resisted, and what I am traces back to it, then blaming me is like blaming a stone for falling. Fault requires that I could have done otherwise. Paul puts it in the mouth of someone who has followed him exactly: “You will say to me then.” Every honest reader has felt it.

Paul does not resolve the logic. What follows in v. 20 is not a rebuttal but a question about who is asking. Paul could have distinguished decree from permission, pointed out that Pharaoh did what he wanted at every stage, or argued that freedom and sovereignty are compatible. He uses none of these. If you came wanting the logic resolved, you won’t get it here, and you are not obtuse for noticing.

What he does instead. He does what God did with Job. Job had a case and asked for a hearing. Out of the whirlwind came questions about the sea, the snow, the wild donkey and the ostrich — and not one word on Job’s question. And Job was satisfied, not because he got the information but because he got the One speaking (Job 42:5). A God whose reasons fitted inside your understanding without remainder would be a God the size of your understanding. People want that God right up until they are in trouble, and then they want a bigger one.

Don’t stop at the potter. If you close the book at v. 21 you have half Paul’s answer, the harsher half. He does give a cause for Israel’s failure, and it is not a decree. It is Israel: “they did not pursue it by faith, but as if it were based on works” (v. 32). And God says, “All day long I have held out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people” (10:21). Paul refuses to resolve the mechanism and then assigns responsibility exactly where the objector feared it could not be assigned. Both halves are his.

A test on a real case. Most people who ask “why does he still find fault?” are not defending Pharaoh. They fear they are trapped in what they are. So take one thing you did wrong this week — one instance, with a time and place. Did you experience it as compulsion? Nobody does. It felt like choosing, because it was. Whatever is true about God’s eternal decree, no one has ever sinned against his own will, and no one will stand before God able to say, “I wanted you and you turned me away.” The answer this chapter finally gives is not that fault is an illusion but that mercy is not an obligation.
verseByVerse.note: Exodus says both that Pharaoh hardened his heart and that God hardened it.

verseByVerse.quote: But who are you, O man, to answer back to God? Will what is molded say to its molder, "Why have you made me like this?" Has the potter no right over the clay, to make out of the same lump one vessel for honorable use and another for dishonorable use?
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Who are you, O man, to answer back to God?” Can the pot say to the potter, “Why have you made me like this?” Has the potter no right to make from the same lump one vessel for honourable use and another for ordinary use? The creature is not in a position to put the Creator on trial.

“O man.” The same address as 2:1. Not an insult but a reminder of category: you are a creature, having this conversation from inside the made world.

Answering back, not asking. The verb means to talk back, contradict, cross-examine. This verse has been used as a gag, wrongly. Paul is not forbidding questions; this chapter is made of them, and he asked two of the hardest himself (vv. 14, 19). Scripture is full of people who put hard questions to God: Job demanded a hearing; Habakkuk asked how long; Jeremiah said, “Righteous are you, O LORD, when I complain to you; yet I would plead my case before you” (Jeremiah 12:1); Mary asked how this could be, and was answered. If this verse has been used to shut down your honest question in grief or doubt, it was misused. What Paul rebukes is summoning God to the stand as defendant and appointing yourself the bench.

Jeremiah’s potter. The image is usually used in the opposite direction from Jeremiah’s. God sent Jeremiah to watch a potter, and “the vessel he was making of clay was spoiled in the potter’s hand, and he reworked it into another vessel, as it seemed good to the potter to do” (Jeremiah 18:4). The clay is spoiled, and the potter does not throw it away; he starts again with the same lump. And God applies it as an appeal: if a nation God has threatened “turns from its evil, I will relent of the disaster that I intended to do to it” (Jeremiah 18:8). This does not blunt Paul — he cites the potter for the potter’s right, and the right is real. But it tells you what kind of potter has it: hands that rework spoiled clay. The other potter passages are the same: Isaiah 29:16 sits in an oracle that ends with the deaf hearing; Isaiah 45:9 beside the promise of freedom for the exiles. None is about God shrugging.

“Out of the same lump.” Not two grades of clay. The chosen were not better stuff. We all came from the same handful of ground, and the difference between two vessels from one lump lies wholly in the potter’s intention, not the clay.

Don’t press the picture. “Honourable and dishonourable use” in a household means the good dish and the ordinary pot; final destinies come in vv. 22–23. Paul uses the same image elsewhere with a person moving between categories: “if anyone cleanses himself from what is dishonorable, he will be a vessel for honorable use” (2 Timothy 2:21). The picture does one job here. It is not a system.

A test. Think of the thing in your life you most want explained. Which do you want more: the explanation, or the God who has it? Many of us find we want the explanation and would take it and go. The demand to be answered can be, underneath, a wish not to need him. Not knowing why is a real grief, and the psalms say so loudly; you are not required to feel resolved. You are required not to climb onto the bench.

The potter’s hands. God formed the first man “of dust from the ground” (Genesis 2:7). There is one occasion in the New Testament when anyone makes clay: Jesus spits on the ground, makes mud, and puts it on the eyes of a man born blind (John 9:6). The Potter took up dust a second time — to give a man sight, while everyone walked past asking whose fault it was.

parallels.desc: shall the potter be regarded as the clay?

verseByVerse.quote: What if God, desiring to show his wrath and to make known his power, has endured with much patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction, in order to make known the riches of his glory for vessels of mercy, which he has prepared beforehand for glory —
verseByVerse.commentary:
What if God, wanting to show his wrath and power, has patiently endured “vessels of wrath prepared for destruction,” in order to make known “the riches of his glory for vessels of mercy, which he has prepared beforehand for glory”? Paul’s weight falls on mercy, which God prepares, and on patience toward those headed for judgment.

Different grammar for the two halves. Of the vessels of mercy: God “prepared beforehand” — active verb, God named, and “beforehand.” Of the vessels of wrath: “prepared for destruction” — passive, no agent named, no “beforehand.” Three differences in one sentence, all one way. Paul had the words to make them match and did not. Don’t claim too much: a passive can still have God behind it. But anyone who presents election and reprobation as two identical acts by the same hand is more symmetrical than the apostle.

What the Reformed confessions teach. Some have held a strict symmetry, as though God works unbelief in the lost the way he works faith in the saved. Arminian readers go the other way: the vessels of wrath are those who have fitted themselves for destruction, and God has decreed nothing about them. The historic Reformed confessions take the path between, and it fits this verse best. Election is God’s active, unconditional choice to save. Reprobation is his decision to pass others by, leave them in the sin they have chosen, and condemn them for that sin (Westminster Confession 3.7). God is sovereign over both, but he is the author of faith and never of sin. The lost are condemned for what they did; the saved are saved for what God did.

An unfinished sentence. “What if God…” never gets its second half. At the hardest point of his hardest chapter, Paul asks and leaves it hanging. If he would not close this sentence, nobody preaching it should close it harder than he did.

Much patience — spent on whom? God “endured with much patience” the vessels of wrath — literally “long-tempered,” the quality that, according to 2:4, is meant to lead to repentance. The patience in this verse is spent entirely on those headed for destruction. If the aim were only to display wrath, there would be no reason to wait, and God waits long. Peter: the Lord “is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish” (2 Peter 3:9).

You were inside that patience. The patience toward some is the room in which mercy reaches others. Every Christian was on the wrong side of that sentence for a while. The delay people demand an explanation for is the delay they were saved during.

A test. Work out roughly how long it was between the first thing you knew was wrong and the day you came to Christ — ten years, thirty, fifty. That interval is “much patience,” measured from inside. You have lived in it and were not consumed. That is not an argument; it is a receipt. Thank God for it.

Two guards. This is not God arranging destruction so the scenery looks better. The sentence lands on v. 23 — riches, glory, mercy prepared beforehand. Wrath is what God endures; mercy is what he prepares. And no one can look at another person and tell which vessel they are. The patience here has not run out — not for the one you’ve given up on, and not for you. As long as it is called “today” (Hebrews 3:13), the invitation is open.

verseByVerse.quote: even us whom he has called, not from the Jews only but also from the Gentiles?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The vessels of mercy are “even us whom he has called, not from the Jews only but also from the Gentiles.” After twenty verses about other people, Paul points at the church in the room: Jews and Gentiles called together by God’s grace.

Suddenly, “us.” For twenty verses everything has been third person — Isaac and Ishmael, Jacob and Esau, Moses, Pharaoh, a potter, two vessels — safely at a distance, the way most readers prefer this chapter. Then Paul writes “us,” and it lands like a hand on the shoulder. The vessels of mercy are not a category. They are the people listening to this letter. And it answers those who say this chapter is only about nations: Paul ends his argument by pointing at a congregation.

Called. The verb runs through the passage: “through Isaac shall your offspring be named” — literally “called” (v. 7); “because of him who calls” (v. 11); “called sons of the living God” (v. 26); and “those whom he predestined he also called” (8:30). That matters practically. You cannot observe an eternal decree; staring where the window should be has driven serious people to despair. But a call happens in time, to a person, at an address. It leaves marks.

Out of both. Called “from the Jews” and “from the Gentiles” — out of both. Neither group is summoned wholesale. The narrowing inside Israel (v. 6) runs inside the Gentile world too. No group you can join carries you in. Any Gentile Christian reading this chapter with quiet satisfaction about Israel has just been included in its terms, and Paul will say so plainly: “do not be arrogant toward the branches” (11:18).

A divided room. The Roman church had a seam down the middle: Jewish believers expelled from Rome under Claudius and now returned, and Gentile believers who had kept the church going in their absence. Each had grievances and a private account of whose church it really was. Paul sends a sentence that awards it to neither: us, called by him, out of the Jews and out of the Gentiles. Election arrives in Romans not as a seminar topic but as the only thing that can settle an argument about seating.

A test. Read v. 24 again. Did you instinctively count yourself in “us”? Many read Romans 9 as spectators — weighing its fairness, worrying about others, assessing God from the gallery. Paul wrote it as a member. If the chapter has felt like a court case you watch rather than a mercy you are inside, this verse is where the seating was assigned.

For the anxious. If you wonder whether “us” includes you, the verse gives you something more useful to examine than your eternal status: a call. Have you heard one — not a voice, but the gospel’s summons that you have found yourself answering, however unevenly? Then answer it again today. The chapter began with a man weeping because his own people would not come, and ends its argument by naming the people who did: a mixed, unlikely, quarrelling congregation in the capital of the empire that would one day kill him.

verseByVerse.quote: As indeed he says in Hosea, "Those who were not my people I will call 'my people,' and her who was not beloved I will call 'beloved.'" "And in the very place where it was said to them, 'You are not my people,' there they will be called 'sons of the living God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God says in Hosea, “Those who were not my people I will call ‘my people,’ and her who was not beloved I will call ‘beloved’… they will be called ‘sons of the living God.’” Words first spoken about unfaithful Israel, Paul now applies to the Gentiles: God makes a people out of those who were not his people.

The names of children. Paul is quoting the names of a man’s children. God told Hosea to marry a woman who would be unfaithful, and she was. Their second child was a daughter, Lo-ruhamah, “No Mercy”; their third a son, Lo-ammi, “Not My People” (Hosea 1:6–9). A prophet had to call his own children by those names in front of neighbours who knew what they meant. The sermon was his family. So when Paul quotes “her who was not beloved I will call ‘beloved,’” he is quoting a little girl’s name being taken off her.

The negative removed. God does not hand out replacement names. He cancels the “no” on the names already given. No Mercy becomes Mercy. Not My People becomes My People.

“In the very place.” Where it was said, “You are not my people,” there they will be called sons of the living God. Not somewhere else after a fresh start where nobody knows. At the same address where the disowning was announced. Most of us would prefer God restored us somewhere new. He tends to do it in the room where it happened, in front of the same people.

Higher than restoration. “My people” again would have been enough. Hosea says “sons of the living God” — not just readmitted but family, and the God is the living one, over against the dead things they had left him for.

Two apostles, one text. Peter does the same with Gentile churches: “Once you were not a people, but now you are God’s people; once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy” (1 Peter 2:10).

A test with a pen. Write down the sentence you believe is truest about yourself when no one is watching — the one that surfaces when the house is quiet. Often it is a name: not wanted, or not forgiven. Notice what makes Hosea different from ordinary comfort. Those names were accurate when given; Israel really had gone after other gods. So God is not saying “you were never really that.” He is saying “you were, and you are not now.” A verdict reversed, not a misprint corrected. Cross out your sentence and write God’s over it.

A guard. The renaming was not free. Hosea was sent to buy his wife back from what she had sold herself into, and Scripture records the price, down to the barley (Hosea 3:2). That is the shape of every renaming God does: Someone goes and pays for the one who left. If mercy can reach that house, whether it can reach Rome — or you — is already settled.
verseByVerse.note: Hosea spoke of the northern tribes of Israel; Paul applies the words to the Gentiles too.

parallels.desc: I will say to Not My People, “You are my people”

verseByVerse.quote: And Isaiah cries out concerning Israel: "Though the number of the sons of Israel be as the sand of the sea, only a remnant of them will be saved, for the Lord will carry out his sentence upon the earth fully and without delay."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaiah cries out about Israel: though they are as many as the sand of the sea, “only a remnant of them will be saved,” for the Lord will carry out his sentence fully and swiftly (Isaiah 10:22–23). The narrowing within Israel was always part of God’s plan, not a failure of it.

“Cries out.” Paul changes his verb. Before, “he says in Hosea”; here, Isaiah “cries out” — a shout, a raised voice. This is a prophet raising his voice about his own nation.

A son named for the doctrine. Isaiah had a son called Shear-jashub, “A remnant shall return,” and God had him bring the boy to meet the king (Isaiah 7:3). The second prophet in four verses whose children were the sermon: Hosea’s were the judgment, Isaiah’s the hope — but a hope that cut both ways. Stress “only a remnant” and it is a threat; stress “a remnant shall return” and it is a promise. To a man secure in his numbers and ancestry, the word is “only.” To a man who has counted the faithful and thinks he has reached the end of them, the word is “a remnant” — there is one.

The sand still matters. Isaiah is not cancelling the promise to Abraham of descendants as the sand (Genesis 22:17). Paul is saying the multitude was never going to arrive by descent. Where it finally goes is chapter 11; this verse is not his last word.

Swift and complete. The end of v. 28 is genuinely difficult in Greek, and translations differ. The sense is that God will bring his word to completion and not let it drag. That too is mercy: a sentence carried out decisively is not left hanging for centuries.

A remnant that returns. The verse just before Paul’s quotation defines the remnant: “A remnant will return, the remnant of Jacob, to the mighty God” (Isaiah 10:21). The remnant is not defined by having survived but by having returned.

A test. Don’t ask whether you are among the few. Ask whether you have returned. Plenty of people stay — never leave the building, never renounce anything, name on a roll somewhere. Staying and returning are not the same act. Turn to God again today.

A guard. Remnant language is easily corrupted. It is the natural vocabulary of every small, embattled, self-congratulating group that has decided everyone else has compromised. Look at what Isaiah’s remnant is: survivors of a catastrophe, people who came out of a burning country with nothing, whose only distinction is that God kept them. There is not a syllable of achievement in it. The moment “remnant” becomes a compliment you pay yourself, it has stopped describing you.

parallels.desc: only a remnant will return

verseByVerse.quote: And as Isaiah predicted, "If the Lord of hosts had not left us offspring, we would have been like Sodom and become like Gomorrah."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaiah also said, “If the Lord of hosts had not left us offspring, we would have been like Sodom and become like Gomorrah” (v. 29, quoting Isaiah 1:9). The surviving remnant exists only because God preserved it. Left to ourselves, nobody would be left at all.

A counterfactual. “If the Lord had not… we would have been.” This is not a lament about how few were kept but a statement about what did not happen. The chapter has pressed a question about those passed over. Isaiah asks the other question: why is anybody here at all? He speaks from inside the wreckage, one of the survivors: we should not be here.

Jerusalem called Sodom. We treat Sodom as somebody else. Read one verse further: “Hear the word of the LORD, you rulers of Sodom! Give ear to the teaching of our God, you people of Gomorrah!” (Isaiah 1:10). Isaiah calls Jerusalem Sodom to its face while the temple is running and the sacrifices offered. On his account the difference between Jerusalem and Sodom was not behaviour. It was that one had seed left in it and the other did not. Abraham could not find ten righteous men in Sodom; Lot was pulled out by the arm; his wife did not make it to the hills (Genesis 19). Sodom is what a place looks like when nothing is kept back.

Seed, not leftovers. Isaiah’s word for what God left is “seed” — in Greek, sperma. A remnant is what is left when something is consumed. A seed is put in the ground on purpose. One looks back at a loss; the other forward to a harvest. God did not salvage a few. He planted. That is why Paul ends the section here, on a word that means a future.

A test. Finish Isaiah’s sentence about yourself: “If the Lord had not left me ______, I would have been ______.” Most people can complete it faster than they expect: a friend who would not give up on you; a church you nearly walked out of; a conscience that would not settle; a year that broke something you were relying on; an illness that stopped you at the moment you were about to do the irreparable thing. Left to ourselves we audit the deficit — wasted years, people not saved, how little remains. Isaiah audits the reprieve. Both are honest; only one is the arithmetic of a man who knows what he escaped. Thank God for your blank.

A guard. This is not a comparison with people who are worse. Isaiah forbids that by calling his own congregation Sodom. Nobody is ranked; everybody is reprieved, and the reprieve is the only distinction anyone has. The section that began with a man swearing he could not stop grieving ends with a prophet saying we should not be alive. The last word is not a verdict on the lost. It is a seed in the ground.

parallels.desc: if the LORD of hosts had not left us a few survivors

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 30–33 — The Stumbling Stone: Israel's Pursuit and Fall
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The chapter ends with a turn from theology to history. The Gentiles, who were not pursuing righteousness, have attained it — by faith. Israel, which pursued the law of righteousness, did not attain it — because they pursued it as if it were by works rather than by faith. They stumbled over the stumbling stone: Christ. The stone God laid in Zion (Isaiah 28:16) was meant to be the foundation of Israel's hope; it became the obstacle over which they fell.

The irony is complete. The people who had every advantage — every covenant privilege, the law, the promises, the patriarchs — failed to reach what the people with no advantage attained. The reason is not their lack of zeal (Paul will say in 10:2 that they have zeal, but not according to knowledge) but their misdirection: seeking a righteousness of their own rather than the righteousness of God. The stumbling stone is not a surprise or a trap; it is the very cornerstone that God announced. But it requires faith to receive it as such.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Stone and the Two Ways

The stone of Romans 9:33 is used in the New Testament as a central Christological image (cf. 1 Peter 2:6–8, Matthew 21:42–44). Christ is simultaneously the cornerstone (the secure foundation for all who believe) and the stumbling stone (the cause of fall for all who refuse). The same Christ who is salvation to the one who believes is judgment to the one who will not. The gospel is never neutral; it is always either the savour of life or the savour of death (2 Corinthians 2:16). There is no third option.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel's pursuit of righteousness by works was not insincere. It was zealous and disciplined. But zeal misdirected is more dangerous than apathy, because it produces a confidence in one's own religious achievement that closes the hand against the gift of grace. Now: The same dynamic plays out in every religious context. The most difficult people to bring to genuine faith are often the most religious — those who have so much invested in their own righteousness that they cannot bring themselves to stand before God empty-handed and receive what only grace can give.

verseByVerse.quote: What shall we say, then? That Gentiles who did not pursue righteousness have attained it, that is, a righteousness that is by faith; but that Israel who pursued a law that would lead to righteousness did not succeed in reaching that law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So what does this mean? Gentiles who were not pursuing righteousness obtained it — a righteousness by faith. Israel, who pursued a law that would lead to righteousness, did not reach that law. They failed not for lack of effort, but because they tried to earn by works what can only be received by faith.

A race with a strange result. “Pursue” is chasing down; “attain” is overtaking and grasping. Picture the result board. Standing at the finish are those who never entered — not training, not on the track, off doing the things chapter 1 described. And they are across the line. Meanwhile the athletes who trained for centuries, knew the course better than anyone alive, and had the rules and the coaching are still out on the track, and the race is over.

They did not reach the law. Paul does not say Israel pursued righteousness and failed to reach righteousness. He says they pursued “a law that would lead to righteousness” and “did not succeed in reaching that law.” What they failed to arrive at was the law itself. The people who studied it, memorised it, fenced it with further rules and died rather than break it did not get to the law — because its destination was a Person and they treated it as a syllabus. “Christ is the end of the law” (10:4).

Not insincerity. “They have a zeal for God” (10:2). Paul had it himself, more than any of them, and used it to arrest Christians. Misdirected zeal is harder to reach than apathy. The indifferent man has nothing invested. The devout man has forty years invested, and every year argues against the one thing asked of him. It is often not the person who has never entered a church who finds grace impossible, but the one who hasn’t missed a Sunday since 1974 — because to receive righteousness as a gift he must agree that the fifty years bought him nothing.

A guard. This is no sneer at serious people. Paul ran hard and will spend four chapters urging detailed obedience. The problem was not that Israel tried but what they tried to produce. A man can sprint with great discipline in a direction that leads nowhere, and the discipline is not the fault.

A test. How do you experience the Christian life? As a distance still to cover — ground to make up, a standard you are closing on, a verdict still ahead? Or as an address you already live at (5:1–2)? Both kinds of Christian work hard, and from outside you can’t tell them apart. But one runs toward the finish and the other from it, and the difference shows the first bad week. If never arriving is your settled experience of God, this verse describes your Tuesday. The Gentiles here did not run a better race. They did not run at all. They were handed it — the only way anyone has ever got it, including the athletes.

verseByVerse.quote: Why? Because they did not pursue it by faith, but as if it were based on works. They have stumbled over the stumbling stone, as it is written, "Behold, I am laying in Zion a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense; and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why did Israel fail? “Because they did not pursue it by faith, but as if it were based on works.” They stumbled over the stumbling stone God laid in Zion — Christ himself. But, as Paul quotes Isaiah, “whoever believes in him will not be put to shame.”

“Why?” — and a real answer. Paul gives a reason, and it is not the potter or God’s hidden will. It is in Israel: they pursued righteousness by works, not faith. At v. 20 Paul refused to resolve the question of fault by argument, and that refusal stands. But it was never his last word. Here he assigns the cause of Israel’s fall to what Israel did. Sovereign mercy is why anyone is in; unbelief is why anyone is out. Paul holds both in one chapter, and a reader who can carry only one will misrepresent him either way.

Two texts welded together. The frame is Isaiah 28:16 — “Behold, I am laying in Zion… whoever believes in him will not be put to shame” (as Paul gives it from the Greek Old Testament). The middle is Isaiah 8:14 — “a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense.” In Isaiah 28 the stone is a tested, precious cornerstone. In Isaiah 8 the LORD himself “will become a sanctuary and a stone of offense” in the same breath. One stone: sanctuary and obstacle. The difference is not in the masonry but in the approach. Come to a foundation stone as a threshold and it holds you for life. Come at it in the dark, at speed, looking elsewhere, and it takes your feet from under you.

Laid on purpose. “I am laying.” Not debris in the road or a trap, but placed deliberately in Zion at the front of the building, where nobody can enter without meeting it.

The offence. Not obscurity; the stone is the most visible thing in the building. A crucified Messiah. Deuteronomy says “a hanged man is cursed by God” (Deuteronomy 21:23), so a crucified Christ was not a lowered expectation but a contradiction in terms (cf. 1 Corinthians 1:23). And yet that is how the chapter opened: Paul wished he could be accursed for his people and could not (v. 3). The stone they tripped over is the one Person who could do what Paul wished, and did. What made him unthinkable is why he is any use to anyone.

The widest sentence in the chapter. After twenty-eight verses of narrowing: “whoever believes in him will not be put to shame.” No lineage, no prior standing, no evidence of having been chosen. It is the one sentence in Romans 9 a frightened reader can act on directly, and Paul put it last. “Shame” is the word of 1:16: “I am not ashamed of the gospel.” Shame is precisely what this stone takes away.

A test. Name your stone — the thing about Christ you have to get past rather than simply accept: his exclusive claim, the wrath of chapter 1, the cross itself, or arriving with empty hands after a lifetime of competence. This verse says it was laid. It is not an obstruction in front of the door. It is the door. Come to it today.

A guard. “Whoever” means whoever. There is no hidden qualifier for those who turn out to be chosen. The man who has just written the most uncompromising paragraph on election in the Bible ends by throwing the door open and standing back. The builders looked at this stone, saw no use for it, and threw it aside (Psalm 118:22). It is holding up everything.

parallels.desc: a stone, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone
a stone of offence

9.text: <sup>1</sup>I am speaking the truth in Christ—I am not lying; my conscience bears me witness in the Holy Spirit—<sup>2</sup>that I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart.<sup>3</sup>For I could wish that I myself were accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh.<sup>4</sup>They are Israelites, and to them belong the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the worship, and the promises.<sup>5</sup>To them belong the patriarchs, and from their race, according to the flesh, is the Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen.<sup>6</sup>But it is not as though the word of God has failed. For not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel,<sup>7</sup>and not all are children of Abraham because they are his offspring, but “Through Isaac shall your offspring be named.”<sup>8</sup>This means that it is not the children of the flesh who are the children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as offspring.<sup>9</sup>For this is what the promise said: “About this time next year I will return, and Sarah shall have a son.”<sup>10</sup>And not only so, but also when Rebekah had conceived children by one man, our forefather Isaac,<sup>11</sup>though they were not yet born and had done nothing either good or bad—in order that God’s purpose of election might continue, not because of works but because of him who calls—<sup>12</sup>she was told, “The older will serve the younger.”<sup>13</sup>As it is written, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.”<sup>14</sup>What shall we say then? Is there injustice on God’s part? By no means!<sup>15</sup>For he says to Moses, “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion.”<sup>16</sup>So then it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy.<sup>17</sup>For the Scripture says to Pharaoh, “For this very purpose I have raised you up, that I might show my power in you, and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth.”<sup>18</sup>So then he has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills.<sup>19</sup>You will say to me then, “Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?”<sup>20</sup>But who are you, O man, to answer back to God? Will what is molded say to its molder, “Why have you made me like this?”<sup>21</sup>Has the potter no right over the clay, to make out of the same lump one vessel for honorable use and another for dishonorable use?<sup>22</sup>What if God, desiring to show his wrath and to make known his power, has endured with much patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction,<sup>23</sup>in order to make known the riches of his glory for vessels of mercy, which he has prepared beforehand for glory—<sup>24</sup>even us whom he has called, not from the Jews only but also from the Gentiles?<sup>25</sup>As indeed he says in Hosea, “Those who were not my people I will call ’my people,’ and her who was not beloved I will call ’beloved.’”<sup>26</sup>“And in the very place where it was said to them, ’You are not my people,’ there they will be called ’sons of the living God.’”<sup>27</sup>And Isaiah cries out concerning Israel: “Though the number of the sons of Israel be as the sand of the sea, only a remnant of them will be saved,<sup>28</sup>for the Lord will carry out his sentence upon the earth fully and without delay.”<sup>29</sup>And as Isaiah predicted, “If the Lord of hosts had not left us offspring, we would have been like Sodom and become like Gomorrah.”<sup>30</sup>What shall we say, then? That Gentiles who did not pursue righteousness have attained it, that is, a righteousness that is by faith;<sup>31</sup>but that Israel who pursued a law that would lead to righteousness did not succeed in reaching that law.<sup>32</sup>Why? Because they did not pursue it by faith, but as if it were based on works. They have stumbled over the stumbling stone,<sup>33</sup>as it is written, “Behold, I am laying in Zion a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense; and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame.”

10.title: Faith Comes by Hearing
10.overview:
Romans 10 moves from the theology of election (chapter 9) to the human experience of faith and the missionary imperative of proclamation. Paul's pastoral heart is again on display: his heart's desire and prayer for Israel is their salvation. Their problem is not a lack of religious commitment but a misdirection of it — a zeal for God that is not according to knowledge, a pursuit of their own righteousness that refuses to submit to the righteousness of God.

The great passage of vv. 9–15 moves from confession and faith to calling on the name of the Lord to preachers sent with good news — a chain that runs from individual conversion back to the sovereign act of apostolic commissioning. The gospel does not reach people automatically; it reaches them through preachers who are sent, who go, who speak. The chapter ends with the sobering testimony of Israel's own scriptures: they have heard, they have understood, and they have not believed. The tragedy of unbelief is complete.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — Righteousness for All Who Call: The Nearness of the Word
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul's pastoral longing for Israel's salvation (v. 1) is the emotional key to the chapter. He is not writing as a detached analyst of Israel's religious failure; he is writing as a broken-hearted brother who knows exactly what his people are missing and cannot stop praying for them. The diagnosis is precise: "a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge." Zeal without knowledge is not a small problem; it is perhaps the most dangerous religious condition possible, because it generates confident misdirection.

The contrast between the righteousness of the law and the righteousness of faith (vv. 5–8) draws on Deuteronomy 30, where Moses speaks of God's word as near to the people — not beyond the sea, not in the heights of heaven, but in their mouths and in their hearts. Paul identifies this nearness with the gospel: "the word of faith that we proclaim." The righteousness of God is not a distant achievement to be scaled by heroic effort; it is a near word to be received by confession and faith.

Two verses stand between the diagnosis and that contrast, and they should not be passed over. They are the hinge of the chapter. Israel, Paul says, being ignorant of the righteousness of God, and seeking to establish their own, did not submit to God’s righteousness (v. 3).

Watch the sequence, because it is a clinical description of how a religious life goes wrong. First not knowing what God was offering; then setting about producing a version of it themselves; and finally — the word that makes it a moral matter rather than a misunderstanding — refusing to submit.

That verb is the surprise. One does not expect righteousness to be something a person submits to. But a righteousness that arrives as a gift has to be received on the giver’s terms, and receiving is precisely what a competent, disciplined, self-respecting person finds hardest. The offence of the gospel is not that it asks too much. It is that it will not let you contribute.

Then v. 4, which the chapter cannot do without: Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes. The word is telos, and it carries both senses at once — the terminus and the goal, where a road stops and what it was built to reach.

Both are true here and neither should be dropped. As a route to righteousness the law has come to its end, because the destination has arrived. And it was always heading there; Christ is not an alternative to the law but the thing it was pointing at, which is why Paul can say elsewhere that he does not overthrow the law but upholds it (3:31).

Note also the last clause, because it is the one that opens the door: to everyone who believes. The universal that will ring three times in vv. 11-13 has already sounded here, before the famous verses begin.

Verses 9–13 are among the most frequently memorised in Paul's letters — "If you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved." The simplicity is staggering. Two things: confession of lordship, belief in resurrection. Both are the expression of the same faith. And the word "all" rings three times: everyone who believes (v. 11), everyone who calls (v. 13), for he is Lord of all and bestows riches on all who call (v. 12). The gospel has no ethnic or social exclusion clause.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Confession of Lordship

Romans 10:9 makes the confession "Jesus is Lord" (Kyrios Iēsous) the central act of Christian profession. In the first-century Roman world, "Kyrios" was the title of Caesar — the one to whom ultimate allegiance was owed. To confess "Jesus is Lord" was therefore not merely a theological statement but a political one: Jesus, not Caesar, holds ultimate authority over my life. The early church was often persecuted for refusing to say "Caesar is Lord" — because they had already given that title to another. Every true Christian confession has this political dimension: it declares a transfer of ultimate allegiance.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Moses's vision of the nearness of God's word (Deuteronomy 30) had originally been given to Israel on the plains of Moab, just before they entered the land — as a word of covenant accessibility. God was not hiding himself; he had given his word and it was near. Paul's application to the gospel makes the same point: the righteousness of God is not a distant achievement but a near word, proclaimed by apostles, received by faith. Now: The simplicity of Romans 10:9 is the permanent rebuke to every complicated scheme of salvation. Salvation does not require a theology degree, a track record of spiritual achievement, or a passage through elaborate ritual. It requires the honest confession of a changed allegiance and the genuine belief in a historical resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: Brothers, my heart's desire and prayer to God for them is that they may be saved. For I bear them witness that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s heart’s desire and prayer is that Israel may be saved. He testifies that they have “a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge.” The hard doctrine of chapter 9 has not cooled his love; it has sent him to prayer.

“Brothers.” The Roman church was by now largely Gentile. Paul asks them to care about Israel’s salvation by opening his heart rather than issuing an order — preparing for his warning in 11:18 not to be arrogant toward the broken branches.

Doctrine, then prayer. Chapter 9 ended with a nation tripping over a stone. Paul’s next act is to pray for them. He does not finish the argument and change the subject; he finishes it and goes to his knees. Grief (9:2–3), doctrine (9:6–29), prayer (10:1), hope (11:23): one man, four movements, no contradiction.

“Heart’s desire.” The word means good pleasure, what you would pick if you could have anything — the word used of God’s own good pleasure in salvation. Paul’s first choice is that these people be saved. Not answered, not proved wrong, which was well within his power. Saved.

A witness for the defence. “I bear them witness” is courtroom language. Paul testifies to what he knows first-hand. He described himself as once “so extremely zealous… for the traditions of my fathers” (Galatians 1:14), “as to zeal, a persecutor of the church” (Philippians 3:6). When he writes of zeal without knowledge, he is describing himself as a young man. He is not a man who never had the disease; he is a survivor of it, and remembers how right it felt.

Sincere and wrong. This is the frightening part. You can be sincere, disciplined, costly, lifelong — and wrong. Israel’s zeal produced martyrs. Paul’s produced arrest warrants and a coat held at a stoning. Sincerity is real, and sincerity is not a saving category.

A test. You already know you are sincere, so ask something more useful: when did you last change your mind about something in your faith because Scripture required it, not because it suited you? Zeal according to knowledge can be corrected, because it answers to something outside itself. Zeal without knowledge has no way to revise; it can only get warmer. If nothing in your convictions has moved in twenty years, that may not be faithfulness. It may mean nothing has been allowed to speak. Read a passage this week asking what it corrects in you.

Two guards. This does not license calling sincere people of other convictions stupid. Paul credits their zeal and wants them saved, not defeated. And knowledge without zeal is not the cure. The chapter that diagnoses misdirected passion was written by a man whose heart’s desire comes first in the sentence.

How Paul was cured. Nobody argued him out of it. He was stopped on a road and shown whom he had been fighting, and his first words were, “Who are you, Lord?” (Acts 9:5). Zeal without knowledge is not cured by less zeal. It is cured by meeting the One you were serving so badly.

verseByVerse.quote: For, being ignorant of the righteousness of God, and seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to God's righteousness. For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not knowing the righteousness that comes from God, Israel tried to establish their own and did not submit to God’s. “For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.” The law was never the road to a right standing with God; it pointed to Christ, and in him it has arrived.

Three verbs. They were ignorant; they sought to establish; they did not submit. “Ignorant” is surprising: these were the most literate religious community of the ancient world, entrusted with God’s words (3:2). It means failing to recognise what was in front of them.

Building or getting under. “Establish” is a builder’s word — to put up, make something stand. “Submit” means to place yourself underneath. One is a man putting up a structure with his own name on it; the other is a man getting under something someone else built. You can’t do both. And what stops a person doing the second is usually not misunderstanding. It is that he has spent thirty years on the first and it is nearly finished.

What it looks like. Picture the man Paul has in mind. He tithes, has never been unfaithful to his wife, looks after his mother, keeps his word, helps the needy, and hasn’t missed a service in eleven years — all genuinely good. Ask what stands between him and God and he won’t sneer at grace. He will just start, somewhere in his answer, to describe himself. Establishing your own righteousness does not feel like arrogance. It feels like diligence.

“End” — goal and finish. The word means both the point where something stops and the point it aimed at. Both are true. The picture is a finishing tape: it ends the race and is the reason the race was run. So the law is not repudiated. Everything it required has been met in a Person. Paul has already said, “we uphold the law” (3:31). And note the qualifier: Christ is the end of the law “for righteousness.” What has ended is the law as the route to a right standing — not the law as God’s word or as a mirror. Nobody is told to stop reading Leviticus, only to stop trying to climb it.

Put down the tools. If Christ is the finish, the project is over. There is nothing left to establish; the only thing to do with a completed building is put down the tools. That is harder than it sounds for someone who has built for decades. The exhaustion of religious people is rarely caused by their sins. It is caused by a construction project God ended long ago, and nobody told them.

A test. Finish this quickly: “I’ve had a good week with God if I have ______.” Most people answer instantly with a list of activities — prayed more, read more, been patient, not lost my temper on Wednesday. Notice what that list is: scaffolding poles, the shape of someone still establishing, surviving in people whose doctrine of grace is perfectly correct. Try ending tomorrow’s prayer by thanking God for Christ’s righteousness rather than reviewing your own.

A guard. The week still matters; Paul will spend chapters 12–15 on how to live. What has changed is what the week is for. It is no longer material for a structure. It is the response of someone who has been given a home. Israel’s tragedy was not wanting righteousness too little but wanting it enough to spend a nation’s history building one, while God held out a finished one the whole time.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that verse 4 can also be read “Christ is the end of the law, that everyone who believes may be justified.” “End” can mean goal as well as termination.

verseByVerse.quote: For Moses writes about the righteousness that is based on the law, that the person who does the commandments shall live by them. But the righteousness based on faith says, "Do not say in your heart, 'Who will ascend into heaven?'" (that is, to bring Christ down)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses describes the righteousness based on the law: “the person who does the commandments shall live by them” (v. 5, quoting Leviticus 18:5). But the righteousness based on faith speaks differently, using Moses’ own words: don’t ask, “Who will ascend into heaven?” — as though you had to bring Christ down. He has already come.

An honest offer. “The person who does the commandments shall live by them” is genuine and means what it says. The law is not a trap; it states honourable terms — do, and live. Paul quotes it for the same purpose in Galatians 3:12. The difficulty was never the offer. It was the doer.

Moses against Moses. Both quotations come from Moses: Leviticus 18:5 and Deuteronomy 30. The contrast is not apostle versus lawgiver, but the lawgiver stating terms, and the same lawgiver describing a word that comes near without anyone having to go and fetch it.

Not out of context. Paul is often accused of raiding Deuteronomy 30. But look where it stands: after the covenant curses of chapter 28, after exile is described in advance, and right after God promises, “the LORD your God will circumcise your heart and the heart of your offspring, so that you will love the LORD your God with all your heart… that you may live” (Deuteronomy 30:6). The nearness Moses speaks of belongs to a passage about restoration after failure, by God’s surgery on the heart. It was never a description of an easy law.

“Do not say in your heart.” Moses uses this formula for sentences never spoken aloud: “Beware lest you say in your heart, ‘My power and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth’” (Deuteronomy 8:17). What is forbidden here is not a public position but an interior sentence.

Its modern form. Almost nobody says “Who will ascend into heaven?” But many Christians said this month: “There must be something more I have to do.” That is the ascent — the reflex that believes the gospel in principle and then quietly assembles a ladder: more discipline, more feeling, a better run of weeks, as though Christ needed fetching down and the fetching were your job.

The climb is unnecessary. Paul does not say the climb is hard. He says it is unnecessary, because the journey has already been made in the opposite direction. Nobody has to bring Christ down. He came down. The ladder is not too short; there is nothing at the top that is not already standing beside you. Next time you hear yourself say “something more,” answer it: he came down.

parallels.desc: by doing them a person shall live
who will ascend to heaven for us?

verseByVerse.quote: "or 'Who will descend into the abyss?'" (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead). But what does it say? "The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart" (that is, the word of faith that we proclaim);
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nor ask, “Who will descend into the abyss?” — as though you had to bring Christ up from the dead. He has been raised. “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart” — that is, the message of faith the apostles preach. Salvation is not far away. It has been brought to you.

An honest note on the text. Deuteronomy 30:13 says “beyond the sea”: “Who will go over the sea for us and bring it to us?” Paul changes it to the realm of the dead. That is not carelessness. It is interpretation of a kind Jewish teachers of his day practised openly, and he signals it each time with “that is.” He is applying the passage, not reciting it. And the change does work. “Over the sea” is merely far. The abyss is the place no one returns from. Up and down are the only two directions a human could travel to reach God, and Paul closes both, because Christ has been to both and come back.

The other interior sentence. If the ascent says “there must be something more I have to do,” the descent says the opposite: “What he did cannot reach as far down as I have gone.” That sentence has kept more people from Christ than atheism. It doesn’t deny the gospel; it holds that this particular case — the thing done at nineteen, the years nobody knows about, the marriage wrecked on purpose — is beneath its range. Paul answers by pointing to where Christ has been: in the grave, and out of it.

“Near.” Not available or obtainable — near, and located precisely: in your mouth and in your heart. Nearer than the church building, the minister, the next conference, the season when things calm down. The gospel is not somewhere you must get to. It is already in the room.

Near because someone said it. “The word of faith that we proclaim.” The word didn’t drift close. Somebody said it aloud. Paul will build six verses on this (vv. 14–17). The nearness of v. 8 and the preacher of v. 15 are one fact seen from two ends.

A test. Name what you privately believe still has to happen before you are right with God. Most people can name it in ten seconds. Which direction does it point — something more to achieve (the ascent) or something too far gone (the descent)? There is no third option, and Paul has closed both before v. 9. Tell God which one you have been saying, and then thank him that the travelling is done.

Two guards. Nearness is not possession; that is why v. 9 calls for confession and belief. A thing can be in your mouth because you were taught it as a child and never believed it. And “in your heart” does not mean the word is your own inner voice, to be found by looking inside. It is near because it was brought and spoken from outside, by someone sent. The whole distance a sinner now stands from God is the width of an open mouth.
verseByVerse.note: Paul applies Moses’ words about the nearness of God’s word to the message about Christ.

parallels.desc: the word is very near you, in your mouth and in your heart

verseByVerse.quote: Because, if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For with the heart one believes and is justified, and with the mouth one confesses and is saved. — Romans 10:9–10
verseByVerse.commentary:
“If you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.” Believing with the heart, a person is justified; confessing with the mouth, a person is saved. One faith: trust inside, spoken outside.

Believe in your heart. In Scripture the heart is the centre of the person — will, affections, thinking. Saving faith is not just a thought in the mind but a conviction at the core that reorients everything. Calvin defined faith as a firm and certain knowledge of God’s kindness toward us, founded on his freely given promise in Christ, revealed to our minds and sealed on our hearts by the Holy Spirit.

What “Jesus is Lord” cost. Around AD 112 Pliny, governor of Bithynia, wrote to Emperor Trajan describing his test for Christians: offer incense and wine before the emperor’s image and curse Christ. Those who did were released. A capital trial came down to one sentence said where witnesses could hear. That is why the mouth is named — not because God needs the syllables, but because the mouth is the organ that costs. “Lord” was Caesar’s title, for the one with final right over your life. Giving it to a crucified Galilean took it off someone else. Christians were killed less for what they privately believed than for what they would not say. Confession is a transfer of allegiance.

Not a password. Jesus blocked that reading: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 7:21). And “no one can say ‘Jesus is Lord’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12:3). The confession does not cause new life. It is the first sound new life makes.

The order reverses. Verse 9 has mouth then heart; verse 10 heart then mouth. In v. 9 Paul follows Moses’ order — “in your mouth and in your heart” (v. 8, quoting Deuteronomy 30:14). In v. 10 he gives the order in which things happen. These are not two requirements to assemble. It is one faith described twice: from inside, trust; from outside, audible. And “justified” and “saved” are not two prizes, one for believing and a better one for speaking, but one rescue named by its effect on your standing and on your future. “You will be saved” points to a coming day; but the verdict is not deferred. It has been given.

“I can’t find the moment I confessed.” For the one converted alone in a hospital bed, or so gradually there is no date, or who cannot speak at all: “confesses” is present tense, a description, not a ceremony you may have failed to perform. The word means “to say the same thing” — to agree with God about his Son where it can be heard. You have done it each time you prayed to him, called him Lord where that was awkward, or told the truth about whose you are when a shorter answer was available. The verse asks not whether there was a moment, but whether there is a mouth that agrees with the heart.

A test. Think of the last time you had a plain chance to say whose you are and let it pass. What were you actually afraid of? Not hell — something much smaller: a change in someone’s expression, a conversation turning heavy, being thought “that sort of person.” That fear is a small piece of what made this sentence dangerous in Rome. Next time, say it.

Why the resurrection? You cannot call a dead man Lord; the title is for someone in office. The raising is God’s verdict on the cross — the Son “declared to be the Son of God in power” (1:4), “raised for our justification” (4:25). The event you are asked to believe is the ground on which you are declared right. And it answers 3:19, where the law speaks “so that every mouth may be stopped.” Seven chapters later, the gospel gives the stopped mouth something to say. Not a defence. A name.
verseByVerse.note: “Jesus is Lord” was the earliest Christian confession. “Lord” is the title the Greek Old Testament used for God’s name.

verseByVerse.quote: For the Scripture says, "Everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame." For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek; for the same Lord is Lord of all, bestowing his riches on all who call on him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Scripture says, “Everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame.” There is no distinction between Jew and Greek: the same Lord is Lord of all and is generous to all who call on him. One Lord, one way, one inexhaustible generosity for every person who calls.

Paul adds a word. He quoted this same line from Isaiah 28:16 at 9:33, and there it lacked the word “everyone” — so do Isaiah and the Greek Old Testament Paul read. Here he adds it, and uses the idea twice more (“all who call,” v. 12; “everyone who calls,” v. 13). The one word he adds to the prophet is the word this paragraph is built on.

The private exceptions clause. “Everyone” is easy to believe in general and hard in particular. Nobody disputes it as doctrine; almost everybody keeps an exception. Sometimes it is another person, a case so long-running that hoping feels like poor judgment. Sometimes, more quietly, it is yourself.

A test. Don’t ask whether you believe “everyone”; you’ll say yes. Listen to how you pray for the person you have privately filed as hopeless. Do you pray as though the promise covers them, or as though applying for an exception? The two prayers sound different. Paul modelled the first at the top of this chapter: his prayer for people who rejected the gospel is “that they may be saved” (10:1). Pray that way for them tonight.

“No distinction” — turned around. Paul used these exact words at 3:22–23 to introduce the worst news in the letter: “there is no distinction: for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” There the phrase levelled everyone onto one floor of ruin. Here it opens a door to all. Nobody is far enough in to be exempt from needing this, and nobody far enough out to be barred from it. The gospel can be for everybody only because the ruin was.

The ground is one God. “The same Lord is Lord of all.” If there were two Lords there could be two ways. There is one. And a Gentile calling on Jesus is not a guest at someone else’s God; he is calling on his own Maker.

No reduced portion. “Bestowing his riches” is present tense: being rich toward all who call. It is not a fixed sum divided among claimants. To the one who came late, or out of wasted years, with the settled sense that what is left will be a reduced share: there is no reduced share. Nobody arriving now is served what earlier arrivals didn’t finish. Only one distinction remains — those who call on him and those who don’t — and nobody is born on the wrong side of that line.

parallels.desc: whoever believes will not be in haste

verseByVerse.quote: For "everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved” (v. 13, quoting Joel 2:32). Paul applies to Jesus a promise about calling on the LORD — Israel’s God. The way of salvation is the cry of someone who has nothing else, calling on Jesus’ name.

The name. In Joel the name is the covenant name of God given at the burning bush — the name a synagogue reader would not pronounce, saying “Adonai” instead. Paul applies that sentence, about that name, to Jesus of Nazareth without a word of justification. A man trained as a Pharisee, who handled the sacred name with great care all his life, hands it to a Galilean executed in his own lifetime — in a subordinate clause, as proof of something else. He is not arguing that Jesus is divine. He is reasoning from it. The highest claim in the chapter is made in its quietest sentence.

Prepared for four verses. “confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord” (v. 9); “the same Lord is Lord of all” (v. 12); now “everyone who calls on the name of the Lord.” The title moves from confession, to scope, to the covenant name of God, without changing hands.

Saved from what? In Joel the promise follows the day of the LORD: the sun turned to darkness and the moon to blood “before the great and awesome day of the LORD comes” (Joel 2:31). It is rescue with a date and a danger. Romans has named the danger: wrath revealed from heaven (1:18), the day of wrath a hard heart stores up (2:5). This verse is the way out of that day, and it has one moving part.

Calling. Not eloquence or correctness, but what a person does with no options left and one name to say. It became the earliest description of Christians: “all those who in every place call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 1:2); in Damascus Saul had authority “to bind all who call on your name” (Acts 9:14). The church’s first name for itself was a verb.

The thief. A man being executed — no time to make amends, nothing to restore, no changed life to point to, hands not even free. He has a mouth and a name: “Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom” (Luke 23:42). He is told, “today.” Paul’s “everyone” is at least that wide.

Two guards. It is not a formula; calling is the sound faith makes, not a lever on God, and lips can say these words with nothing behind them (Matthew 7:21). And for the one who called and felt nothing back: the promise is “will be saved,” not “will feel saved.” God attaches himself to the calling, not the sensation. Many calls he answered were made by people sure they spoke into an empty room.

A test. Remember not the best prayer you ever prayed but the shortest one you meant — two or three words at an hour you would rather not describe. That is the verb in this verse, and it is all that is asked. In Joel the name was too holy to pronounce. In Paul it is the one thing a dying man can still get out. Call on it today.

parallels.desc: everyone who calls on the name of the LORD shall be saved

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–21 — The Sent Preacher and Israel's Unbelief
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The logic of the gospel creates a missionary chain that runs backwards from salvation to sending: how can anyone call on one in whom they have not believed? How can they believe in one they have not heard? How can they hear without someone preaching? How can anyone preach unless they are sent? Paul quotes Isaiah 52:7 — "How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the good news!" — and the beauty he celebrates is not aesthetic but teleological: the feet that carry the gospel are beautiful because of what they carry and what their arrival means for those who hear.

The rhetorical questions tighten the logic inexorably: sending → preaching → hearing → believing → calling → saved. Remove any link and the chain breaks. This is Paul's theological argument for the absolute necessity of gospel proclamation. The sovereignty of God in election does not make preaching unnecessary; it makes preaching the instrument through which God calls his elect. "Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ" (v. 17). The word is the means; the Spirit works through the means; the elect hear and believe. Preach.

The chain does not then run smoothly to its conclusion, and v. 16 is where Paul says so: But they have not all obeyed the gospel. Every link held. They were sent, they preached, Israel heard — and it was not believed. Paul reaches for Isaiah again, and the line he takes is the first verse of Isaiah 53, in the middle of the fourth Servant Song: Lord, who has believed what he has heard from us? (Isaiah 53:1). It stands immediately before the description of the man despised and rejected, pierced for our transgressions. So the unbelief being grieved here is not a late development. It was written into the prophecy of the cross itself: the servant was foretold as one who would not be believed.

The chapter ends with the testimony of Israel's own scriptures against Israel's unbelief. Have they not heard? Yes — all the earth has heard (v. 18). Did they not understand? Yes — Moses had already anticipated a day when Israel would be provoked to jealousy by a foolish nation (v. 19; Deuteronomy 32:21).

And then Isaiah, whom Paul says is so bold as to put it like this: I have been found by those who did not seek me; I have shown myself to those who did not ask for me (v. 20; Isaiah 65:1). That is the hardest sentence in the chapter for anyone who assumes that finding God is the reward for looking for him. God turns up among people who were not enquiring, while the people who held the oracles do not come. Israel's rejection is not ignorance; it is disobedience (v. 21) — the stretching out of God's hands to a disobedient and contrary people. The love of God remains; the response of Israel does not.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Necessity of Preaching

Romans 10:14–17 is the most important New Testament text on the theology of preaching. Preaching is not one option among many for communicating the gospel; it is the divinely appointed means by which faith comes. The Spirit of God works through the proclaimed word — the word heard, the word believed — to create the faith that saves. This is why the Reformed tradition has always given preaching the central place in worship: not as a performance or an educational exercise but as the means of grace through which God speaks and through which his people hear. "Faith comes from hearing" — and hearing requires a preacher, and a preacher requires a sending. The missionary imperative is embedded in the very logic of salvation.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The "beautiful feet" of Isaiah 52:7 originally referred to the herald who would bring to Jerusalem the news that the exile was over — Babylon had fallen, and God's people were coming home. Paul applies this image to the heralds of the new exodus: those who proclaim that sin, death, and the wrath of God have been overcome in Christ. The gospel is the announcement that the exile from God is over; the journey home has begun. Now: In an age that has substituted social media presence, personal authenticity, and lifestyle witness for the proclamation of the gospel, Romans 10:14–17 is a direct challenge: people are not saved by our online presence or our admirable lives. They are saved by hearing the word of Christ. We must preach — in whatever form that takes in our cultural moment — because faith comes by hearing.

verseByVerse.quote: How then will they call on him in whom they have not believed? And how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard? And how are they to hear without someone preaching? And how are they to preach unless they are sent? As it is written, 'How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the good news!' — Romans 10:14–15
verseByVerse.commentary:
How can people call on someone they have not believed? Believe in someone they have never heard of? Hear without a preacher? Preach unless sent? “How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the good news!” For anyone to be saved, the gospel must be carried and spoken.

The chain runs backwards. Paul has said everyone who calls will be saved. So he works upstream: what must have happened for anyone to call? Belief; hearing; preaching; sending. The chain ends at a passive verb — “unless they are sent.” Somebody else acts first. No one in the sequence appoints himself, and the sending finally comes from God, arriving in ordinary shoe leather.

Election and preaching. That settles a common objection: if God has chosen his people, isn’t preaching a formality? Paul argues the reverse. The God who appointed the harvest appointed the plough, and no farmer certain of a crop leaves the seed in the barn. Election doesn’t make proclamation optional; it makes it worth doing, because God’s word “shall not return to me empty” (Isaiah 55:11).

The word got near through a mouth. “The word is near you, in your mouth” (v. 8). But ask how it got into your mouth: it was in someone else’s first.

Beautiful feet. Isaiah 52 pictures a city waiting for news with no way to get it; word travelled at the speed of a man’s legs. What a watchman sees first, as a runner crests the ridge, is feet. “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news” (Isaiah 52:7). Nobody thought feet beautiful; they were the dirtiest part of a person, washed by a household slave. They are lovely because of what is attached further up. And the herald shouts: peace, good news, salvation, and “Your God reigns” — the exile is over; there has been a change of government; you can go home. That is the announcement of v. 9. The herald on the ridge cries “Your God reigns”; the believer at the bottom says “Jesus is Lord.”

A question. Who told you? Not who taught you later — who first put it into words in your hearing? A parent, a colleague, a teacher, someone who said it badly and said it anyway. You stand at the end of a line of feet and can usually name the last pair. Then ask: who told them? And who will you tell?

A guard. This passage is often used for pressure, which is not what it does. The verb is passive, so no one must manufacture a calling not given; the chain needs senders as well as goers. Nor are you responsible for the result; the next verse says preaching and believing are two things. What it establishes is that the message must travel, and that people are not saved by the light they already have. Creation leaves a person without excuse (1:20); only the gospel saves.

Can people be saved without hearing? Some Christians hold a wider hope: that God may save people who respond to the light of creation or conscience, or who meet Christ at the moment of death. They point to Cornelius (Acts 10), to 2:14–16, and to Psalm 19, which Paul himself quotes in v. 18. But Cornelius is the strongest case against it. Devout as he was, an angel told him to send for Peter, who “will declare to you a message by which you will be saved” (Acts 11:14). Scripture gives no promise to those who never hear; it gives a command to go. What God does with infants and those unable to understand is a different question (cf. 7:9).

Who are the sent? Paul has in mind heralds sent to proclaim publicly, and the church still recognizes and sends such people, as the church at Antioch sent Barnabas and Saul (Acts 13:1–3). But ordinary Christians need no commission to speak of Christ. When persecution scattered the Jerusalem church, “those who were scattered went about preaching the word” (Acts 8:4), and every believer is to be “prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you” (1 Pet 3:15). The public ministry of the word belongs to those the church sends; the witness belongs to all. There was probably nothing striking about the person who told you. The beauty was in what they carried.

parallels.desc: how beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news

verseByVerse.quote: But they have not all obeyed the gospel. For Isaiah says, 'Lord, who has believed what he has heard from us?' — Romans 10:16
verseByVerse.commentary:
But not all have obeyed the gospel. As Isaiah said, “Lord, who has believed what he has heard from us?” Faithful preaching does not guarantee faith. The messenger’s task is faithfulness; the results belong to God.

“Not all.” Paul does not write that Israel has not obeyed but “not all.” That keeps the remnant standing, explains why chapter 11 can ask whether God has rejected his people and answer no, and stops this becoming a verdict on a whole nation. And it is the same Greek word as the “everyone” of vv. 11–13, turned over. The word that was a promise has become a measurement, and the measurement comes back short.

Where Isaiah says it. “Who has believed what he has heard from us?” is the first line of Isaiah 53. The next lines describe a man with “no form or majesty that we should look at him… despised and rejected… pierced for our transgressions.” So it is not a complaint about a hard audience; it is the preface to the report, and the report is a crucified man. The difficulty was never poor delivery. It is what the message says — the stone of 9:33.

“Obeyed.” You don’t normally obey news; nobody obeys a weather forecast. But this news announces a change of government (v. 15), and such an announcement puts you under someone. That is why unbelief in this chapter is described as refusal, not error: “they did not submit” (v. 3), “not all obeyed” (v. 16), “a disobedient and contrary people” (v. 21).

For the one who has kept telling. The person most likely to read this verse hard is not a preacher but a mother who has told her son for eleven years, a man whose brother changes the subject, someone who brought a friend to church and watched him go quietly cold. Look at Isaiah’s commission: “Go, and say to this people: ‘Keep on hearing, but do not understand’” (Isaiah 6:9). He asked, “How long, O Lord?” and was told, “Until cities lie waste without inhabitant” (Isaiah 6:11). If faithfulness were measured by response, Isaiah failed for a lifetime, and so did Paul with his own people.

A guard. “Results belong to God” is true and is also the standard excuse of the lazy and cold. Look at how Isaiah’s despair is phrased: “Lord, who has believed…?” It is not a shrug to an audience but a grief handed upward. Paul’s own response to his people’s unbelief was to pray (v. 1).

A test. When the person who won’t believe comes up, listen to what you say about them when they aren’t in the room. Is it Isaiah’s sentence, with “Lord” at the front and a real ache behind it? Or a verdict, given to someone else, about a case you have privately closed? The words can be almost identical. Only one is still praying. Turn it back into prayer today.

parallels.desc: who has believed what he has heard from us?

verseByVerse.quote: So faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ. — Romans 10:17
verseByVerse.commentary:
“So faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ.” Faith is not produced by argument, feeling or social pressure alone. The Holy Spirit creates it through the message about Christ, when it is heard.

“So” — drawn from Isaiah. Paul draws this from the verse he just quoted. Isaiah’s “what he has heard from us” uses a word meaning both the act of hearing and the report heard. If faith is what was missing when the report went out, faith is what comes by the report.

A specific message. This is not a general recommendation of listening. Faith comes through a message with content: “the word of Christ.” Not a word about God in general, not encouragement or religious atmosphere. The report is about him, and no other report does this.
