That is why careful, faithful exposition of what Scripture actually says has always been central in the Reformed tradition: it is the word of Christ that creates faith.

“I wish I had more faith.” Almost everyone says it, and tries to fix it inwardly — concentrating, resolving, trying to feel more certain. It doesn’t work, because faith is not a substance you press harder on. It is a response, and a response needs something to respond to.

A test, run backwards. Think of the season when your faith was thickest — not happiest, thickest, when God was most obviously real — and ask what you were doing in the weeks before. Then think of the thinnest stretch and ask what had quietly stopped. The answers are rarely mysterious. Under the word, faith thickens; away from it, it thins, so gradually that the person it happens to is usually the last to notice. Put yourself under the word this week — daily, and on Sunday.

Two guards. Hearing is necessary, not automatic; v. 16 says not all who heard obeyed, and 2:13 said hearers of the law are not justified. You can sit under preaching for forty years without receiving it. And “hearing” is not about ears. The housebound believer with a Bible open, the deaf believer watching an interpreter, the prisoner reading in a cell — the word of Christ is arriving, and does there what it does in a full church. What the verse rules out is faith coming from anywhere other than the message.

Christ still speaking. Paul writes elsewhere that Christ “came and preached peace to you who were far off” (Ephesians 2:17) — to people in Asia Minor who never saw him in the flesh. He preached to them through messengers. So the sermon next Sunday, imperfectly delivered by a tired man with a cold, is not merely a report about a distant event. It is the risen Christ still speaking. That is why the preacher’s business is to get out of the way. Someone else is talking.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “the word of God.”

verseByVerse.quote: But I ask, have they not heard? Indeed they have, for "Their voice has gone out to all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world." But I ask, did Israel not understand? First Moses says, "I will make you jealous of those who are not a nation; with a foolish nation I will make you angry."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Have they not heard? They have: “Their voice has gone out to all the earth.” Did Israel not understand? Moses foretold it: “I will make you jealous of those who are not a nation.” Israel cannot plead that the message never reached them; and God’s turning to the Gentiles was meant to win Israel back.

Who has heard? Paul is not claiming every human being has now heard the gospel. Five chapters later he says his ambition is “to preach the gospel, not where Christ has already been named” (15:20), because whole regions have not yet been told (15:21). The point is that Israel cannot plead ignorance. The message had been announced in their synagogues, in their language, by their own countrymen, for a generation.

Borrowing the sky. Psalm 19 is about the heavens: “The heavens declare the glory of God… their voice goes out through all the earth.” A testimony with no translator and no border. Paul is not proving from a psalm about stars that the gospel has reached every village. He borrows its picture of reach: the announcement has gone out the way daylight goes out. And it closes a circle from 1:20, where the sky left people without excuse. Now the message that can save has travelled the same roads.

Moses: measure for measure. Deuteronomy 32:21 in full: “They have made me jealous with what is no god; they have provoked me to anger with their idols. So I will make them jealous with those who are no people; I will provoke them to anger with a foolish nation.” Israel gave God’s love to a no-god; God gives his love to a no-people. The Gentiles are not the better party promoted. They are chosen precisely because nobody counted them.

In their hymnbook. This is the Song of Moses, which Moses was told to teach Israel by heart before they entered the land, as a witness against them in a future they had not yet lived (Deuteronomy 31:19–21). Israel had sung it for centuries. Did Israel not understand? They had it memorised.

Jealousy to win back. God does not say he will replace them but make them jealous — worth doing only if you mean to get someone back. Paul makes this explicit: his Gentile ministry aims to “make my fellow Jews jealous, and thus save some of them” (11:14). Not punishment but a recovery operation conducted in public.

A test. Jealousy works only on something that looks worth having. Nobody envies a life that seems joyless, anxious and duty-bound. Would anyone watching you at close range — at home, unedited, when things go wrong — want what you have? This is not a call to perform contentment; that provokes only suspicion. It is a call to go and get some, from the word v. 17 just named, so that there is something to envy.

A guard for Gentiles. The terms are “no people” and “a foolish nation.” The grafted branch has no grounds for looking down at the broken one, as chapter 11 will say at length (11:18–20). Refused by the people he had carried for fifteen centuries, God did not withdraw. He went and was visibly loved somewhere else, in front of them — a strange thing to do unless you mean to be missed.

parallels.desc: their voice goes out through all the earth
I will make them jealous with those who are no people

verseByVerse.quote: Then Isaiah is so bold as to say, "I have been found by those who did not seek me; I have shown myself to those who did not ask for me." But of Israel he says, "All day long I have held out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaiah boldly says, “I have been found by those who did not seek me; I have shown myself to those who did not ask for me.” But of Israel: “All day long I have held out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people.” God was found by those not looking, and held out his arms all day to those who refused him.

“So bold as to say.” The verb means to throw caution aside. The outrage was not that God saves Gentiles — Isaiah says so often — but the manner: God let himself be found by people who weren’t looking. For some readers this is the best sentence in the chapter. People frightened by chapter 9, quietly sure they are not chosen, usually offer the same evidence against themselves: I didn’t really want this; I came late, or badly, or for the wrong reasons. Verse 20 removes that evidence. Not seeking is the qualification of those God says found him.

Consecutive verses. Verse 20 is Isaiah 65:1 and verse 21 is Isaiah 65:2. Paul didn’t hunt for a counterweight; he kept reading, and sovereign grace and human refusal lay side by side in one paragraph. That answers a damaging way of reading chapter 9. Close the book at the potter and you have a God who settles everything over people’s heads. A chapter later the same apostle ends with God in a doorway with arms out, and assigns the loss to a people who would not come. “Contrary” means answering back — the very posture 9:20 said the clay had no standing for, now shown to be what the clay did. Both stand.

Arms out all day. Hold your arms straight out and see how long before your shoulders burn. Two minutes is hard. “All day long I have held out my hands.” Picture a parent in a doorway, arms open from morning to dark, while a child walks past again and again. Jesus said the same over the same city: “How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!” (Luke 13:34). Not could not — would not.

Where the hands went. Isaiah was not writing about the cross, and it would be dishonest to say so. But a Christian cannot read this without seeing where those hands went in the end: held out, outside the walls of the city they were held out to, nailed open, for six hours.

A test before you pray tonight. When you come back to God after neglect, what posture do you picture him in? Most people picture folded arms, a turned back, or at best cool patience. This verse says arms out — and says it of people refusing him at the time. Whatever you imagine, the text has described his posture, and it is not the one you are bracing for. Come.

An honest word. A day has an evening. Romans has warned against reading God’s patience as indifference (2:4–5). “All day long” measures extraordinary endurance; it is not a promise the arms will never come down. Yet the chapter ends not with a bolted door but a posture still held, and the very next sentence asks whether God has rejected his people and answers, “By no means!” (11:1). The hands are still out because the argument is not finished.

parallels.desc: I was ready to be found by those who did not seek me
I spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people

10.text: <sup>1</sup>Brothers, my heart’s desire and prayer to God for them is that they may be saved.<sup>2</sup>For I bear them witness that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge.<sup>3</sup>For, being ignorant of the righteousness of God, and seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to God’s righteousness.<sup>4</sup>For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.<sup>5</sup>For Moses writes about the righteousness that is based on the law, that the person who does the commandments shall live by them.<sup>6</sup>But the righteousness based on faith says, “Do not say in your heart, ’Who will ascend into heaven?’” (that is, to bring Christ down)<sup>7</sup>“or ’Who will descend into the abyss?’” (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead).<sup>8</sup>But what does it say? “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart” (that is, the word of faith that we proclaim);<sup>9</sup>because, if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.<sup>10</sup>For with the heart one believes and is justified, and with the mouth one confesses and is saved.<sup>11</sup>For the Scripture says, “Everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame.”<sup>12</sup>For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek; for the same Lord is Lord of all, bestowing his riches on all who call on him.<sup>13</sup>For “everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.”<sup>14</sup>How then will they call on him in whom they have not believed? And how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard? And how are they to hear without someone preaching?<sup>15</sup>And how are they to preach unless they are sent? As it is written, “How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the good news!”<sup>16</sup>But they have not all obeyed the gospel. For Isaiah says, “Lord, who has believed what he has heard from us?”<sup>17</sup>So faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ.<sup>18</sup>But I ask, have they not heard? Indeed they have, for “Their voice has gone out to all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.”<sup>19</sup>But I ask, did Israel not understand? First Moses says, “I will make you jealous of those who are not a nation; with a foolish nation I will make you angry.”<sup>20</sup>Then Isaiah is so bold as to say, “I have been found by those who did not seek me; I have shown myself to those who did not ask for me.”<sup>21</sup>But of Israel he says, “All day long I have held out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people.”

11.title: The Mystery of Israel and the Doxology of Grace
11.overview:
Romans 11 completes the great argument about Israel that began in chapter 9. Paul has shown that God's word has not failed (chapter 9) and that Israel has heard and not believed (chapter 10). Now he asks: has God rejected his people? The answer is again the most emphatic negative in the letter: By no means! God has not cast away the people he foreknew. The evidence: Paul himself is a Jew, a descendant of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin — and he has believed. The remnant is real.

But the chapter moves beyond the remnant to the mystery: Israel's hardening has served the purpose of Gentile inclusion, and Gentile inclusion is the means by which Israel will eventually be provoked to jealousy and saved. The olive tree image (vv. 17–24) holds the whole argument together: natural branches were broken off; wild branches were grafted in; the natural branches can and will be grafted back in. The God of the olive tree is the God of Israel's future. And that future ends not in permanent rejection but in the breathtaking statement: "all Israel will be saved" (v. 26).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Remnant: God Has Not Rejected His People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"Has God rejected his people? By no means!" The vehemence of Paul's denial is significant — the same mē genoito he has used throughout the letter for the most outrageous misunderstandings of the gospel. The question of Israel's rejection is in the same category as the question of whether God is unjust (9:14) or whether we should sin that grace may abound (6:1). The answer is the same: unthinkable.

Paul's primary evidence is himself. He is a Jew. He has believed in Jesus as Messiah. Therefore God has not totally rejected Israel, because here is at least one Israelite who has been saved — and not the most promising one, either. The former persecutor of the church, the man who breathed threats and murder against the disciples of Jesus, stands as Exhibit A for the continued saving purposes of God toward Israel.

The parallel with Elijah (vv. 2–4) is instructive: when Elijah was convinced he was the only faithful Israelite left, God corrected him — seven thousand had not bowed to Baal. The prophet's perception of total abandonment was wrong. Paul draws the application: there is a remnant chosen by grace. Not by works, not by ancestry — by grace. And where grace operates, it is no longer works; the two principles are mutually exclusive. The remnant is real, small though it appears.

Then comes the harder half of the section, and it is not an appendix to the remnant — it is the same breath. What then? Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking. The elect obtained it, but the rest were hardened (v. 7). Three parties in one line: Israel as a whole, the elect within it, and the rest. Paul has just insisted that God has not rejected his people; he now says that most of them are hardened. The chapter is written by a man who saw no contradiction between those two sentences, and it cannot be read by anyone who holds only one of them.

The hardening is given scriptural warrant from two places welded together (v. 8) — God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that would not see and ears that would not hear, Isaiah 29:10 joined to Deuteronomy 29:4. The Deuteronomy setting repays knowing. Moses stands at the end of the wilderness years reciting what the people have watched with their own eyes: the plagues, the sea, forty years of bread out of the sky. His verdict on all of it is that to this day the LORD has not given you a heart to understand. Evidence was never the missing ingredient.

Then David (vv. 9–10), and the psalm is not chosen at random. Psalm 69 is the psalm of the righteous sufferer, the one the evangelists reach for to describe the cross — zeal for your house has consumed me; for my thirst they gave me sour wine to drink. Paul turns its imprecation on those who rejected the very sufferer it was describing. And notice what is asked to become a snare: their table. Not their enemies, not their circumstances. Their provision. The privileges listed back in 9:4–5 are the things they trip over.

None of which is the section’s last word, and it would misrepresent Paul to stop here. His very next sentence asks whether they stumbled in order that they might fall, and answers it with the same violent negative this section opened with.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Remnant Principle in Scripture

The remnant theology of Romans 11:1–10 runs through the entire Old Testament: Isaiah's "remnant of Israel" (Isaiah 10:20–22), Micah's "remnant of Jacob," the faithful seven thousand in Elijah's day. God has never saved the entire nation of Israel simply by virtue of their physical membership in the covenant people; he has always worked through a called, believing remnant within the larger community. This remnant is not self-selecting; it is chosen by grace. Paul's point is that this has always been God's method — the new covenant does not represent a change in approach but a clarification and fulfilment of the approach God has always taken.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The seven thousand who had not bowed to Baal were invisible to Elijah — unknown to him, underground, silent. The remnant of God is often invisible to human perception. The prophet who declares the cause lost may be wrong; God's remnant is not necessarily visible or audible. Now: In seasons when the church appears to be in irreversible decline — when the statistics are grim and the cultural momentum runs entirely against Christian faith — the Elijah phenomenon is a perpetual danger: "I alone am left." The church is always smaller than it should be and larger than it appears. God preserves what he has promised to preserve.

verseByVerse.quote: I ask, then, has God rejected his people? By no means! For I myself am an Israelite, a descendant of Abraham, a member of the tribe of Benjamin. God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Has God rejected his people? “By no means!” Paul himself is the proof: an Israelite, from Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin, and a believer. “God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew.” God set his love on Israel beforehand, and their present unbelief cannot cancel it.

The question his argument forced. Chapter 10 ended with God’s hands held out all day to a people who would not come. Any reader is forming the sentence: then that is the end of them. Paul asks it aloud before anyone else can, and recoils with his strongest negative — kept for conclusions that would wreck the gospel (3:31; 6:1; 9:14). The argument follows in the next breath, and its first piece is startling.

He points at himself. Not at the thousands of Jewish believers in Jerusalem, which would have been statistically stronger, but one man, named — and the one with the worst record: the man who held the coats while Stephen was stoned and approved of it (Acts 7:58; 8:1), who then dragged believers from their houses. The proof that God has not finished with Israel is a Jew who had done his best to finish the church.

Benjamin. The smallest tribe. Saul, its most famous son, protested his anointing: “Am I not a Benjaminite, from the least of the tribes of Israel?” (1 Samuel 9:21). Paul opens a section on a remnant by naming himself from the tribe that was itself a remnant. Smallness has never been evidence that God has left the building.

“Whom he foreknew.” Not that God knew in advance how they would turn out — that would be cold comfort, since how they turned out is the problem. To “know” here is to have set your regard on someone: “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you” (Jeremiah 1:5). The same verb opens the chain of 8:29. The relationship did not begin with them, so it does not end with them.

For the one who thinks God has finished with them. The person reading this most slowly may not be thinking about Israel but about themselves — after the same sin the ninth time, after years of nothing. Watch Paul’s method. He does not look inward or take anyone’s spiritual temperature. He points to a person and a history: something God did, at a date, to a man not looking for it.

A test. When the fear comes that you are finished, what do you go and look at? Most of us look at our feelings — like checking the weather to find out whether you are married. Write down instead one thing God has done that you could testify to in court: an event, not a mood. A day. A change you did not manufacture. That kind of evidence does not move when you do.

A guard. What Paul establishes here is precise: God has not rejected his people, and the proof is Jewish people who believe in Jesus. It is a remnant argument. The larger claim about Israel’s future comes at v. 26, and he says nothing here about territory or politics. Taking less than he says empties the chapter; taking more borrows his authority for something he did not write. Whatever holds Israel, it is plainly not Israel’s grip.

parallels.desc: the LORD will not forsake his people

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not know what the Scripture says of Elijah, how he appeals to God against Israel? "Lord, they have killed your prophets, they have demolished your altars, and I alone am left, and they seek my life." But what is God's reply to him? "I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elijah complained to God against Israel: “They have killed your prophets… and I alone am left.” God answered: “I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal.” The faithful were invisible to Elijah, but not to God — and it was God who had kept them.

After the triumph. Elijah had just won the greatest public victory in the Old Testament: Carmel, the nation watching, the prophets of Baal crying to a god who did not answer, fire from a clear sky on a soaked altar. Then one threat from Jezebel, and he ran a day’s journey into the wilderness, sat under a broom tree, and asked to die. The collapse came after success, not failure. The dangerous ground is often the week after the thing went well, when the adrenaline drains and one piece of bad news arrives. Anyone who has crashed on Monday after a Sunday that went beautifully has been under that tree.

Sleep and food first. God did not correct his theology. He let him sleep, fed him, let him sleep again, fed him again (1 Kings 19:5–8). Only after forty days’ walking came “the sound of a low whisper” and the number. Some of what presents as a crisis of faith is a body that hasn’t been fed or slept, and God treats it accordingly first. Look after yourself before you conclude the worst.

Intercession in reverse. Elijah “appeals to God against Israel.” The prophet’s office was to plead for the people; here he prosecutes them. Despair rarely stays private. Given time it builds a case, usually against the people you were called to.

Despair edits the file. “I alone am left” was not just overstatement. A chapter earlier Obadiah had told Elijah to his face that he had hidden “a hundred men of the LORD’s prophets by fifties in a cave and fed them with bread and water” (1 Kings 18:13). Elijah knew, and still said he was the only one.

“I have kept for myself.” God does not say seven thousand stood firm, but that he kept them, for himself. Their survival is a statement about his grip, not their stamina — which is exactly Paul’s point, since the remnant is about to be defined by grace. And their faithfulness is described only negatively: they “have not bowed the knee.” No movement, no platform — just people who, when everyone else bent, did not. If your obedience feels like nothing more than things you did not do, you are in the register God chose to count.

You cannot see the whole board. When the cause looks lost — grim statistics, a hostile culture, your church greying — the Elijah reflex is not to say things are hard but to assume you see everything. You don’t. The church is always smaller than it should be and larger than it appears, and God has never felt obliged to introduce you to the seven thousand.

A test. Think of the last time you said, “there’s nobody left.” Then count. Name the people you know who have not bowed — not the impressive ones, the quiet ones: the colleague who won’t join in, the woman who has visited the same housebound member for nine years, the embarrassed teenager who goes anyway. Most people who do this honestly are surprised. Thank God for them, and tell one of them.

A guard. Remnant doctrine has a smug cousin: the small faithful group that has begun to enjoy being small. Nobody in the seven thousand knew they were being counted, and the man sure he had the roll was the one who had it wrong. And God sent Elijah back down with three errands — two kings to anoint and a successor to call (1 Kings 19:15–16). The cure for a man who wanted to die was food, a fact, and a list of things to do on Thursday.

parallels.desc: I, even I only, am left
seven thousand who have not bowed to Baal

verseByVerse.quote: So too at the present time there is a remnant, chosen by grace. But if it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works; otherwise grace would no longer be grace. — Romans 11:5–6
verseByVerse.commentary:
So now too there is a remnant, “chosen by grace.” And if it is by grace, it is not by works; otherwise grace would no longer be grace. The remnant exists because God chose freely, not because some were better.

“At the present time.” Elijah is not just a nice parallel from long ago. What was true on that mountain is happening in Paul’s own decade. The remnant is not God’s emergency measure for a bad generation. It is the ordinary shape of how he has always saved: never a whole nation by birth, always a people kept within it.

“Chosen by grace.” Literally, “according to the election of grace.” There is a choosing underneath the remnant, and it is made of the same stuff as grace. The remnant is not the group that turned out better. It is the group that was chosen, by a God whose choosing is gift all the way down.

No mixing. Verse 6 closes off the compromise every religious person reaches for: mostly grace, with some contribution. Grace and works are not ingredients to blend; they are rival accounts of where the outcome came from. Being given a house is different from buying one at a discount. Make the discount ninety-nine per cent; the deed still says “sold,” and the buyer can still say what he paid. Grace is not a very large discount. It is a different kind of transaction.

Why say the obvious? Because the instinct never quits. Grace will not stay where you put it — agreed on Sunday, quietly renegotiated by Wednesday, and the renegotiation comes disguised as seriousness.

Where it hides. Listen to how you explain other people’s faith. “She was always a seeker.” “He had a good upbringing.” “They were the sort who would respond.” Each is a small denial of verse 6 — locating something in the person that explains the outcome. And the same instinct runs the other way about those who haven’t come: “he was always hard; that family was never going to.”

A test. Take the last two or three people you know who came to faith and notice the explanation you reached for. If it was a fact about them, you told yourself the story verse 6 rules out. That is the seed of the arrogance Paul confronts twelve verses later, when the Gentile reader starts explaining why the branches were broken off. Thank God instead for what he did.

A guard. This does not make obedience optional; the man who wrote v. 6 wrote chapter 12. Works are evidence, never the ground (see on 2:7–8). What v. 6 forbids is not effort but invoicing. Nobody in the remnant is there for a reason he could name. That makes it a remnant, not an élite.

verseByVerse.quote: What then? Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking. The elect obtained it, but the rest were hardened, as it is written, "God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that would not see and ears that would not hear, down to this very day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking. The elect obtained it; the rest were hardened, as Scripture says: “God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that would not see and ears that would not hear, down to this very day.” The hardening is God’s judicial response to a refusal already made.

They were seeking. This is not a nation that stopped caring. They were still in the synagogue, still keeping the calendar, still with “a zeal for God” (10:2). Set that beside 10:20, where God was found by people not looking at all. The searchers missed it; those not searching were found. Seeking is not the same as receiving. A person can look very hard in a direction he has already decided the answer must lie.

The failure. Paul has said it twice: they sought it “as if it were based on works” (9:32) and would not submit to righteousness as a gift (10:3). What they wanted arrived in a form they had ruled out in advance, and it went past them.

A test. Name something you are asking God for. Now name the form you have privately decided the answer must take. Most of us have one and have never said it aloud. What would have to be true for you to recognise the answer in another shape — slower, smaller, through someone you don’t like, or as a door closing? Israel’s tragedy was not indifference. It was a specification. Tell God you will take his answer in his shape.

Hardened — by whom? Paul writes “were hardened,” with no agent named, the same reticence as 9:22. But he doesn’t hide behind the grammar, because the next line says “God gave them a spirit of stupor.” We should not be tidier than he is.

The picture behind it. Isaiah: “Be drunk, but not with wine; stagger, but not with strong drink! For the LORD has poured out upon you a spirit of deep sleep” (Isaiah 29:9–10). Not blindness that knows itself, but a stupor — a man certain he is thinking clearly whose gait tells everyone else he is not. And Moses: “to this day the LORD has not given you a heart to understand or eyes to see or ears to hear” (Deuteronomy 29:4). Something withheld, not added. An understanding heart is a gift, never standard equipment, and the judgment at its most terrible is God declining to supply what was never owed (cf. 1:24). And “to this very day” has been accurate about two different days fourteen centuries apart.

Two guards. To the reader wondering whether he is among the hardened: Paul gives not a feeling but a fact a few verses later: “if they do not continue in their unbelief, [they] will be grafted in, for God has the power to graft them in again” (v. 23). He does not treat hardening as beyond appeal. And to anyone tempted to file someone else under “hardened” and stop praying: nobody watching Saul of Tarsus collect his warrants would have put him anywhere but the second column. He is the one holding the pen.

parallels.desc: the LORD has not given you eyes to see
a spirit of deep sleep

verseByVerse.quote: And David says, "Let their table become a snare and a trap, a stumbling block and a retribution for them; let their eyes be darkened so that they cannot see, and bend their backs forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
David says, “Let their table become a snare and a trap… let their eyes be darkened… and bend their backs forever” (vv. 9–10, quoting Psalm 69:22–23). The privileges meant to lead Israel to Christ became, when Christ was refused, the occasion of their stumbling.

A hard prayer. A modern reader flinches: David asks God to darken people’s eyes, and an apostle quotes it approvingly. Three things in the text make it bearable. The man praying is not nursing a grudge; the hostility is aimed past him at God: “it is for your sake that I have borne reproach” (Psalm 69:7). An imprecation is the opposite of vengeance: a refusal to act, handing the case to the only Judge entitled to hear it. And Paul is not giving us a prayer to use on our neighbours. He is producing evidence that Scripture said this would happen.

The vinegar psalm. Psalm 69 is the one the Gospels use for the crucifixion; it supplies the sour wine on a sponge (John 19:28–29). The psalm that gave the vinegar at Golgotha gives the verdict here. The sufferer and the one rejected are the same figure.

A snare at the table. A snare is set where the animal habitually feeds, on the path it takes without thinking. The “table” was Israel’s place of provision — sacrifices, feasts, Passover, the whole covenant by which God fed them. The trap is in the dining room. And “bend their backs” is the posture of a slave under a load — bitter, because the law was given to people just brought out of slavery. The commandments that were a rescue became a weight, not because they changed but because of what people made them carry.

The One who saw that back. “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest… For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:28–30). Addressed to exactly this posture, by the One the psalm was about.

“Forever”? The word means continually, quoted from a lament, not a verdict on Israel’s last day. Paul knows he will soon write that they can be grafted in again (v. 23). These verses describe a condition, not a closed case.

Your table. What traps a settled Christian is rarely what he already knows is dangerous. It is the privilege: the Bible knowledge that has made him unteachable; the church role that has become his name; the doctrinal precision that began as reverence and now runs on contempt. All good; all his table.

A test. Don’t audit your sins; that ground is guarded. Ask which part of your religious life you have never examined because it is so obviously good. That is where nobody watches, and where this snare is set. A trap at a table only endangers those who keep sitting there. Get up and follow the One who was offered the vinegar.

parallels.desc: let their own table before them become a snare

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–24 — The Olive Tree: Gentiles Grafted In, Israel Recoverable
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The section does not begin at the tree. It begins with a question about the difference between two ways of going down: did they stumble in order that they might fall? (v. 11). The distinction is the whole argument. A stumble is what happens on the way somewhere — you go down, and you get up. A fall, in the sense Paul is denying, is terminal. His answer is the same violent negative that opened the chapter.

What follows is the mechanism, and it is stranger than a consolation. Their trespass has meant salvation for the Gentiles, and that Gentile salvation is aimed back at Israel — so as to make Israel jealous, which is Moses’ own word from Deuteronomy 32:21, quoted a chapter earlier (10:19). Then the arithmetic of v. 12: if their failure has meant riches for the world, how much more their full inclusion. Paul is reasoning from the lesser to the greater, and the reasoning only works if there is a fullness still to come.

Verses 13–14 are more startling than they look, and they are addressed to Gentiles explicitly. Paul says he makes much of his Gentile ministry precisely in order to provoke his own people and save some of them. The apostle to the Gentiles is running a strategy whose second target is Israel; the two ministries are not in competition, and the Gentile church is, without knowing it, part of how God intends to reach the synagogue.

Then two images before the tree. If their rejection meant reconciliation for the world, their acceptance will mean life from the dead (v. 15) — a phrase Paul does not explain, and which readers have taken either as the general resurrection at the end or as a quickening of such magnitude that no smaller word would do. And v. 16: if the firstfruits of the dough are holy, so is the whole lump; if the root is holy, so are the branches. That is the offering of Numbers 15:20–21, where a consecrated portion makes the batch consecrated — a part standing for a whole, which is exactly what a remnant is and exactly what the tree is about to illustrate.

The olive tree is one of the most evocative images in the letter. The cultivated olive tree is Israel — the covenant people, rooted in the patriarchs, sustained by the promises of God. Natural branches (unbelieving Jews) have been broken off — not because God has given up on the tree, but because of unbelief. Wild branches (believing Gentiles) have been grafted in — not because of their natural superiority but purely by grace, "grafted in contrary to nature" (v. 24). The tree itself, its root and its sap, remains unchanged; what changes is which branches are bearing fruit on it.

Paul's warning to the Gentile believers is sharp and pointed: "Do not be arrogant toward the branches" (v. 18). The Gentile who imagines that the Jewish people have been permanently and finally replaced, that God has transferred his covenant purposes entirely and irreversibly to the Gentile church, has not been paying attention to chapters 9–11. God is able to graft the natural branches back in (v. 23). Indeed, he has said he will. The mercy shown to Gentiles is not a reversal of God's purposes for Israel; it is part of the very mechanism by which those purposes will ultimately be fulfilled.

The warning against Gentile pride is not merely a pastoral nicety; it is a theological corrective to supersessionism — the view that God has permanently replaced Israel with the church, that the covenant promises to Abraham and his physical descendants are entirely and exhaustively fulfilled in the Gentile church. Romans 11 will not allow this. The natural branches can be grafted back in; the God of the olive tree has not changed his mind about the tree.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Olive Tree and the Question of Supersessionism

Romans 11:17–24 is the central text in the debate between supersessionism (the church has entirely replaced Israel as the covenant people) and its alternatives. The text resists the supersessionist reading: unbelieving Jews are broken off branches — not dead stumps — and can be grafted back in. The root and richness of the olive tree (the Abrahamic covenant and its promises) remain; what changes is which branches are currently bearing fruit. The Reformed tradition has generally held to a form of "fulfilment theology" — the church is the continuation and fulfilment of Israel — while resisting the conclusion that God's purposes for ethnic Israel are entirely exhausted. Romans 11:25–29 will make this explicit.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Gentile believers in Rome were apparently in danger of looking down on Jewish unbelief with a degree of spiritual smugness. Paul's corrective is immediate: you stand only by faith; the one who broke off natural branches can break off wild ones too. The Gentile's security in the olive tree rests on the same grace that brought him in — and that grace is not a possession he holds, but a gift he receives. Now: Two thousand years of church history have produced exactly the Gentile arrogance Paul warned against — anti-Semitism often wrapped in theological language, the assumption that God has finished with the Jewish people. Romans 11 stands against this permanently. God has not and will not abandon the people he foreknew.

verseByVerse.quote: So I ask, did they stumble in order that they might fall? By no means! Rather, through their trespass salvation has come to the Gentiles, so as to make Israel jealous. Now if their trespass means riches for the world, and if their failure means riches for the Gentiles, how much more will their full inclusion mean!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Did Israel stumble so as to fall for good? “By no means!” Through their trespass salvation came to the Gentiles, to make Israel jealous. And if their failure brought riches to the world, how much more will their “full inclusion” bring!

Stumble, not fall. A stumble interrupts a journey; the man who trips is still going somewhere. A fall, as denied here, ends the travelling. Paul does not deny that the stumble had a purpose. He denies the purpose was the fall.

It had street names. They tripped over the stone in Zion (9:32–33). And the result was happening city by city: Paul preaches in the synagogue, is thrown out, and turns to the Gentiles — at Pisidian Antioch, at Corinth, and later at Rome itself (Acts 13:46; 18:6; 28:28).

Jealousy means love remains. Nobody is jealous over something he never wanted. For the provocation to work, the affection must still be there underneath, buried under centuries of refusal but not extinguished. The emotion God intends to stir is evidence of a bond never cut. You can’t make someone jealous of a house they were glad to leave.

Two fullnesses. “Full inclusion” is the word “fullness,” used again at v. 25 of the Gentiles. One fullness at each end of the mystery. And the argument is lesser-to-greater, as at 5:9–10: if the accident produced this much, wait for the intention.

Call sin sin. Paul says riches came “through their trespass.” He does not soften the noun. What God used is still called sin in the same sentence its results are called riches. That is the guard 8:28 needs and seldom gets.

A test. Many of us have an episode we can no longer name honestly, because good came out of it — the marriage that ended, the betrayal, the failure that redirected a life. We start calling it “a blessing in disguise,” and something in us knows that isn’t true and quietly stops trusting the whole account. Say both sentences aloud, in order: “That was wrong. God brought this out of it.” If God can draw the salvation of the nations out of a trespass, the question is not whether he can work with your wreckage, but what he will do when he has something to work with.

verseByVerse.quote: Now I am speaking to you Gentiles. Inasmuch then as I am an apostle to the Gentiles, I magnify my ministry in order somehow to make my fellow Jews jealous, and thus save some of them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul turns to the Gentiles in the church: as apostle to the Gentiles he magnifies his ministry, hoping to make his fellow Jews jealous “and thus save some of them.” His Gentile mission and his hope for Israel serve each other.

He turns his head. “Now I am speaking to you Gentiles.” Claudius had expelled the Jews from Rome years earlier; when they returned, the church had carried on without them and become thoroughly Gentile. That seam runs under the letter and is why chapters 9–11 exist. Paul is speaking to people with Jewish believers sitting behind them who used to lead.

“I magnify my ministry.” Paul deliberately makes much of his work, and says why: he wants it to look like something worth having, because people are watching whom no argument will reach.

“Some.” The man who wished himself accursed for his people (9:3) works with an expectation of “some.” A healthy servant of God holds both: a hope with no ceiling and an estimate with no fantasy. He isn’t managing disappointment in advance. He just isn’t lying to himself about next year.

The modern target. Paul’s hardest audience had heard, grown up inside it, and concluded they knew exactly what it was. Every church has such people: the one raised in it who is finished with it, the minister’s son, the woman who can quote more Scripture than you and won’t go back. You don’t argue them in; they have had the arguments. What Paul reaches for is a spectacle: people visibly better off for the thing they walked away from. Not a performance of happiness, which they will detect at once, but something duller and harder — being demonstrably better off, over years, in the parts of life they can see.

A test. Think of the person you know who has heard it all and is done. What has passed between you recently — argument, or evidence? If everything you have offered is a case, you have been doing the one thing the apostle to the Gentiles decided not to rely on. Show them, this month, what Christ is doing in you, and pray for them by name.

verseByVerse.quote: For if their rejection means the reconciliation of the world, what will their acceptance mean but life from the dead? If the dough offered as firstfruits is holy, so is the whole lump, and if the root is holy, so are the branches.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If Israel’s rejection brought reconciliation to the world, their acceptance will be “life from the dead.” And if the first portion of dough is holy, so is the whole lump; if the root is holy, so are the branches. Israel’s future rests on God’s promises to the patriarchs.

“Life from the dead.” Paul does not explain it, and careful readers take it two ways. Some read it literally: Israel’s acceptance stands so close to the end that the general resurrection follows. Others read it as the strongest metaphor available — a quickening far beyond ordinary revival, Ezekiel’s dry bones standing up. Either fits, but the second is more likely: Paul does not use his usual phrase for the resurrection, and v. 12 speaks of “riches for the world,” suggesting an outpouring of new life among the nations rather than the end itself. Hold it with an open hand.

The feel of it. One other place uses the phrase of a person: the father explaining the music to his resentful elder son: “It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found” (Luke 15:32). That is the note — a door opening on a party someone had stopped expecting.

The dough. Under Numbers 15:20–21 a woman baking from the new harvest gives a lump of the first batch to God before any is baked. Then the whole batch is holy — not each loaf consecrated separately, but because the first piece stood for the rest.

The root. The picture shifts from bread to a plant. Dough is inert; a root is alive and feeding. Branches are holy because they are attached to something holy that nourishes them. Bread cannot be broken off and grafted back — hence the tree that follows. The root is the patriarchs and the promises made to them; Israel is “beloved for the sake of their forefathers” (v. 28) — promises from a God who “swore by himself” because he had no one greater to swear by (Hebrews 6:13).

For the late convert. Some Christians feel their faith is second-hand — no believing family, converted late, always aware of others who have had it since childhood. The holiness here never comes up out of a branch. It comes through the root, and a branch attached last Tuesday draws the same sap as one there sixty years.

A test. What is your assurance resting on right now — a fact about the root, or a fact about your branch? The promise God made, or the health of your own attachment? Both feel like faith from inside. Only one holds in a bad month. Go back to the promise today.
verseByVerse.note: The first portion of dough was offered to God, and it made the whole batch holy. The “root” is the patriarchs.

parallels.desc: a loaf from the first of your dough

verseByVerse.quote: But if some of the branches were broken off, and you, although a wild olive shoot, were grafted in among the others and now share in the nourishing root of the olive tree, do not be arrogant toward the branches. If you are, remember it is not you who support the root, but the root that supports you. — Romans 11:17–18
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some branches were broken off, and you Gentiles, a wild olive shoot, were grafted in and now share the nourishing root. So do not be arrogant toward the branches: you do not support the root; the root supports you. Gentile believers draw life from Israel’s promises, and the right response is humility.

Backwards horticulture. Normally a cultivated cutting is grafted onto hardy wild rootstock. Paul describes the reverse and calls it “contrary to nature” (v. 24). He is not wrong about farming. He points to the one feature nobody would do on purpose — the feature that makes it grace.

“Some.” Not the tree felled, not all the branches. The same care as “save some” (v. 14) and the “partial” hardening of v. 25. Paul is exact about quantities where everyone else reaches for totals.

The branch congratulating itself. “It is not you who support the root, but the root that supports you.” Picture it: a branch held six feet off the ground by something it did not make, cannot see, and could not survive ten minutes without, forming a view about its own contribution.

Is the olive tree Israel or the church? It is one tree: the one people of God, rooted in the promises to Abraham. Some have read the passage as saying the church has simply replaced Israel, so that the Jewish people have no further place in God’s purposes. Dispensational Christians speak instead of two peoples of God with two programmes, Israel and the church. Paul’s picture fits neither. Gentile believers are grafted into Israel’s tree; they do not plant a new one, and they do not grow beside the old one. Unbelieving Jews were broken off, but they can be grafted back in (vv. 23–24). So the church is not Israel’s replacement but Israel continued, with the Gentiles added, which is how Paul can tell Gentile believers that they are “fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God” (Eph 2:19).

An inventory. Name something in your faith that you invented. The Scriptures came through Israel. The God you pray to introduced himself to Abraham, Moses and the prophets. The words you use when you have none of your own are often a psalm by a Jewish king. Your Messiah was circumcised on the eighth day. Nothing on the list is yours; all of it came down the trunk.

The church did not heed this. It must be said plainly. The sin Paul forbids here — Gentile Christians holding Jewish people in contempt — became over the centuries a settled habit of Christendom, dressed in theology and eventually in far worse than words. Romans 11 is a warning given early, in writing, by an apostle, and disregarded. And “do not be arrogant” is a present command: stop it, or don’t carry on. Paul is interrupting something already under way in the room.

A test. How do you speak and think of Jewish people, and of those outside the church generally? Pray this week for Jewish friends and neighbours by name, as people loved for the patriarchs’ sake, whom God can graft in again.
verseByVerse.note: Israel is often pictured as God’s olive tree.

parallels.desc: a green olive tree

verseByVerse.quote: Then you will say, "Branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in." That is true. They were broken off because of their unbelief, but you stand fast through faith. So do not become proud, but fear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You will say, “Branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in.” True — but they were broken off for unbelief, and you stand by faith. “So do not become proud, but fear.” The same principle that removed unbelieving Israel could remove a proud Gentile.

“That is true.” Paul puts the boast in the Gentile’s mouth and, instead of denying it, concedes it. The doctrine in the boast is correct. What he refuses is the inference. That means orthodoxy is no defence. A man can have election exactly right and still draw from it a conclusion Paul answers with “fear.”

Through faith, not because of it. “Broken off because of their unbelief, but you stand fast through faith.” Not because of your faith, as if it were a qualification replacing their lineage. Faith is the manner of holding on, not a possession that entitles you. Nobody stands on his grip. He stands on what he grips.

Two kinds of fear. Three chapters ago Paul said, “you did not receive the spirit of slavery to fall back into fear” (8:15). No contradiction. The fear he forbade is a slave’s fear of not knowing whether he is owned. The fear he commands is the alertness of someone standing somewhere high who understands what is holding him up. One makes you check the rope; the other makes you refuse to climb, or pretend you aren’t on a cliff. It is what Paul means by “work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you” (Philippians 2:12–13). That fear is not the opposite of assurance; it is assurance paying attention. “Let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Corinthians 10:12).

A test. Take a position you hold confidently as biblical — about who is in and who is out, about a group that has gone wrong, about the tradition you left. What does it make you feel toward the people it excludes? If anything in the family of satisfaction, you are the man of v. 19, and Paul’s reply is the same: yes, that is true — now be afraid. Then pray for them.

parallels.desc: let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed

verseByVerse.quote: For if God did not spare the natural branches, neither will he spare you. Note then the kindness and the severity of God: severity toward those who have fallen, but God's kindness to you, provided you continue in his kindness. Otherwise you too will be cut off.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If God did not spare the natural branches, he will not spare you either. “Note then the kindness and the severity of God”: severity toward those who fell, kindness toward you — “provided you continue in his kindness.” Otherwise you too will be cut off.

“Note” — look. Paul turns your head and holds it: look at both, and don’t look away from either.

Severity. The word comes from “to cut off sharply” — a sheer rock face, an edge with nothing gradual. Paul uses it in a paragraph about branches cut off. And “kindness” is the word of 2:4, the kindness meant to lead to repentance. Neither is new information.

One without the other. Many of us have a God who is one and not the other. A God of all kindness can’t account for a cross — no crisis grave enough to require it. A God of all severity can’t account for your continued existence, and the person who holds him usually lives braced. Paul puts both in one sentence because a God who is only one is not the God who is there.

Can a true believer be cut off? Arminian Christians take the verse as a warning that individuals who once truly believed may fall away and be lost. Others read it only of Gentiles as a group, who could be broken off as Israel was. But the “you” here is singular, so the warning reaches each person, and it should not be blunted. It does not mean that one whom God has justified may yet be lost. Those broken off are those who do not continue, and those who do not continue show that their faith was never living: “if they had been of us, they would have continued with us” (1 John 2:19). For the true believer the warning is one of the means by which God keeps him continuing, and the promise of 8:30 stands: those he justified, he also glorified. Nobody has been frightened out of the kingdom by Romans 11:22. Many have been woken up by it.

A test. Read the verse twice and notice which clause you had to make yourself slow down for. Most of us glide over one. If “severity” is the word your eye skips, the God you picture is smaller and safer than the One who cut branches from his own tree. If “kindness” feels as if it must have conditions attached, you have been living under a sentence Christ already served. Pray for the half you skipped.

verseByVerse.quote: And even they, if they do not continue in their unbelief, will be grafted in, for God has the power to graft them in again. For if you were cut from what is by nature a wild olive tree, and grafted, contrary to nature, into a cultivated olive tree, how much more will these, the natural branches, be grafted back into their own olive tree.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even unbelieving Israel, if they do not continue in unbelief, will be grafted in, “for God has the power to graft them in again.” If a wild branch could be grafted into a cultivated tree against nature, how much more will the natural branches be grafted back into “their own olive tree.”

The obstacle is not God’s ability. “God has the power.” In every conversation about a hardened person, ours included, the unspoken assumption is that the case has become too difficult — too many years, too much said, too settled. Paul answers the question nobody asked aloud by stating that God is able, which shows what the doubt was really about.

The harder miracle already happened. The Gentile believer accepts that he was cut from a wild tree and grafted, against nature, into a cultivated one. Then he has granted the harder of the two. Putting a branch back on the tree it grew on is not the astonishing operation. His own presence there is.

“Their own olive tree.” After all the grafting and warning, the tree is still described as theirs. The guest has been given a great deal, but not the deeds.

One condition. “If they do not continue in their unbelief.” Not the years, not the history, not a life spent elsewhere. One thing keeps anyone out, and it is the one thing that can stop (cf. 2 Corinthians 3:16).

A test. Most readers have someone in mind raised inside the faith and now outside it, about whom a quiet verdict has been reached: too far in, too long out. Read v. 24 with that person in view. The branch that once grew on the tree is the case Paul calls easier. He is not promising an outcome; it would be cruel to pretend so. He is telling you which column the case belongs in. Name what you have privately filed as impossible — and pray for it again, remembering the more remarkable grafting has already happened, to you.
verseByVerse.note: Growers normally grafted a cultivated branch onto wild stock; grafting a wild branch into a cultivated tree is, as Paul says, “contrary to nature.”

parallels.desc: when one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–36 — The Mystery, the Promise, and the Doxology
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul reveals a mystery so that the Gentile believers will not become proud: a partial hardening has come on Israel until the full number of Gentiles has come in, and in this way all Israel will be saved, as the prophets foretold of a Deliverer from Zion who will remove ungodliness from Jacob. As regards the gospel, Israel is at present opposed to it for the Gentiles’ sake; as regards God’s choice, they are loved because of the patriarchs, for God does not take back his gifts and call. Just as Gentiles once disobeyed and now have received mercy, so Israel has disobeyed so that they too may receive mercy; God has shut everyone up in disobedience in order to have mercy on all. Paul ends in wonder at the depth of God’s riches, wisdom and knowledge, whose ways no one can trace or advise: all things are from him, through him and to him, and to him be glory for ever.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Irrevocability of God's Covenant Purposes

Romans 11:29 — "the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable" — is the theological capstone of chapters 9–11 and one of the most important statements about God's faithfulness in Scripture. The word translated "irrevocable" (ametamelēta) means without repentance — God does not change his mind about what he has given and whom he has called. Applied to Israel: whatever the full meaning of "all Israel will be saved" (v. 26), it means at minimum that God has not and will not permanently and finally abandon the people he chose. Applied to the individual Christian: the calling and justification God has effected in her life will not be revoked. The golden chain of 8:29–30 and the irrevocability of 11:29 are two sides of the same coin.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The doxology of vv. 33–36 was Paul's own response to the argument he had just made. Having argued through three chapters about divine sovereignty, human responsibility, the mystery of Israel, and the purposes of God — he does not end with a systematic summary. He ends with worship. This is the correct response to the depth of God: not the mastery of a doctrine but the surrender of a doxology. Now: In an age that demands that every theological mystery be resolved into a satisfying rational system, the doxology of Romans 11:33–36 is the necessary reminder: we are not God. The depths of his wisdom and knowledge exceed our categories. The only posture that is finally appropriate before the mystery of divine election and human salvation is the posture Paul strikes: "From him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory forever."

verseByVerse.quote: Lest you be wise in your own sight, I do not want you to be unaware of this mystery, brothers: a partial hardening has come upon Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in. And in this way all Israel will be saved, as it is written, "The Deliverer will come from Zion, he will banish ungodliness from Jacob"; — Romans 11:25–26
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul reveals a “mystery” so the Gentiles will not be proud: a partial hardening has come on Israel “until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in. And in this way all Israel will be saved,” as Scripture says, “The Deliverer will come from Zion.” Israel’s hardening is partial and temporary; God has not finished with his ancient people.

What does “all Israel” mean? Each view has its reasons. Those who take “all Israel” as the whole church of Jews and Gentiles point to 9:6, “not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel,” to Galatians 6:16, and to the words “in this way,” which describe how Israel is saved rather than when. Those who take it as the elect among the Jews throughout history point to the remnant of vv. 1–10. But in this chapter Israel has consistently meant the Jewish people, set over against the Gentiles; v. 25 contrasts Israel’s hardening with the Gentiles’ coming in; and the full inclusion of v. 12 looks for something greater than a remnant. So the more likely reading is a great future turning of Jewish people to Christ. And “in this way” means it will happen as God has always worked, through the gospel and by faith, when the Deliverer banishes ungodliness from Jacob.

The dispensational scheme, or the modern state? Does this support the dispensational scheme, or make the modern state of Israel a fulfilment of prophecy? No. What Paul promises is forgiveness: “when I take away their sins” (v. 27). He says nothing of territory, a rebuilt temple or a thousand-year reign, and a future turning of Jews to Christ fits the amillennial view as easily as any other. Christians may pray for the Jewish people and judge the nation’s politics as they would any other nation’s. What Paul teaches us to long for is that they come to their Messiah.

Medicine for conceit. “Lest you be wise in your own sight.” The greatest disclosure about the future in the letter is given for a pastoral reason: to stop Christians thinking too well of themselves. A reader who leaves vv. 25–26 with a firmer timetable and no change in how he regards anyone has taken the medicine and kept the disease.

“Partial” and “until.” The hardening is “in part” — Paul keeps writing fractions. And “until” is temporal, with an end written into the clause that announces it, which a permanent rejection would not have.

The same door. Paul adapts Isaiah 59:20 as he adapted Deuteronomy at 10:6–8, openly. What matters is the content: a Deliverer comes, ungodliness is banished, sins are taken away (v. 27). That rules out a popular reading the text will not carry: that Israel might be saved on a separate track, without Christ. Chapter 10 insisted on one name to call on and one message to be brought. Paul does not now provide a second door. The hope is enormous, and it is the same hope, by the same means, as everyone else’s.

A test. Take a doctrine you hold firmly — election, the end times, whatever your tradition has made you certain of — and ask what holding it has done to you. Has it made you gentler with those who have it wrong, slower to write anyone off? If it has mostly made you surer you are right, you are holding it in exactly the posture v. 25 was written to prevent.
verseByVerse.note: A “mystery” in the New Testament is something once hidden and now revealed by God. Interpreters differ over whether “all Israel” means the Jewish people as a whole before the end, or the whole company of God’s people, Jew and Gentile. The more natural reading in context is the first: a future turning of the Jewish people to Christ.

parallels.desc: a Redeemer will come to Zion

verseByVerse.quote: "and this will be my covenant with them when I take away their sins." As regards the gospel, they are enemies for your sake. But as regards election, they are beloved for the sake of their forefathers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s covenant is “when I take away their sins.” Regarding the gospel, Israel are enemies — for the Gentiles’ sake. Regarding election, they are “beloved for the sake of their forefathers.” Both are true at once, and the second will prevail.

The promise is forgiveness. “This will be my covenant with them when I take away their sins” (v. 27; cf. Isaiah 27:9; Jeremiah 31:33–34). Not territory or a political settlement. The guarantee of Israel’s future is the removal of sin — what Paul has offered everyone since chapter 3.

“Enemies for your sake.” Not merely enemies, to be looked down on, but enemies in a way that worked to your advantage. The hostility a proud Gentile might feel superior to is what opened the door he walked through. The only posture left is gratitude, which cannot be combined with contempt.

Loved on someone else’s account. “Beloved for the sake of their forefathers” — not for anything in the present generation, but because of promises made to men dead nearly two thousand years. Before calling that arbitrary, notice it is the only way anyone in Romans is loved. Nobody is accepted on his own account. Every Christian is loved because of Another’s obedience, held because of promises made before he was born. Israel’s case is the gospel’s logic applied to a nation.

Two truths about one person. Paul holds two true things about the same people in one sentence and lets neither cancel the other. Most of us can’t do it for an afternoon about one relative. The person who wronged us becomes just “the one who wronged me”; the person we love becomes someone whose faults we must minimise to keep loving him. Verse 28 does neither.

A test. Take the person you are most tangled with and write both halves in one line, joined by “and,” not “but”: what is actually wrong, and what is actually true of them and of your bond. If you can’t get both onto the page without one softening, you have found the work. Paul managed it about people who had tried to have him killed. Pray for that person with both halves in view.

parallels.desc: when he takes away his sin

verseByVerse.quote: For the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable. For just as you were at one time disobedient to God but now have received mercy because of their disobedience,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“The gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable.” God has no second thoughts about what he gives or whom he calls. Gentiles were once disobedient and received mercy through Israel’s disobedience; God’s mercy works through and despite human failure.

Without regret. The Greek word is built on “to regret,” with a negative: without-regret. It is not mainly that God is unable to take a thing back, but that he has no second thoughts about having given it.

A familiar human regret. The reference you wrote for someone who then embarrassed you. The trust you extended and watched being spent. The money you gave “as a gift,” and the cold feeling months later when you saw how it was used. Regret that attaches itself to generosity afterwards is one of the most ordinary emotions there is. Paul says there is none of it in God (cf. Numbers 23:19).

About Israel, and about you. In context this is about Israel — the gifts and calling of 9:4–5, which have not been withdrawn. Applying it to the individual believer is legitimate, because it is the same God and the same logic as 8:29–30, but it is an extension, and should be named as one.

A test. Many Christians carry a private theory about what would finally exhaust God’s patience with them — a specific thing, usually unnamed. Name yours. Verse 29 does not answer by assessing whether your item qualifies. It denies the category exists. God does not sit down afterwards and wish he had chosen differently. Thank him for that today.

parallels.desc: God is not man, that he should lie

verseByVerse.quote: so they too have now been disobedient in order that by the mercy shown to you they also may now receive mercy. For God has consigned all to disobedience, that he may have mercy on all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel has now been disobedient so that, by the mercy shown to the Gentiles, they too may receive mercy. “For God has consigned all to disobedience, that he may have mercy on all.” Everyone is shut in by sin together, so that everyone who is saved is saved by mercy alone.

A prison word. “Consigned” means shut up together, locked in with no way out — the word of Galatians 3:22, where Scripture “imprisoned everything under sin.” Not a courtroom but a cell with the whole human race in it, Jew and Gentile, every exit tried and locked.

Locked in, to be let out. “That he may have mercy.” The confinement is the means, not the end. God closed every other door so that the only one left opens from outside. Nobody in that room can be told he took the second-best way out; there was no other.

No senior partner. You were disobedient and received mercy; they are disobedient and will receive mercy. Both groups reached it by roads of exactly equal dignity — none.

Does “all” mean everyone is finally saved? No, and the letter forbids that reading. The same apostle hopes to save “some” (v. 14) and grieved in chapter 9 over people he expected to be lost. The two “alls” are the same width, and the argument since chapter 9 has been about two groups, not every individual: Jew and Gentile alike are shut in; Jew and Gentile alike are shown mercy (see on 5:18–19).

Nobody is a special case. What the verse destroys is the idea of a scale on which some are further down. The door was locked on all of us at the same time, from the same side, by Someone who had already decided how the story ends. If you think you are beyond mercy, you are in the same room as everyone else — and the door opens from outside. Knock on it today.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit the second “now.”

verseByVerse.quote: Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!” After three chapters of argument, Paul ends not with a formula but with worship. God is greater than our understanding — and more merciful than we feared.

Footprints you can’t follow. “Inscrutable” is built on the word for footprint: his ways cannot be tracked. You can see where he has been but not reconstruct the route. Israel’s hymnbook said it of the Red Sea: “Your way was through the sea, your path through the great waters; yet your footprints were unseen” (Psalm 77:19). The least deniable act in their history left no tracks.

Not a conversation-stopper. This verse is often used to end discussion. But Paul has just reasoned harder than anyone in Scripture. The doxology comes at the end of the argument, not instead of it. It is what a mind sounds like when it has gone as far as it can and found the country still opening ahead. Reaching for v. 33 at the start, to avoid the work, quotes Paul’s conclusion while refusing his method.

Depth, not muddle. Paul leaves real questions standing — why these and not those, how hardening and responsibility fit, what “life from the dead” means. He neither apologises nor papers over them. He looks at the unexplained remainder and calls it depth, a word of praise. A muddle is something you have failed to sort out. A depth is something you have come to the edge of.

Where the argument ends. Eleven chapters of the tightest reasoning in Scripture — wrath, law, Abraham’s faith, two Adams, the Spirit, the potter, the olive tree — end in a man running out of words before God and saying so. The riches were always going to be deeper than the reasoning. That is not the argument’s failure; it is what it was for.

A test. Take the hardest unanswered question this section raised for you. Instead of setting it aside or forcing an answer, bring it to God in praise: tell him what you do not understand, and thank him for what you do. Let this verse be your prayer.

parallels.desc: my thoughts are not your thoughts

verseByVerse.quote: "For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?” (v. 34, quoting Isaiah 40:13). No one has advised God or improved his plans. And for the anxious, that is comfort: no one has ever briefed him against you.

Said to exiles. Isaiah 40 was addressed to a beaten, deported people whose complaint is quoted a few verses later: “My way is hidden from the LORD, and my right is disregarded by my God” (Isaiah 40:27). They were not arguing that God was too free. They were afraid he had lost track of them.

Comfort, not rebuke. To such people, the news that nobody has instructed God means his handling of their case has not been delegated, advised, or worked out from partial information. And quieter still: if nobody has been God’s counsellor, nobody has successfully briefed him against you. No one got to him first. There is no version of your file he was handed by someone else.

Built, not blurted. The three questions of vv. 34–35 answer the three nouns of v. 33 in reverse: knowledge (“who has known his mind”), wisdom (“who has been his counselor”), riches (“who has given a gift to him”). Paul is no less careful in worship than in argument.

The mind that decided. He has never been advised or revised a decision because information reached him late. And this is the mind that decided, without anyone suggesting it, to save the ungodly at the cost of his own Son. When you feel your situation is hidden from God, read Isaiah 40:27–31 and rest on the mind that needs no counsellor.

parallels.desc: who has measured the Spirit of the LORD?

verseByVerse.quote: "Or who has given a gift to him that he might be repaid?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Who has given a gift to him that he might be repaid?” (v. 35; cf. Job 41:11). No one has put God in debt. Everything we receive from him is gift, never payment — which is exactly what makes it love.

Said to Job. God speaks from the whirlwind: “Who has first given to me, that I should repay him? Whatever is under the whole heaven is mine” (Job 41:11). It is said to a man who wanted an accounting and who was, by the book’s own verdict, more nearly right than his friends. Even to him: there is no ledger in which he could be the creditor.

The background hum. The instinct this kills is rarely admitted aloud: the faint sense, after a stretch of obedience, that something is now owed — that a year of faithful service has bought protection, that God shouldn’t let this happen to someone who has been doing what you have. It is not a stated belief. It becomes audible the moment life goes wrong.

If God owed you. You would have a claim. But a debt paid is not a gift given, and a God settling an account with you would not be loving you. Think of a friend who visits because he owes you, and one who visits because he wanted to see you. Everything that makes the second visit worth anything is the absence of obligation (cf. 1 Corinthians 4:7).

A test. When something hard happens, listen for the sentence “I don’t deserve this” in the sense of “I’ve earned better.” Replace it with thanks for one specific gift you never earned. Verse 35 guarantees that nothing you have ever received from God was a payment.

parallels.desc: who has first given to me, that I should repay him?

verseByVerse.quote: For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory forever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory forever. Amen.” Everything comes from God, is sustained by God, and exists for God. So all glory belongs to him.

Three prepositions, three closed doors. From him: nothing brought itself into being. Through him: nothing keeps itself going. To him: nothing is its own point. Together they leave no room for the idea the letter has dismantled since 1:21 — that a creature might be the origin, sustainer or end of anything (cf. 1 Corinthians 8:6; Colossians 1:16–17).

Amen at both ends. Chapter 9 opened in grief, and Paul broke off to bless God: “God over all, blessed forever. Amen” (9:5). Here he says “Amen” again. Chapters 9–11 begin with worship over a sorrow and end with worship over a resolution.

Why praise, with questions still standing? Paul’s difficulties did not all dissolve; some are still on the page. He arrives at praise because the God he could not fully trace turned out, when the argument was done, to be more merciful than he had feared — a God who shut everyone in so he could let everyone out, and has not taken back a single thing he gave.

Everything going home. The chapter that asked whether God had rejected his people ends with everything in existence going home to him: every galaxy and atom, every kingdom that rose and fell, every hour of every life, including the unrecorded ones. There is no fourth preposition and nothing outside the three.

A test. Take one ordinary thing in your day — your work, a meal, a person — and say over it: from him, through him, to him. Then do it for him. That is how “to him be glory” becomes more than a closing line. Amen.

11.text: <sup>1</sup>I ask, then, has God rejected his people? By no means! For I myself am an Israelite, a descendant of Abraham, a member of the tribe of Benjamin.<sup>2</sup>God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew. Do you not know what the Scripture says of Elijah, how he appeals to God against Israel?<sup>3</sup>“Lord, they have killed your prophets, they have demolished your altars, and I alone am left, and they seek my life.”<sup>4</sup>But what is God’s reply to him? “I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal.”<sup>5</sup>So too at the present time there is a remnant, chosen by grace.<sup>6</sup>But if it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works; otherwise grace would no longer be grace.<sup>7</sup>What then? Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking. The elect obtained it, but the rest were hardened,<sup>8</sup>as it is written, “God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that would not see and ears that would not hear, down to this very day.”<sup>9</sup>And David says, “Let their table become a snare and a trap, a stumbling block and a retribution for them;<sup>10</sup>let their eyes be darkened so that they cannot see, and bend their backs forever.”<sup>11</sup>So I ask, did they stumble in order that they might fall? By no means! Rather, through their trespass salvation has come to the Gentiles, so as to make Israel jealous.<sup>12</sup>Now if their trespass means riches for the world, and if their failure means riches for the Gentiles, how much more will their full inclusion mean!<sup>13</sup>Now I am speaking to you Gentiles. Inasmuch then as I am an apostle to the Gentiles, I magnify my ministry<sup>14</sup>in order somehow to make my fellow Jews jealous, and thus save some of them.<sup>15</sup>For if their rejection means the reconciliation of the world, what will their acceptance mean but life from the dead?<sup>16</sup>If the dough offered as firstfruits is holy, so is the whole lump, and if the root is holy, so are the branches.<sup>17</sup>But if some of the branches were broken off, and you, although a wild olive shoot, were grafted in among the others and now share in the nourishing root of the olive tree,<sup>18</sup>do not be arrogant toward the branches.
