13.title: Citizens of Two Kingdoms
13.overview:
Romans 13 addresses two dimensions of the Christian's life in the world that might seem unrelated but are theologically connected: the relationship to governing authorities (vv. 1–7) and the debt of love that fulfils the whole law (vv. 8–14). Both passages apply the gospel-transformed mind of 12:2 to concrete social realities. The Christian is not a free agent owing nothing to anyone; she is embedded in a created order (civil government) and a moral order (the law of love) that place real obligations on her life.

The passage on governing authorities is one of the most important and most abused in the New Testament — used to justify passive submission to every form of political power, and also to justify every form of political resistance. Paul's point is neither absolutist submission nor automatic resistance; it is the theological grounding of civil authority in God's own ordering of human society, combined with the practical obligation to honour, obey, and pay taxes to those who wield legitimate authority.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Governing Authorities: God's Servant for Good
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"Let every person be subject to the governing authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been instituted by God" (v. 1). The theological foundation is clear: civil government is not a human invention that God tolerates; it is an ordering of human society that God has established for the good of human beings. The magistrate, the soldier, the tax official — in their legitimate exercise of authority, they are God's servants (diakonos — the same word used for church deacons) for the maintenance of order, the punishment of evil, and the commendation of good.

The context matters: Paul is writing to Rome under the early Nero, before the persecutions of the 60s. The Roman state, for all its paganism, provided the remarkable infrastructure of law, roads, and relative peace (the Pax Romana) that enabled the gospel to spread across the empire. Paul is not asking the Roman Christians to endorse every policy of the emperor; he is asking them not to be revolutionaries — not to treat their citizenship in the kingdom of God as a license to ignore or undermine the civil order that God has established.

The limits of this submission are implied by the rest of Scripture (Acts 5:29 — "We must obey God rather than men") and by Paul's own record of civil disobedience. When the governing authority commands what God forbids, or forbids what God commands, the Christian must obey God. But the default posture is submission, because the default function of civil government — even imperfect civil government — is the ordering of human life in a fallen world for the common good.

Three things in the passage should not be passed over. The first is v. 2, which supplies the sanction: whoever resists the authority resists what God has appointed, and those who resist will incur judgment. Paul is not merely recommending civic good manners. He is saying that the ordering itself has God behind it, so that contempt for it is not a neutral act.

The second is the second half of v. 4, and it is the hinge on which the previous chapter turns. The magistrate does not bear the sword in vain; he is an avenger who carries out God’s wrath on the wrongdoer. A few verses earlier Paul forbade the Christian to avenge himself and told him to give place to the wrath (12:19). He now names the office through which some of that wrath is administered in the present. Vengeance was not abolished when it was taken out of your hands. It was relocated.

The third is v. 5, which gives the motive: submission is owed not only to avoid God’s wrath but also for the sake of conscience. That distinguishes the Christian citizen from the merely prudent one. Fear of penalty produces compliance wherever penalties are likely; conscience produces the same behaviour where no one is watching and nothing would follow.
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Kingdoms and Civil Authority

The Reformation developed the doctrine of the two kingdoms — the kingdom of God's left hand (civil government) and the kingdom of his right hand (the church) — as the theological framework for understanding passages like Romans 13. God governs the civil sphere through natural law and common grace, using even unbelieving rulers to maintain order and restrain evil. God governs the church through Word and Spirit. The two kingdoms are distinct but not separate; the Christian citizen participates in both, with different modes of loyalty appropriate to each. Luther and Calvin both insisted on the legitimacy and dignity of civil authority while limiting its scope: Caesar has his domain; Christ has his; and the two must never be confused.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Roman Christians were tempted, for obvious reasons, to view the imperial state with suspicion or hostility — an institution that had crucified their Lord and would eventually persecute them. Paul's command to submit was not politically naive; it was theologically grounded. God uses even imperfect and eventually hostile governments to structure human life. The Christian who refuses all civil order in the name of heavenly citizenship has not understood the two-kingdom distinction. Now: In democracies, Romans 13 applies to the obligation of citizens to participate in civil society — paying taxes, respecting legitimate authority, working through legal channels to promote justice. It does not require silent compliance with injustice; the Christian who uses the legitimate tools of civil society to oppose evil is not violating v. 1 but fulfilling v. 4's vision of government as a servant of good.

verseByVerse.quote: Let every person be subject to the governing authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been instituted by God. Therefore whoever resists the authorities resists what God has appointed, and those who resist will incur judgment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone is to be subject to the governing authorities, because all authority comes from God and existing authorities are appointed by him. To resist that order is to resist God’s arrangement. Civil government as such is God’s institution for order and justice, even when rulers do not acknowledge him.

Subject, not simply obey. Paul does not use the word for obeying (used of children and slaves elsewhere) but one about rank and order: place yourself under an arrangement. A person can be genuinely subject to an order and still refuse a particular command within it — which is exactly what the martyrs did when they refused to sacrifice and then did not run away.

What it does not say. It does not say every ruler is good, every command must be carried out, or a government may not be criticised, voted out or taken to court. And it does not say whatever a state does is God’s will. Paul grounds his argument on what government is for (vv. 3–4), and an argument from function does not cover a government that has inverted its function.

Scripture refuses the absolutist reading. The Hebrew midwives disobeyed a royal order to kill infants, and “God dealt well with the midwives” (Exodus 1:20). Three men refused to bow to the king’s image and told him so (Daniel 3:18). Daniel kept praying against an explicit statute (Daniel 6:10). The apostles told their nation’s supreme council, “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). None is treated as a lapse. And the same empire appears twice: in Romans 13 Rome is God’s servant for good; in Revelation 13 the imperial power is a beast that makes war on the saints (Revelation 13:7). A state is an ordinance of God and can become a monster, and the Christian must know which he is looking at.

Paul knew. He wrote “he does not bear the sword in vain” (v. 4) about the government that, by consistent church tradition, later executed him with the sword on no just charge. The sentence was never a compliment to Rome. It was a claim about God.

“Resists.” The word is military — to range yourself in battle order against something. Not the citizen who thinks the government wrong, campaigns, petitions, or refuses a specific unjust demand, but settled hostility to ordered authority itself, on the grounds that belonging to another kingdom releases you from this one. That temptation comes in opposite political costumes, with the same reasoning: my citizenship is in heaven, so these arrangements have no claim on me. Paul answers: they have a claim because they have an Author, and the alternative to imperfect order is not freedom but the strong doing as they please with the weak.

A guard. This passage has been used by slaveholders against abolitionists, by governments against people they were crushing, and by individuals telling someone under their power that resistance is sin. That is misuse, and the text refutes it: v. 4 defines authority by its service to your good, and the order Paul says to submit to is one whose own laws forbid what is being done to you. Reporting a crime is not resisting God’s ordinance. It is using it.

May Christians ever resist a tyrant by force? Many Christians, including most of the early church, answered no, beyond refusing to obey sinful commands. Calvin allowed that lower magistrates, such as estates and parliaments, have a duty to restrain a king who tyrannizes his people (Institutes 4.20.31), and later Reformed writers such as Samuel Rutherford built on that to justify armed resistance led by lawful authorities. The more likely reading of Paul is close to Calvin’s. Private Christians are not to take up arms against their government on their own authority. But where lawful authorities resist a ruler who has turned against the good he exists to serve (v. 4), they are not resisting God’s ordinance but upholding it. Such cases are rare and grave, and Paul wrote these words under Nero.

A test. Take what you are angriest at your government about and sort it: something you dislike, something unjust, or something that requires you personally to sin. The first is politics, and Paul says nothing about it here. The second calls for every lawful means you have. Only the third is the martyr’s question, and it is rarer than our rhetoric suggests. A Christian who treats the first as the third spends the credibility he will need if the third ever comes. Meanwhile, pray for those in authority (1 Timothy 2:1–2).
verseByVerse.note: Paul wrote under the emperor Nero, in the early, better years of his rule. Jesus had said, “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s.”

parallels.desc: by me kings reign

verseByVerse.quote: For rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad. Would you have no fear of the one who is in authority? Then do what is good, and you will receive his approval, for he is God's servant for your good. But if you do wrong, be afraid, for he does not bear the sword in vain. For he is the servant of God, an avenger who carries out God's wrath on the wrongdoer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rulers are not a terror to good conduct but to bad. Do good and you will have their approval, for the ruler is “God’s servant for your good.” But if you do wrong, be afraid: “he does not bear the sword in vain,” for he is God’s servant, “an avenger who carries out God’s wrath on the wrongdoer.”

Does this support capital punishment? The sword was the instrument of execution, and the ruler who bears it is “an avenger who carries out God’s wrath on the wrongdoer.” Behind it stands God’s word to Noah, before Moses: “Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed” (Gen 9:6). Some Christians read the sword more generally, as the state’s power to punish, and oppose the death penalty because courts make mistakes and because Christ calls us to mercy. Those concerns about justice are serious, but the more likely reading is that Scripture permits the state to put murderers to death. It permits rather than requires it in every case, and it requires that it be done justly.

May a Christian serve as a soldier or police officer? Yes. If the ruler is God’s servant in bearing the sword, a believer may serve in that office. When soldiers asked John the Baptist what to do, he did not tell them to leave the army but to be honest and content (Luke 3:14), and Jesus praised the faith of a centurion (Matt 8:10). Christian pacifists cite “all who take the sword will perish by the sword” (Matt 26:52), but that was a rebuke to Peter for using it to resist God’s plan, not a ruling on lawful office. A Christian in uniform must still refuse an unjust order.

Where the wrath went. In 12:19 Paul told the wronged Christian, “never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God.” Here the magistrate is “an avenger” who carries out God’s wrath — the same word family. The avenging forbidden you in 12:19 is assigned to the officer in 13:4. Wrath was never cancelled when it was taken out of your hands. You were asked to stop being the one who settles it, and here Paul tells you where some of it has gone: it has an address, a payroll and an office in your city.

Read the two together. Alone, 12:19 sounds like abolishing justice; alone, 13:4 sounds like sanctifying state force. Together: justice is real and matters enormously, and you personally are not authorised to administer it.

An argument from function. “Rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad” describes what authority is for, and the case rests on it. A ruler who becomes a terror to good conduct is doing the opposite, and Paul’s argument cannot be stretched to bless him. The passage grounds authority; it does not immunise it.

For the wronged. If someone has committed a crime against you, going to the police is not a failure of Romans 12 or a lapse in forgiveness. Paul has just called that officer God’s servant. You are not taking the matter into your own hands; you are handing it to the hands appointed for it.

Approval too. The half nobody quotes: “you will receive his approval.” The state is meant to praise what is good, not only punish what is bad (1 Peter 2:14). Any account of government from this passage that produces only fear has read half of it. If you hold authority — at work, at home, in public office — commend good conduct as readily as you correct bad.
verseByVerse.note: The sword stood for the government’s power to punish, including capital punishment.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore one must be in subjection, not only to avoid God's wrath but also for the sake of conscience. — Romans 13:5
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two motivations for submission to governing authority: avoiding wrath (the practical, external consequence of resistance) and conscience (the internal moral awareness of what is right). Paul ranks them in order of depth: the external deterrent of punishment may keep people in line; the internal conviction of conscience operates even when punishment is unlikely. The Christian is called to the deeper motivation — to submit not merely because resistance would bring trouble, but because the conscience, properly formed, recognises the legitimate claim of God-ordained authority.

This does not mean every law is just or that the conscience must rubber-stamp every government action. The same conscience that recognises the legitimacy of civil authority also recognises its limits. When Peter and John said We must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29), they were appealing to the same conscience Paul is invoking here — the conscience that knows a higher authority than Caesar. Conscience, properly informed by Scripture, is not the servant of the state but of God.

The word is syneidēsis, the co-knowing faculty Paul described back at 2:14–15 as an internal courtroom where thoughts accuse and sometimes excuse. It is the same faculty, now applied to the traffic of ordinary civic life, and the point is that a Christian is not law-abiding for the reason most people are.

The difference shows up wherever the penalty disappears. An empty road at three in the morning, a red light, no cameras and no other car within a mile. Nothing whatever will happen if you go. Almost everybody knows exactly what they do at that junction, and it is one of the few completely honest facts a person has about themselves, because there is nobody to perform for.

That is the whole distinction in v. 5. Fear of consequence is a real motive and Paul does not sneer at it; he lists it first. But it produces a citizen who is dependable in proportion to the likelihood of being caught, which is not a citizen at all so much as a calculation. Conscience produces the same conduct at the empty junction as at the busy one.

And the same faculty is what sets the limit, which is why this verse and Acts 5:29 are not in tension. A conscience that can be overruled by a statute is not a conscience; it is a licence. The reason Peter could refuse the council is the same reason Paul can tell you to pay your taxes without being watched — in both cases the man is answering to somebody who is not in the room.

verseByVerse.quote: For because of this you also pay taxes, for the authorities are ministers of God, attending to this very thing. Pay to all what is owed to them: taxes to whom taxes are owed, revenue to whom revenue is owed, respect to whom respect is owed, honor to whom honor is owed. — Romans 13:6–7
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus had already said it: render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s (Matthew 22:21). Paul applies the principle: pay your taxes, pay your customs, show respect, show honour — not because you endorse every use of that tax revenue, but because you recognise the legitimate function of the authority that levies it. Civil life requires contribution; the Christian is not exempt from the obligations of the community she inhabits.

The fourfold list — taxes, revenue, respect, honour — covers the material and the social dimensions of civic obligation. The Christian is a good citizen not out of mere law-abiding compliance but out of a theology of creational order: God has established the civil sphere; it makes legitimate claims; those claims are, within their proper scope, to be honoured.

Verse 6 uses a word for the authorities that ought to stop the reader. In v. 4 they were diakonos, servants. Here they are leitourgoi — the term for those who perform a public religious duty, the word behind our liturgy, used in the Greek Old Testament of priests serving at the altar. Paul has just described the revenue service as a liturgical order. The clerk processing a tax return is doing, without knowing it, a species of the thing a priest does.

And they are said to be attending to this very thing — a verb Paul used a chapter ago in 12:12, where the Christian is to be constant, persistent, stubbornly devoted in prayer. The official at his desk persists at his post with the same word used of the believer at his prayers. It is an extraordinarily high view of an extraordinarily dull job.

None of which was written in comfortable circumstances. Tacitus records serious public grievance over indirect taxation in Rome in the late 50s, with the emperor considering abolishing the levies outright — and Romans was written within a year or two of it. Paul is not offering a general principle in a calm season. He is telling a small, suspect congregation in the capital to keep paying, on time, into a treasury that funded the games, the temples of the gods, and eventually the machinery that would kill them.

But notice the limit sitting inside the command. Pay what is owed — which concedes that not everything demanded is owed. The saying of Jesus behind it has the same shape and is usually quoted only half-way. Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s is not the whole sentence; the second clause, and to God the things that are God’s, is a boundary drawn around the first. Caesar may have the coin with his face on it. He may not have the man made in the image of God.

The fourfold list is worth reading slowly for what it costs. Taxes and revenue are money, and money is the easy half — it leaves the account and the matter ends. Respect and honour are harder, because they are owed to a person, sometimes to a person you did not vote for and do not admire.

Which is the practical edge, and it lands close to home. Paul does not say honour the ones who deserve it. He says pay what is owed to the office. So the test is simply how you speak about the people currently in power when you are among people who agree with you — the car, the meal table, the group chat. That is where this verse is actually kept or broken, and almost nobody thinks of it as a Romans 13 question at all.
verseByVerse.note: “Taxes” were direct taxes; “revenue” meant customs and tolls.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–14 — Love Fulfils the Law: Put on Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"Owe no one anything, except to love each other, for the one who loves another has fulfilled the law" (v. 8). The transition from taxes and respect to love is sudden but logical: both are obligations owed to those among whom we live. But the debt of love is unique — it is a debt that is perpetually owed and perpetually paid but never fully discharged. You can pay a tax and be done with it; you can never be done with the obligation to love, because the opportunities to love are inexhaustible and the command is perpetual.

Paul's claim is audacious: love fulfils the entire law. The specific commandments — do not commit adultery, do not murder, do not steal, do not covet — are all "summed up" in this word: love your neighbour as yourself (quoting Leviticus 19:18). This does not make the specific commandments irrelevant; it establishes their theological root. Love is the soil from which all the particular expressions of right conduct grow. The person who truly loves her neighbour will not steal from him, will not lie to him, will not commit adultery against him. Love is not a substitute for the law's specific demands; it is the power that fulfils them from within.

The passage closes with the urgency of eschatological time: "the night is far gone; the day is at hand" (v. 12). The Christian lives in the interim between the first coming of Christ (which inaugurated the day of salvation) and his return (which will complete it). This is not time to sleep; it is time to wake, to lay aside the works of darkness, to put on the armour of light — and supremely to "put on the Lord Jesus Christ" (v. 14). The Christian life is not moral self-improvement; it is the clothing of oneself in Christ, day by day, until the transformation is complete.

Between the dawn and the clothing stands v. 13, which supplies the specifics: let us walk properly as in the daytime, not in orgies and drunkenness, not in sexual immorality and sensuality, not in quarreling and jealousy. Three pairs, and the order of them is the sting. The list begins where anyone would expect a vice list to begin and ends somewhere entirely respectable — with arguing and envy, which are set down in the same sentence, under the same heading, as the drunken procession through the streets.
verseByVerse.theology:
Love as the Fulfilment of the Law

Romans 13:8–10 gives the summary of the second table of the law: love your neighbour as yourself. This is not a replacement of the law with an undefined sentiment; it is the identification of the animating principle from which all the law's specific demands flow. The Reformed tradition has insisted that love and law are not opposites — love is the motive; the law is the guide. The renewed person who loves God supremely and her neighbour genuinely will want to know concretely what that love requires in specific situations, and the law provides exactly that: the concrete shape of love in action.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul's command to "put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh" (v. 14) was the verse that Augustine read in the garden in Milan in 386 AD, at the moment of his conversion. He had been struggling with the inability to break free from sexual sin; these words fell on him with the weight of divine command and divine grace simultaneously. The verse is still doing what it did to Augustine: convicting, commanding, and empowering. Now: The urgency of vv. 11–14 is the urgency of the gospel in every age: the window of this life is short; the return of Christ is certain; the works of darkness are not appropriate wear for people who are children of light. Every day lived in unrepentant sin is a wasted day; every day lived in Christ is a day that will outlast the sun.

verseByVerse.quote: Owe no one anything, except to love each other, for the one who loves another has fulfilled the law. For the commandments, "You shall not commit adultery, You shall not murder, You shall not steal, You shall not covet," and any other commandment, are summed up in this word: "You shall love your neighbor as yourself."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Owe no one anything except to love — the one debt that can never be fully discharged, because love is always more possible, always more costly, always more demanded. Paul lists four of the Ten Commandments (the second table, governing human relationships) and then reduces them to the single summary: love your neighbor as yourself (Leviticus 19:18). This is not an abolition of the commandments — it is their compression into the single principle that underlies all of them. Love does not replace the law; it fulfills it by going to its root.

The move from taxes to love is not the change of subject it appears to be, because Paul is still using the same word. Verse 7 said pay everyone what is owed; verse 8 opens owe no one anything. Same root, consecutive sentences. He has been talking about debts all along, and he now names the one item on the account that never clears.

Does Owe no one anything mean that all borrowing is sin? No. The context is paying what is due, taxes, revenue, respect (v. 7), and the command is to leave no debt unpaid. The law regulated lending rather than forbidding it (Exod 22:25; Deut 15:7–8), and Jesus said do not refuse the one who would borrow from you (Matt 5:42). What Scripture condemns is failing to repay: The wicked borrows but does not pay back (Ps 37:21). It also warns that the borrower is the slave of the lender (Prov 22:7). So a Christian may take a mortgage or a loan he can repay, should keep its terms, and should be slow to borrow for what he cannot afford.

And does as yourself command us to love ourselves first? No. It assumes the care for ourselves that everyone already has: no one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it (Eph 5:29). That care becomes the measure of what we owe our neighbour. The command is not to build up self-love but to give others what we naturally give ourselves (cf. Matt 7:12).

That is the strange and rather beautiful thing about the exception clause. Every other obligation in this passage can be discharged. You can pay the tax, settle the bill, return the tool, and the matter is closed; there is a real satisfaction in owing nobody anything. Nobody has ever reached that position with this debt. It is charged again every morning, to the same people, at the same rate.

And the commandments he chooses to sum up are all from the second table — the ones about the neighbour — which is worth noticing before anyone concludes Paul has replaced religion with ethics. He is not summarising the whole law here; he is summarising the half of it that deals with the person next to you. The first table is not in view because it is not in dispute.

He also ends the list with coveting, which is the one nobody can see you break — the commandment that made the difference back in chapter 7. It sits here as the proof that this is not a code of external conduct. You can satisfy the other three by simply not doing things. You cannot satisfy that one without something happening inside.

So a test, and it is uncomfortably specific. Bring to mind the person in your church you find hardest — not an enemy, just the one you would rather not sit near. The debt is owed to them this week at exactly the same rate as to the people you like, and unlike a tax it cannot be paid by anyone else on your behalf. Most of us are not refusing to pay it. We have simply arranged our lives so the invoice rarely arrives.

parallels.desc: love your neighbour as yourself

verseByVerse.quote: Love does no wrong to a neighbor; therefore love is the fulfilling of the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love does no wrong to a neighbour — a negative definition, but comprehensive: every wrong that the law prohibits is a failure of love. And the converse: where love is genuinely present, the law’s prohibitions are naturally kept. This is the new covenant internalization of the law: not the external constraint of a code but the internal motivation of love for God and neighbor, which produces from within the behavior the law demanded from without. The fulfillment of the law is not abolition but achievement — love achieving from the inside what the law could only command from the outside.

The negative form of the definition is a mercy, and it is worth seeing why. Positive definitions of love cannot be checked. Ask whether you loved your wife enough this week and there is no answer, only a mood — and the answer you give will depend mostly on how tired you are. Paul’s version can be checked. Have I done this person wrong? That is a question with a yes or a no, and it can be asked about a specific Tuesday.

Which makes v. 10 the most usable sentence in the chapter for anyone trying to examine themselves without either flattery or despair. It gives you a floor you can stand on and measure from.

But a floor is what it is, and the guard matters. This verse must never be turned into “as long as I have harmed nobody, I have loved.” A man can go a whole year wronging no one and loving nobody; the coldest people most of us know are perfectly innocent of this list. Paul has already put the ceiling in place one chapter earlier, where love feeds the enemy and blesses the persecutor (12:20, 12:14) — which is a great deal more than not wronging him. Verse 10 tells you where love starts. It does not tell you where it stops.

verseByVerse.quote: Besides this you know the time, that the hour has come for you to wake from sleep. For salvation is nearer to us now than when we first believed. The night is far gone; the day is at hand. So then let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light. — Romans 13:11–12
verseByVerse.commentary:
The eschatological urgency of vv. 11–12 grounds the ethics of vv. 8–14 in the reality of the coming consummation. The command to love is not merely good advice for social harmony; it is the appropriate way to live in the time between the first coming of Christ (which inaugurated the day of salvation) and his return (which will complete it). Salvation is nearer to us now than when we first believed — every day that passes brings the return of Christ closer. This is not reason for anxiety but for alertness.

The night is far gone; the day is at hand — the Christian lives in the overlap of the ages: the old age of darkness and death is passing away; the new age of light and life has already broken in with the resurrection of Christ. The ethics of the new age — love, light, putting on Christ — are the appropriate clothing for people who are living in the dawning of the day. To live in the works of darkness (v. 12) is to dress for a night that is already ending.

Verse 12 ends with a command, and it is the point of the whole image: let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light. Both verbs are clothing verbs — strip off, put on — and the second is the very verb Paul will use two verses later of putting on Christ himself. Verses 12 and 14 are one metaphor, not two.

The word rendered armour is simply the word for weapons or equipment, and Paul has used it in this letter before: present your members to God as instruments for righteousness (6:13). Same word. What was handed over as equipment in chapter 6 is what you get dressed in here. The Christian is not issued a costume for the daylight. He is issued kit.

Notice too that Paul says you know the time, and the word is not clock time but kairos — the decisive moment, the hour that has a character to it. His argument is not that the readers need new information. It is that they already possess it and are living as though they did not, which is the ordinary condition of most Christians most of the time.

Which raises the honest difficulty, and it should not be stepped around. Paul says salvation is nearer than when we first believed, and the day is at hand — and two thousand years have gone by. Did he simply get it wrong? The sentence itself is the answer, because it is not a calculation but a comparison, and it is true every time it is read. It was true for him. It is truer for you than it was for him. And for each of us the day arrives at our own death if it has not arrived before, which no one has ever had grounds to think was far off.

Keep the picture of waking literal for a moment, because it is exact. Nothing in the room changes when a person wakes. The furniture is where it was, the light is what it was; the only difference is that someone is now present to it. Paul is not asking for new circumstances. He is asking for someone to be awake inside the ones already there.

So the test is what you did with the last hour before you slept and the first fifteen minutes after you woke — the two stretches nobody plans and nobody sees. We arrange our public hours carefully. Those two are where the actual dressing happens, and most of us have never once considered them a spiritual question.

verseByVerse.quote: Let us walk properly as in the daytime, not in orgies and drunkenness, not in sexual immorality and sensuality, not in quarreling and jealousy. But put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its desires. — Romans 13:13–14
verseByVerse.commentary:
Live decently, “as in the daytime” — not in drunken revelry, sexual immorality and sensuality, or quarrelling and jealousy. Instead, “put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh.” Clothe yourself in Christ, and don’t arrange your life to feed old desires.

As in daylight. “Walk properly as in the daytime” — behave now as you would if it were already light. Everyone understands this: there is a category of things people do at one in the morning that they would not do at eleven, in the same street, in front of the same neighbours.

The list ends with the respectable. Three pairs: orgies and drunkenness; sexual immorality and sensuality; quarrelling and jealousy. It begins where you’d expect and ends, without changing tone, with arguing and envy. The man who has never been drunk and whose sexual conduct is beyond reproach, but who cannot let a disagreement go — who keeps score, needs to be right, runs a commentary on someone at church — is named in the same breath as the drunk in the street. Paul does not grade them. We do. And every sin listed is social; this is still the argument from v. 8 about the debt of love. The vice list is what unpaid love looks like on a Friday night.

Augustine in the garden. In 386 a North African professor of rhetoric, thirty-one, sat weeping in a garden in Milan, convinced of Christianity but unable to break with a sexual habit; he had prayed, famously, “give me chastity and continence, but not yet.” He heard a child’s voice chanting, “Take up and read.” He opened Paul and read these two verses. He tells us he needed to read no further; the shadows of doubt were gone (Confessions 8.12). Notice what did it: not a promise or a doctrine, but a plain prohibition and a plain command. He had known the doctrine for years. He had never obeyed the sentence.

Put on Christ. Like putting on clothes, so that what others see is Christ rather than the old self. Not pretence but identity: dressing in who you now are (Galatians 3:27; Colossians 3:10–14). And not qualities extracted from Christ and copied, but Christ himself. He was stripped so that there would be something for the guilty to wear.

No provision. “Provision” is a word for forethought, the same root as “give thought to do what is honorable” (12:17). You plan for good in a calm hour, and you plan for the flesh in a calm hour too, usually without admitting it: the route home past the place, the app left installed, the second bottle bought “just in case,” the evening arranged so that being alone is inevitable. Nobody falls at the moment of temptation. They fall at the moment of provisioning, days earlier, which felt like nothing.

A test. Go looking for your provisions, not your sins. Name one arrangement in your life whose only real function is to keep a door open. Close that one thing tonight — not the sin, the arrangement. It is a much smaller act, and it is what this verse asks.
verseByVerse.note: Augustine was converted on reading these verses in a garden in Milan in AD 386.

For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been instituted by God.<sup>2</sup>Therefore whoever resists the authorities resists what God has appointed, and those who resist will incur judgment.<sup>3</sup>For rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad.
