14.title: The Weak and the Strong: Liberty and Love
14.overview:
Romans 14–15 address a specific pastoral conflict in the Roman church: tension between Jewish Christians who maintained food laws and Sabbath observances ("the weak in faith") and Gentile Christians who felt free from such regulations ("the strong"). But Paul's treatment of this specific conflict generates principles that apply to every generation's version of the same tension: the conflict between Christian liberty and Christian love, between what I am free to do and what love requires me to do for the sake of my brother.

The governing principle is not the extension of legal restriction to those who are free, nor the dismissal of sensitive consciences as mere scrupulosity. It is love — the willingness to limit one's own legitimate freedom for the sake of the weaker brother's conscience and the unity of the body. Paul himself is clearly among "the strong" (15:1 — "we who are strong"), but his pastoral concern is to protect the weak while educating them toward greater freedom, without allowing either group to destroy the other with contempt or judgment.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — Welcome the Weak: Do Not Judge or Despise
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"As for the one who is weak in faith, welcome him, but not to quarrel over opinions" (v. 1). The command is striking in both its positive and its negative dimensions. Positively: welcome him — bring him into the full fellowship of the community, do not treat his scruples as a reason for exclusion. Negatively: not to quarrel over opinions — do not make his welcome the occasion for pressuring him to adopt your view or defend your freedom. The welcome is genuine; the agenda of the welcome is his good, not your point-scoring.

The specific examples Paul uses — one person eats only vegetables, another observes certain days as special — are illustrations of a broader principle. The particulars may be first-century Jewish food laws and Sabbath observances; the principle is the obligation of both the strong and the weak to refrain from the two characteristic sins their positions generate: the strong's temptation to despise the scrupulous (treating their sensitivity as weakness or intellectual failure), and the weak's temptation to judge the free (condemning as sinful what God has declared clean).

"Each of us will give an account of himself to God" (v. 12) — the eschatological horizon is the great leveller. Neither the strong nor the weak will stand before God and be assessed on the basis of whether they were free in matters of food and days. They will give an account of themselves — whether they served Christ, whether they loved their brother, whether they built up the body. The things that divide them now will be irrelevant then; what will matter then should be what governs them now.

Four things in the section are worth adding, because the ground between the opening command and v. 12 is where the argument is actually made. The first is v. 4, which supplies the reason judging is out of order: Who are you to pass judgment on the servant of another? The picture is a domestic household. You do not discipline another man’s staff, however sure you are that they are doing it wrong, because they were not hired by you and do not answer to you.

And that verse ends in a promise rather than a rebuke — he will be upheld, for the Lord is able to make him stand. Paul’s confidence is not that the disputed practice does not matter but that the disputed brother is being personally held up by someone competent. God is already at work on the person you were about to correct.

The second is v. 6, and it is the criterion the whole section turns on. Both parties — the one who observes the day and the one who does not, the one who eats and the one who abstains — are described as acting in honour of the Lord, and both are said to give thanks to God. Paul is not calling the difference trivial. He is pointing out that the same thanksgiving is going up from both sides of the table.

The third is v. 9, which grounds the whole thing in the gospel rather than in tolerance: to this end Christ died and lived again, that he might be Lord both of the dead and of the living. The purpose of the cross and resurrection is stated here as lordship — which settles who is entitled to rule another believer’s conscience, and the answer is the one who paid for it. And the fourth is vv. 10–11, where the argument is sealed with Isaiah 45:23: every knee bowing, every tongue confessing, the strong and the weak side by side at the same tribunal, neither of them presiding.
verseByVerse.theology:
Adiaphora and the Conscience

The Reformed tradition uses the term adiaphora (things indifferent) for matters that Scripture neither commands nor prohibits — the territory of Romans 14. In these matters, Christian liberty is real: what God has declared clean is clean; what the gospel has freed the conscience from need not be re-enslaved. But liberty is not the highest value; love is. Calvin insisted that in matters of adiaphora, the strong must exercise their freedom with sensitivity to the weaker conscience — not capitulating to every scruple indefinitely, but never using freedom as a weapon against the brother Christ died for.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The specific tensions in Rome were between Jewish and Gentile believers over Torah food laws and calendar observances — real, living issues that threatened the unity of a church in which both groups worshipped together. Paul does not resolve the tension by declaring one group right and the other wrong; he transcends it by pointing both groups to a standard higher than their own position: the lordship of Christ (v. 8) and the coming judgment (v. 12). Now: Every generation of the church has its equivalent of the Romans 14 debate: alcohol, entertainment, dress, worship style, political engagement. The principles are the same: welcome the brother with differing scruples; do not quarrel over opinions; do not despise; do not judge; remember that each will give account to God and not to you.

verseByVerse.quote: As for the one who is weak in faith, welcome him, but not to quarrel over opinions. One person believes he may eat anything, while the weak person eats only vegetables.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Welcome the one who is “weak in faith,” but not to argue over disputed matters. One believes he may eat anything; the weak eats only vegetables. The “weak” here is the believer whose conscience still binds him in matters God has left free — and he is to be received warmly, not worked on.

Weak means more rules, not fewer. Get this straight or every instruction lands on the wrong person. “Weak in faith” does not mean lax or half-hearted. It means the man with more scruples: who cannot eat the meat, cannot ignore the day, cannot do the permitted thing without his conscience objecting. We usually call the strict Christian “strong” and the relaxed one “weak.” Paul’s labels run the other way.

How do you tell a disputable matter from a real sin? This chapter is about things God has neither commanded nor forbidden: food and drink, special days, and similar matters on which believers may differ before the Lord. Three questions sort them. Does Scripture command it or forbid it? Is the gospel itself at stake? Is anyone being told that he must do this to be right with God? Where the answer to all three is no, this chapter governs, and the strong bear with the weak. But where Scripture calls something sin, no appeal to liberty or conscience can make it a disputable matter. And where the gospel is at stake, the strong must not yield: when false brothers wanted Titus circumcised, Paul says, “we did not yield in submission even for a moment” (Gal 2:5). Bearing with a weak conscience is love; letting it rule the church is not.

Why vegetables. A scrupulous believer in Rome — likely a Jewish Christian, or someone who had left idol worship — could not easily know how an animal was slaughtered or whether market meat had passed through a temple. The only way to be sure was to eat no meat at all. A tender conscience over-corrects because it cannot bear the risk.

Welcome, as God welcomed. The same verb appears in v. 3 (“God has welcomed him”) and 15:7 (“welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you”). This is not politeness at the edge of the room. It is the hospitality God has already shown the person you find difficult.

Not with a project. “But not to quarrel over opinions.” You can receive someone warmly with the settled aim of working on him — being hospitable at him. Welcome with a project attached is not what is commanded, and the person receiving it can always tell.

For the weak reader. If you recognise yourself as the weak brother, the term names one thing only: a conscience not yet free where God has granted freedom. It says nothing about your sincerity, salvation or love for Christ; you are scrupulous because you fear displeasing God, which is not a contemptible reason. And almost every command in this chapter is aimed at the strong, on your behalf. Paul does not spend a verse telling you to hurry up.

A test for the strong. Think of a fellow believer whose conscience is tighter than yours on some matter. When did you last welcome him without trying to change him? Invite him this week, and leave the matter alone.
verseByVerse.note: The “weak” probably include Jewish believers who kept the food laws, and others who avoided meat that might have been offered to idols.

verseByVerse.quote: Let not the one who eats despise the one who abstains, and let not the one who abstains pass judgment on the one who eats, for God has welcomed him. Who are you to pass judgment on the servant of another? It is before his own master that he stands or falls. And he will be upheld, for the Lord is able to make him stand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two sins named and forbidden: the strong despising the weak (treating their scruples as ridiculous), and the weak judging the strong (treating their freedom as sin). Both errors arise from the same source: forgetting that the other person is God’s servant, not yours. God has welcomed him — the ground of mutual acceptance is not agreement on secondary matters but shared reception by the same God. The one who judges another’s servant oversteps: the servant’s accountability is to his own master, and that master is able to make him stand.

Does this mean Christians must never judge? No. Paul forbids condemning a brother over matters God has left open. Elsewhere he commands the church to judge sin among its members (1 Cor 5:12–13), pronounces a curse on those who preach another gospel (Gal 1:8–9), and at the end of this letter tells the Romans to watch out for those who cause divisions and create obstacles contrary to the doctrine that you have been taught (16:17). The question is not whether to judge but what: sin and false teaching, yes; another believer’s conscience on a disputable matter, no.

The two sins are assigned with real precision, and the precision is worth pausing on. Paul does not warn both parties about both dangers. The one who eats is told not to despise; the one who abstains is told not to judge. Each temptation is matched to the position that produces it.

That is exactly how it works. Freedom does not tempt a person to condemn; it tempts him to find the other man faintly ridiculous. The word is exoutheneō, to count as nothing — the amused dismissal, the raised eyebrow, the anecdote told later about how strict so-and-so is. Scruple does not tempt a person to sneer; it tempts him to convict. Neither party is usually in any danger of the other’s sin, which is why each so easily believes himself innocent.

Then the household image in v. 4, and it is domestic rather than abstract. The word is the one for a house-servant. You may think another family’s arrangements peculiar; you do not walk into their kitchen and start correcting their staff. Not because standards do not matter, but because it is not your household and they did not take instruction from you.

And the verse ends somewhere unexpected. Having asked who you think you are, Paul does not finish by saying the servant may well fall and that will be his own affair. He says he will be upheld, for the Lord is able to make him stand. The apostle’s confidence runs toward the very person you were worried about. Somebody competent already has hold of him.

Which is the practical relief hidden in this passage, if you will take it. A great deal of the anxiety Christians carry about other Christians is really a quiet doubt about whether God is managing them properly. Paul’s answer is that he is, and that your supervision was never part of the arrangement.

A test, then, and it sorts the two sins neatly. Think of a believer whose practice differs from yours on something Scripture does not settle. Now notice which reflex arrives first — the urge to laugh, or the urge to convict. Whichever it is tells you which of the two groups you are actually in, whatever you would have said about yourself.

verseByVerse.quote: One person esteems one day as better than another, while another esteems all days alike. Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind. The one who observes the day, observes it in honor of the Lord. The one who eats, eats in honor of the Lord, since he gives thanks to God, while the one who abstains, abstains in honor of the Lord and gives thanks to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The criterion Paul offers is not practice but orientation: is it done in honour of the Lord? If the observer of days honors the Lord in his observance, and the non-observer honors the Lord in his freedom, both are standing before the same God in the same posture of gratitude. Thanksgiving is the common ground: both the one who eats and the one who abstains give thanks to God. Where thanksgiving is present, the adiaphora (indifferent things) become matters of conscience, not grounds of division.

Does this mean the Sabbath no longer binds? Many Reformed Christians, following the Westminster Confession, hold that the fourth commandment is a creation ordinance (Gen 2:3) and part of the moral law, now kept on the Lord’s Day; on that view Paul is speaking only of Jewish festivals and ceremonial days, not the weekly day of rest. The more likely reading is that the Sabbath is among the days in view. Paul names it outright in Colossians, where festivals, new moons and Sabbaths are a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ (Col 2:16–17). The Sabbath rest is fulfilled in Christ, in whom we rest from our works (Heb 4:9–10). That does not make Sunday worship optional. Christians gathered on the first day of the week from the beginning (Acts 20:7), and the command not to neglect meeting together stands (Heb 10:25); but they gather as a privilege of the resurrection, not under Sabbath law. Christmas and Easter belong to this chapter: a church may keep them gladly, and no one may bind another’s conscience by them.

Notice what Paul does not say in v. 5. He does not say the matter is unimportant, and he does not say do as you please. He says each one should be fully convinced in his own mind — a strong verb, meaning to be filled up to full assurance. Both the freedom and the scruple are required to have been thought about.

That rules out the position most people actually occupy, which is neither conviction nor liberty but inheritance. A great many Christian practices are held for no reason anyone can now state — it is how we were raised, it is what our church does, it is what the people we admire do. Paul is not asking everyone to reach the same conclusion. He is asking everyone to have reached their own, which is a more demanding request than it sounds and falls equally on both parties.

It is also worth registering how remarkable this is coming from Paul. He is not neutral on the question; he says plainly nine verses later that he is persuaded nothing is unclean, and he is one of the strong. Yet here he defends the right of a man to reach the opposite practical conclusion and act on it before God. He will argue for his view. He will not legislate it.

Then v. 6 gives the common ground, and it is not agreement. It is thanksgiving. The one who eats gives thanks; the one who abstains gives thanks. Two men do opposite things at the same table and both of them say grace over it, and Paul treats that as the decisive fact about both.

Which yields a test sharper than any argument about the practice itself: can you give thanks for it? Not can you defend it, not can you find someone who agrees — can you actually thank God for this specific thing, out loud, without the sentence going strange in your mouth. Liberty that cannot say grace over what it is doing has stopped being liberty somewhere, and scruple that cannot thank God for the freedom it is declining has become something other than conscience.
verseByVerse.note: The days in question were probably the Sabbath and Jewish festivals.

verseByVerse.quote: For none of us lives to himself, and none of us dies to himself. For if we live, we live to the Lord, and if we die, we die to the Lord. So then, whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord's.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The theological ground of the previous verses: no Christian is autonomous. The live to yourself option has been closed by the gospel. Every choice — what to eat, what day to observe, but also every life decision — is made in the presence of the Lord to whom we belong. Death itself is to the Lord. The Christian does not even die for themselves: they die into the arms of the one who owns them. This total lordship of Christ over life and death is the basis of Christian ethics: we are not free to live as if we belonged to ourselves.

It is worth stopping to notice where this sentence has ended up, because almost every reader meets it somewhere other than here. Whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord’s is read at gravesides. It is carved on stones. It is said quietly to people in hospital rooms at three in the morning.

And Paul wrote it about a disagreement over vegetables.

That is not a deflation of the verse; it is the point of it. Faced with a squabble about menus and calendars, Paul does not reach for a rule of thumb or a compromise. He reaches for the largest thing he knows — that a Christian is owned in life and in death — and he puts it underneath the smallest possible quarrel. The size of the argument he brings is a measure of how seriously he takes the damage the quarrel can do.

The repetition carries it: to the Lord, to the Lord, the Lord’s. Three times in a single verse. Both parties keep claiming to be right; Paul keeps answering that neither of them is his own. And ownership is the one fact that settles a dispute between equals, because it does not decide who is correct. It decides who has standing to rule.

verseByVerse.quote: For to this end Christ died and lived again, that he might be Lord both of the dead and of the living.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The death and resurrection of Christ are here given their ethical purpose: so that Christ might be Lord of all — the living and the dead. His lordship was not incidental to his dying and rising; it was the aim. He died to purchase lordship over those who had been enslaved to sin and death; he rose to exercise that lordship as the living, reigning king. This verse is the christological foundation of Romans 14: disputes over food and days are ultimately about whether Christ is Lord of every aspect of life — and he is, over all.

Consider what Paul has just done to settle a dispute about dinner. He has gone to the death and resurrection of the Son of God. Not as an illustration, and not as a general appeal to take things seriously — as the actual argument. To this end Christ died and lived again: this was what it was for.

Which quietly disqualifies both sides of the quarrel. If the purpose of the cross was that Christ should be Lord, then every attempt by one believer to take charge of another’s conscience in a matter God has left open is an encroachment on the thing Calvary was transacted to secure. The strong man imposing his freedom and the weak man imposing his scruple are making the same mistake, from opposite ends.

And there is a comfort here that runs well past the argument it was written for. He is Lord both of the dead and of the living, in that order. The believers you have buried have not passed out of his jurisdiction into some neutral territory. They are still his, under the same lordship, on the same terms — which is why Paul can say a verse earlier that we die to the Lord and mean something more than a pious figure of speech.

To this end Christ died and lived again: that he might be Lord both of the dead and of the living. He went into the one country from which no ruler had ever returned, and he came back, and he came back holding the keys. The dead are not outside his jurisdiction. They are not lost, or filed away, or waiting in some neutral territory beyond his reach.

Every believer who has ever been buried is at this moment under the same Lord as every believer still drawing breath. He rules both countries, because he has lived in both.

verseByVerse.quote: Why do you pass judgment on your brother? Or you, why do you despise your brother? For we will all stand before the judgment seat of God; for it is written, "As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The judgment seat silences human judging of one another. Why judge your brother when you will both stand before the same Judge? Why despise him when you will bow beside him at the same throne? Isaiah 45:23 — a text about the universal acknowledgment of the one true God — guarantees that every person who has ever lived will bow before God. The eschatological reality of universal accountability relativizes every present claim to superiority: at the judgment seat, the strong and the weak stand exactly level.

Will believers be judged? Yes: we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ (2 Cor 5:10). But not to decide whether they are saved. That was settled when they believed: whoever believes does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life (John 5:24; cf. 8:1). What is examined is their life and service. Some will receive reward, and others will suffer loss, though they themselves are saved (1 Cor 3:15). Nor does every knee bowing mean that all will be saved. Believers will bow in worship; the rest will bow because they must.

The word for judgment seat is bēma, and it was a piece of ordinary civic furniture: the raised stone platform in a Greek city from which a magistrate gave his ruling. Paul had stood on the wrong side of one himself, in Corinth, when Gallio heard the case against him and dismissed it (Acts 18:12–16). He is not reaching for a vague image of accountability. He is describing a place where you are the one standing and someone else is seated.

The Greek also puts a weight the English cannot. Both questions begin with an emphatic you — you, why do you judge your brother? and you, why do you despise yours? He is turning to each party in the room by name, and the effect is of a man pointing.

Then the quotation, which is doing more than proving that everyone is accountable. Isaiah 45:23 is spoken by the God who has just said there is no other, and Paul elsewhere takes the same verse and applies it to Jesus, at whose name every knee bows (Philippians 2:10–11). So the scene at the end is not a courtroom with an unknown judge. It is the one before whom you will bow beside the brother you were correcting.

And that is the argument. Not that judgment is unpleasant, but that the seat is occupied. Every act of judging another believer over an open question is an attempt to sit somewhere that already has someone in it.

parallels.desc: to me every knee shall bow

verseByVerse.quote: So then each of us will give an account of himself to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The conclusion is personal and singular: each one, individually, gives account of themselves. Not of their neighbor, not of the person whose practice differed from theirs — of themselves. This is the great leveler of inter-Christian judgment: the energy spent evaluating another’s conscience before God would be better spent examining one’s own. The day of accounting is coming, and on that day the questions will be personal, not comparative.

The Greek presses the reflexive hard: each of us will give an account concerning himself. Whatever else is asked, you will not be asked about him.

Which removes at a stroke the defence most of us have quietly prepared. Nearly every account we give of ourselves is comparative — I am not as strict as him, I am not as careless as her, at least I have never. It works well in conversation because there is always someone available to be worse. It will not be admissible, because the other party will be busy giving his own account, about himself, at the same moment.

So here is the test, and it takes a minute. Try describing your own spiritual condition without mentioning another Christian, a church you left, a movement you disagree with, or a generation you think has gone wrong. Just yourself, to God. Most of us discover how much of our self-assessment was actually about somebody else — and that is precisely the material that will not be there to lean on.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–23 — Do Not Cause a Brother to Stumble
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"Therefore let us not pass judgment on one another any longer, but rather decide never to put a stumbling block or hindrance in the way of a brother" (v. 13). The second half of chapter 14 moves from the mutual prohibition of judging and despising to the positive obligation of the strong: limit your freedom in cases where exercising it would damage your brother's conscience and lead him into sin. The governing concern is his welfare, not your rights.

Paul's theological grounding of this obligation is striking: "By what you eat, do not destroy the one for whom Christ died" (v. 15). Christ died for the weak brother. The price paid for his soul is the blood of the Son of God. The strong believer who uses her freedom to demolish someone Christ purchased at infinite cost has committed something far more serious than poor table manners. She has treated as worthless what God treated as worth his Son.

The kingdom of God principle of v. 17 is the positive vision behind the self-limitation: "For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit." The things that matter most — right standing before God, harmony in the body, Spirit-given joy — are not determined by what we eat. The strong person who surrenders her food freedom for the sake of a brother's peace and joy has not lost anything that matters; she has demonstrated something that matters supremely: she cares more about his joy in the Holy Spirit than about her right to eat what she pleases.

Verses 13, 15 and 17 carry the section, and the rest of it carries the argument. Verse 14 is the pivot, and it is the boldest sentence in the chapter: I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself, but it is unclean for anyone who thinks it unclean. Both halves are asserted. The thing really is clean, and it really is defiling for the man whose conscience says otherwise — which is why the answer to his scruple is teaching rather than pressure.

Verses 16 and 19–21 then supply the working rules. Do not let the good thing you possess — your liberty — get itself a bad name (v. 16). Pursue what makes for peace and for building up (v. 19). And the counterpart: do not, for the sake of food, demolish the work of God (v. 20). Paul is running a construction metaphor across these verses, and the choice he puts to the strong is whether their freedom is putting walls up or taking them down.

Verse 22 turns to the free man personally: the faith that you have, keep between yourself and God. Not conceal your convictions, but stop parading a liberty — and then a beatitude for the man who can act without a backward glance at himself.

And v. 23 closes the chapter with the sentence that has travelled furthest from it: whatever does not proceed from faith is sin. In context it is about a specific man doing a specific thing while divided in his own mind. It has been made to carry a great deal more than that.
verseByVerse.theology:
Christian Liberty and the Law of Love

Romans 14:13–23 establishes the fundamental principle of Christian ethics in matters of liberty: freedom is real, but love is higher. The freedom the gospel gives is not a license to do everything the law permits without regard to others; it is the freedom to serve. The one who is free in Christ is freed from the bondage of sin and law — freed for the service of God and neighbour. To use freedom as a weapon against a brother's conscience is a misuse of freedom as fundamental as legalism; it is just as self-centred, only differently oriented.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The specific issue of meat offered to idols (closely related to the Romans 14 situation, developed more fully in 1 Corinthians 8–10) was a genuine and daily challenge in the first-century city. Much of the meat available in the marketplace had passed through a pagan temple. The strong knew the idol was nothing; the weak felt defiled. Paul's principle: your knowledge does not give you the right to wound your brother's conscience. Now: The strong Christian in every age is tempted to treat her freedom as a badge of theological maturity to be displayed rather than a gift to be managed with care. The test of genuine maturity is not the willingness to exercise freedom but the willingness to limit it out of love — to choose the brother's conscience over personal preference, his joy over your rights.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore let us not pass judgment on one another any longer, but rather decide never to put a stumbling block or hindrance in the way of a brother. I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself, but it is unclean for anyone who thinks it unclean. — Romans 14:13–14
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stop judging one another, and decide instead never to put a stumbling block in a brother’s way. Paul knows in the Lord Jesus that no food is unclean in itself — but it is unclean for anyone who thinks it unclean. Being right about freedom does not license using it carelessly.

Judge this instead. Paul uses the same verb twice in opposite directions: “let us not pass judgment on one another… but rather decide” — judge this. He does not tell them to stop making judgments. He tells them to make one about themselves: resolve never to put an obstacle in a brother’s path.

Not offence but damage. A stumbling block is what your foot catches on; a “hindrance” was the trigger of a trap. Neither means “giving offence” in the modern sense. The danger is not that the weak brother is annoyed by your steak, but that he eats one against his conscience, because you made it awkward not to, and something in him gives way.

Paul’s own view. “I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus.” Not a preference, but very probably his Master’s ruling: nothing entering a person from outside defiles him — “Thus he declared all foods clean” (Mark 7:19). Paul is not innovating; he is agreeing.

Both halves true. “But it is unclean for anyone who thinks it unclean.” The food is objectively clean, and genuinely defiling for that man. Paul doesn’t say the weak brother is imagining his problem. Conscience does not create reality — believing meat unclean doesn’t make it so. But conscience does create obligation. It is not infallible, and it is binding. A man who acts against it has done wrong even when the act itself was harmless.

The remedy is not pressure. If the problem is that he thinks it unclean, the only real cure is that he comes to think otherwise — by teaching, time, and the example of people he trusts. Getting him to do the thing while he still believes it wrong doesn’t free him. It damages the instrument.

A test. On the matter where you are confident you are right and a fellow believer is wrong: are you trying to change his mind, or his behaviour? The first is what this verse allows. The second is what most of us actually attempt, because it is quicker. Choose the slower way this week — patience, explanation, and your own example.

verseByVerse.quote: For if your brother is grieved by what you eat, you are no longer walking in love. By what you eat, do not destroy the one for whom Christ died.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not destroy the one for whom Christ died — the weight of these words is immense. Christ gave his life for the person whose conscience you are injuring; you are risking their spiritual ruin for the sake of a meal. The measure of cost is staggering: Christ’s life on one side of the scale; your dinner on the other. Love for the brother is not sentiment — it is the refusal to allow the exercise of freedom to undo in practice what the cross accomplished in principle.

The verb is worth naming because Paul reached for the largest one available. Destroy is the word used across the New Testament for ruin and perishing — the opposite of being saved. He could have said upset, or discourage, or set back. He chose the word for wreckage, and he attached it to a plate of food.

What that looks like in practice is less dramatic than the word suggests and more serious than it feels. It is not usually a single catastrophe. It is a man persuaded to act against his conscience once, in company, to avoid looking foolish — and a conscience overridden once is a good deal easier to override the second time. What has been damaged is not his opinion about meat. It is the instrument by which he says no to anything.

Paul is not here teaching that the strong can undo the work of God in one of the elect; the man who wrote that nothing in all creation can separate us from the love of God (8:39) is not contradicting himself over dinner. He is doing what Scripture consistently does with real dangers — naming them at full strength, to people who are in a position to cause them.

And note the phrase that decides the matter: you are no longer walking in love. Not “you have broken a rule”. The strong man in this scene has done nothing forbidden; his theology is correct and his dinner is lawful. He has simply stopped walking in love somewhere between being right and being at the table, and Paul treats that as the thing that has gone wrong.

verseByVerse.quote: So do not let what you regard as good be spoken of as evil. For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not let what you regard as good be spoken of as evil — Christian freedom is real, but it can be exercised in ways that cause it to be maligned. The strong believer who insists on their freedom at the expense of the weak’s conscience has allowed a good thing to become a bad example. The kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking — Paul relativizes the debate by locating what actually matters: righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. These are the marks of the kingdom; food and drink are not.

The good that is in danger of being spoken ill of is the liberty itself. That is the sting of v. 16 and it is easy to miss: Paul is not warning the strong that they will get a bad name. He is warning them that Christian freedom will. A right thing, handled without love, becomes the very thing people point at as evidence that the doctrine produces bad men.

Then the triad, and its three members are not the private inward states we usually take them for. Read them in the argument they sit in. Peace here is peace between the two parties at the table. Joy is the joy of a brother who has not been trampled. Even righteousness is being contrasted with a menu — right standing and right dealing rather than dietary correctness. Paul is describing what a room looks like, not what a soul feels like.

Which is where the verse becomes uncomfortable, because every generation keeps a list of things the kingdom is not made of and every generation’s list is longer than Paul’s. His was food and drink. Ours runs to music, translations, schooling, dress, politics, and the precise vocabulary a person uses about matters on which we already agree.

So the test is external and easy to run. Suppose someone observed your congregation for a month with no access to its statement of faith. What would they conclude the thing was about — from the conversations after the service, from what generates heat, from what people are known for? If the answer is not somewhere near righteousness, peace and joy, the answer is somewhere near food and drink, whatever the modern equivalent has turned out to be.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever thus serves Christ is acceptable to God and approved by men. So then let us pursue what makes for peace and for mutual upbuilding.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one who serves Christ in the kingdom’s real currency — righteousness, peace, joy — earns approval both from God and from people. The pursuit Paul commends is peace and mutual upbuilding (oikodomē — edification, the building up of the community). This is the constructive alternative to judging and despising: actively building each other up. Every choice about the exercise of freedom should be filtered through this question: does this contribute to the peace and upbuilding of the body?

The verb Paul chooses for the pursuing is the chase-word he used twice in back-to-back verses two chapters ago — seeking hospitality, and those who persecute you (12:13–14). Peace is not something you refrain your way into. It is hunted down, which implies it moves.

And upbuilding is a builder’s noun. Paul thinks of a congregation as a site with work going on, where every action either adds a course of bricks or removes one. That is the picture he will complete a verse later with its opposite, when he tells them not to demolish.

Which reframes the question the strong believer is actually asking. The instinctive question about a disputed freedom is “am I allowed?” — and in this chapter the answer is usually yes, which is exactly why the question is useless. Paul substitutes a different one: what will this build? A thing can be entirely permitted and still take a wall down, and the permission is no help at all in that situation.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not, for the sake of food, destroy the work of God. Everything is indeed clean, but it is wrong for anyone to make another stumble by what he eats. It is good not to eat meat or drink wine or do anything that causes your brother to stumble.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not, for the sake of food, destroy the work of God — the stakes are clarified. The work of God being built in a person’s soul through faith is more valuable than any freedom. If my exercise of freedom causes my brother to stumble — to act against his conscience, or to fall away — I have chosen food over a person for whom Christ died. The principle of voluntary limitation for the sake of the weaker brother is not weakness but Christlikeness: the one who was rich became poor for our sake (2 Corinthians 8:9).

The word for destroy here is the builder’s opposite of v. 19 — to pull down what has been put up. Paul has now set the two side by side: build up (v. 19), demolish (v. 20). And what is being demolished is not the weak brother’s opinion or his comfort. It is called the work of God. Someone else has been building in that man, patiently, for years, and the warning is about walking onto that site with a hammer over a question of lunch.

Then v. 21, which needs handling carefully because it has been made to do work Paul did not give it. It is good not to eat meat or drink wine or do anything that causes your brother to stumble. That sentence has been quoted for two centuries as a standing rule about alcohol, and read that way it turns the chapter upside down.

Notice what Paul does not say. He does not say wine is unclean — he has just insisted in v. 20 that everything is indeed clean, and in v. 14 that nothing is unclean in itself. What he says is that abstaining is good where it prevents a brother stumbling. The abstinence is voluntary, situational, and adopted for somebody else’s sake.

Which is precisely why it cannot become a law. The moment the strong man’s self-limitation is turned into a rule binding everyone, it has stopped being an act of love and become the very thing this chapter forbids — a scruple imposed on another man’s conscience. The chapter asks the free to restrain themselves. It never asks them to legislate the restraint.

So the practical form of it is smaller and harder than a policy. It is the decision, made quietly and usually noticed by nobody, that at this table, with this person, on this evening, you will not have the thing you are perfectly entitled to have. And you will not announce that you are not having it, which is the part most of us fail.

verseByVerse.quote: The faith that you have, keep between yourself and God. Blessed is the one who has no reason to pass judgment on himself for what he approves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Keep between yourself and God — freedom that cannot be exercised without wounding another’s conscience is to be kept private, a matter between the believer and God rather than a public assertion. The beatitude that closes the verse is striking: blessed is the person who has no reason for self-condemnation in what they approve. The conscience at peace — not because it is lax, but because it has been calibrated by the gospel and is living in accordance with that calibration — is the mark of mature Christian freedom.

It is worth being clear about what this is not. Paul is not telling the strong to hide their convictions, be evasive, or pretend to scruples they do not have — he has just stated his own position in the plainest terms in v. 14. What he is forbidding is the display. There is a kind of liberty that is not enjoyed so much as exhibited, and needs an audience of the scrupulous to be fully satisfying.

Then the beatitude, and it is one of the most quietly attractive sentences in the letter: blessed is the one who has no reason to pass judgment on himself for what he approves. The happy man is the one who can do the thing and then simply get on with the evening — no small internal argument afterwards, no rehearsing of the justification, no wondering at midnight whether it was all right.

That is a real and underrated mercy, and it is worth naming for the scrupulous reader who has never had it. A great many sincere Christians conduct a running trial of themselves over things God has not forbidden, and the verdict is always appealed. Paul calls the man free of that blessed — which tells you that God regards a settled conscience as a gift and not as laxity.

One guard, though, because the sentence can be misread as “if you feel fine, you are fine.” Paul is speaking of a conscience calibrated by the gospel, not of one that has simply gone quiet — and Scripture knows the other kind, the conscience that stops objecting because it has been ignored for long enough — consciences that are seared (1 Timothy 4:2). The absence of self-accusation is a blessing when it comes from clarity. It is a symptom when it comes from numbness, and the difference is usually visible to everyone except the man himself.

verseByVerse.quote: But whoever has doubts is condemned if he eats, because the eating is not from faith. For whatever does not proceed from faith is sin. — Romans 14:23
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever eats with doubts is condemned, because he is not acting from faith — “for whatever does not proceed from faith is sin.” Do not do the disputed thing while you believe it is wrong; and do not push others to do so before their conscience is persuaded.

A divided man. “Has doubts” means divided — at war with himself. He is eating while half of him objects, and Paul says the verdict on that is in. Not because the food was wrong; Paul has twice said it is not (vv. 14, 20). The condemnation attaches to the division, not the dinner.

A sentence that travelled. “Whatever does not proceed from faith is sin” has done great work in theology. Augustine used it to deny that unbelievers’ virtues please God, and the Reformers used it to show that no act, however decent, pleases God apart from faith (cf. Hebrews 11:6). That is not a distortion; the principle reaches that far.

What it does not mean. Read outside its room, it terrifies people. It does not mean every act not preceded by a conscious act of faith is damnable, or you would sin every time you changed gear. It does not mean you must feel certain before acting; feelings of certainty are not faith and often accompany foolishness. And it does not make being unsure about a hard question sinful; Paul has spent a chapter making room for the unsure.

What it does mean. In context: do not do the disputed thing while you believe it to be wrong. A man eats what he thinks unclean because the company made it awkward not to, and acts on the pressure of the room rather than his conviction before God.

The cure is conviction. Not paralysis. Verse 5 gave the answer: “Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind.” The cure for doubt is not to stop acting but to stop being divided — to find out, be taught, reach a settled position, then act from it. That is more work than either abstaining or complying.

For the strong. Don’t pressure the weak to act before their conscience has been taught. Freedom that bypasses conscience is not liberation but another bondage. Real growth moves the conscience forward through teaching, example and patient community, not through the bulldozer of the confident majority.

A test. Is there something you are doing while part of you believes it is wrong? Either stop, or go to Scripture and wise counsel until you are genuinely persuaded one way or the other — then act in faith. The chapter that began with welcoming a man with a tighter conscience ends by insisting that his conscience must not be violated, not even by a truth. That is what Paul means by strength.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts insert 16:25–27 here, at the end of chapter 14. Others place it after 15:33, and a few omit it. The variation probably shows that the letter circulated in more than one form in the early church; but the doxology is found in almost all manuscripts, and its natural place is at the close of the letter, where the ESV prints it.
